papers.abstract: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.
authors: Xiwei Liu, Yulong Li, Xuhui Li, Xinlin Zhuang, Zhixiang Lu, Haolin Yang, Jianxu Chen, Yifan Lu, Zhiran Zhang, Yutong Xie
bullets: Introduces 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, starting from a single view.
Compares each model’s exploration with same-budget random walks and oracle routes to separate purposeful seeking from spatial reasoning.
Uses 3D-verified questions, masked-evidence abstention tests, and human verification of over 95% of sampled questions.
Across 23 VLMs, the strongest models seek evidence purposefully but lose useful information through limited memory.
Weaker and specialized models perform near random exploration or fail to reason from gathered evidence.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces ActSpace-Bench, a novel benchmark for evaluating active exploration and spatial reasoning capabilities of VLMs in 3D indoor scenes, directly addressing the gap in 'active spatial intelligence' and highlighting memory limitations during exploration.
papers.title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning
papers.tldr: ActSpace-Bench evaluates whether vision-language models can purposefully navigate real indoor spaces to gather evidence for spatial questions, revealing strong evidence-seeking but major memory and reasoning limitations.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation demands reliable execution across interdependent stages, yet standalone World-Action Models (WAMs) suffer from compounding physical errors, while stateless Vision-Language Model (VLM) supervision incurs prohibitive chunkwise latency and lacks 3D spatial persistence. We present EmboEagle, a closed-loop agentic framework that unifies subtask-conditioned WAM control, latent-space adaptive supervision, and memory-guided geometric recovery. First, we adapt sequential WAMs via decoupled two-stage flow matching that preserves cross-stage visual history while calibrating truncated action supervision at subtask boundaries. Second, without an auxiliary vision encoder, we distill teacher intervention decisions into a lightweight routing gate driven solely by the WAM Action Expert's pre- and post-chunk latent transitions and subtask embeddings. Third, upon invocation, the VLM decouples diagnostic status from discrete routing actions and executes parameterized recovery primitives grounded in structured memory (initial references, active grasp bindings, and tool traces), followed by mandatory post-repair verification. Across RMBench and LIBERO-Mem, EmboEagle achieves 91.3\% and 90.6\% average success, surpassing the strongest baselines by 8.0 and 9.8 percentage points, while boosting real-world success over VoLoAgent under identical executor weights. Moreover, adaptive gating cuts VLM calls by 74.2\% versus chunkwise monitoring (91.3\% vs. 93.7\% success).
authors: Fan Xu, Zhongtao Wang, Hao Wu, Yitong Zhu, Wenzhuo Ma, Long Li, Zhuohao Li, Zhisheng Chen, Rui Su, Kun Wang, Xian Wu, Wanli Ouyang

Uses decoupled two-stage flow matching to preserve visual history and calibrate action supervision at subtask boundaries.
Learns a lightweight intervention gate from WAM latent transitions and subtask embeddings, without an auxiliary vision encoder.
Uses structured memory and parameterized recovery primitives, with mandatory post-repair verification.
Achieves 91.3% and 90.6% average success on RMBench and LIBERO-Mem, while reducing VLM calls by 74.2% versus chunkwise monitoring.

papers.abstract: Active 3D reconstruction aims to allocate a sparse view budget to recover complete geometry and high-fidelity renderings. However, existing methods degrade sharply in multi-room homes: myopic next-best-view scoring gives transit no credit for distant rooms and over-polishes irreducible nearby residuals, whereas dense mappers reach far rooms only by streaming thousands of frames. We propose ROAM-GS, a training-free active multi-room reconstruction framework that couples persistent goals with selective views: each decision selects a goal and a variable-horizon prefix toward it, capturing only at its endpoint. A Surface Reconstruction Memory scores poses by projecting post-update defects and viewing directions. Persistent goals credit transit with their remaining value and are released once arrivals stop measurably improving them. Without per-scene tuning, ROAM-GS achieves state-of-the-art multi-room reconstruction while preserving single-room Replica fidelity, raising mean coverage from 74% to 93% on HSSD and from 47% to 96% (+11.7 dB PSNR) on HM3D, and matching 90-minute dense mapping using $173\times$ fewer views.
authors: Jiawei Jiang, Haonan Zhou, Wendi Hu, Jiabei Hu, Yina Xiang, Kaiyue Zhou, Gaoang Wang
bullets: Addresses myopic view selection, which neglects distant rooms and over-focuses on nearby irreducible errors.
Uses a training-free planner that selects a goal and a variable-length transit path, capturing only at the endpoint.
A Surface Reconstruction Memory scores candidate poses using projected post-update defects and viewing directions.
Persistent goals assign value to transit and are released when further arrivals stop improving reconstruction.
Raises coverage from 74% to 93% on HSSD and 47% to 96% on HM3D, while matching dense mapping with 173× fewer views.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ROAM-GS. Persistent goals (top) keep a target region rg through search, travel, and observe until an arrival capture measurably improves it. Selective views (bottom) truncate the path to the goal view at variable horizons: only the prefix endpoint (orange) is captured, while query poses (hollow) are credited from memory. The joint score S = B + V selects the goal and prefix, and the agent captures once at qπ .

papers.abstract: Long-horizon, history-dependent robotic manipulation often requires acting on visual cues that have disappeared, such as an object indicated earlier or a target hidden under a moving cup. The key challenge is to maintain what past evidence means for the next action as the scene changes. We introduce Recurrent Memory Reasoning (RMR), an explicit reasoning step that connects memory to action inside a vision-language-action model (VLA), with no external reasoning model. At each update, the VLA first infers an event from visual evidence, then revises the task state and grounds a subgoal in the current scene to guide action generation. Carrying the state and subgoal across updates lets remembered identities and task progress determine the current target, doubling RoboMME success over an otherwise identical model without recurrence. Joint training lets one VLA both reason and act; because its memory decisions are text tokens with exact likelihoods, GRPO refines them from rollout rewards without making action generation stochastic. Among the compared methods, RMR-VLA achieves the best results on RoboMME (66.46% overall, 79.83% on the Reference category) and LIBERO-Mem (90.08%).
authors: Yiheng Du, Jingqi Tian, Xu Jiang, Jiexuan Zhang, Shuyu Wang, Zecheng Tang, Jian Zhang
bullets: Maintains task state and subgoals across visual updates so remembered object identities and progress guide current actions.
At each update, infers an event, revises the task state, grounds a subgoal in the current scene, and generates an action.
Jointly trains one VLA to reason and act without an external reasoning model.
Uses exact likelihoods of memory text tokens for GRPO refinement from rollout rewards while keeping action generation deterministic.
Reports 66.46% on RoboMME, 79.83% on its Reference category, and 90.08% on LIBERO-Mem; it doubles RoboMME success versus an otherwise identical non-recurrent model.

papers.abstract: Robot agents built on frontier vision-language models now solve most robot memory benchmarks. Does this mean they can remember what they need in a home, where people and machines keep moving things? Existing memory benchmarks cannot answer this question, because they pause the simulator while the model thinks: nothing can change during a decision, so whatever the robot remembers is still true when it acts. We introduce RoboLiveMem, a benchmark that runs the same memory tasks twice, once with the world paused while the model thinks and once with the world running. It contains 29 task families in three tiers, from 16 realistic BEHAVIOR-1K scenes of homes, workshops and a restaurant to controlled ManiSkill tasks. Every task mixes real changes with harmless look-alikes and runs without any change, so that no fixed strategy succeeds, and most tasks have a twin that keeps the change in view, which separates forgetting from acting too late. Testing 16 models on 34,176 episodes, we find three surprises. (1) Paused results hide the problem: when a remembered object changes in a realistic scene, the 8 Claude and GPT models succeed in 97% of episodes on average with the world paused, but in only 50% with the world running, and their ranking changes: Claude Opus 5.5, which never fails when paused, succeeds in 44%. (2) Speed is not the fix: slower models do no worse, and models given only 2 s per decision still fall at least 36 points below their paused success. (3) Models see the change but act on camera frames from before it ended. Looking again just before acting closes most of the realistic gap, yet when identical objects are swapped several times, all nine models we test still lose points to memory.
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Yuyou Zhang, Janet Wang, Ming Liu, Yijiang Li, Yikai Wang, Weirui Ye, Ding Zhao, Jihun Hamm
bullets: Introduces a benchmark that compares robot memory with the environment paused versus continuously changing.
Covers 29 task families across realistic BEHAVIOR-1K scenes and controlled ManiSkill tasks, including distractor changes and no-change cases.
Across 34,176 episodes and 16 models, realistic changed-object success drops from 97% when paused to 50% when the world runs.
Slower reasoning does not solve the problem; models often perceive changes but act using stale pre-change camera frames.
Looking again before acting largely closes the realistic gap, but repeated swaps of identical objects still expose memory failures.

papers.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of scene-level memory design for efficient navigation across sessions and successive object goals. Recent methods commonly represent a scene using scene graphs or image--text records. However, dense scene-graph representations impose substantial reasoning and context overhead on multimodal large language models, while image--text records cannot be directly converted into executable geometric routes. To address these limitations, we propose SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system equipped with a structured spatial memory constructed by the agent. The memory consists of an area-segmented occupancy map annotated with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes. This map guides the agent toward unvisited areas and provides executable routes to known locations. For multi-session navigation, we introduce agent-guided relocalization, whereby the agent infers an area prior from current observations and stored memory records to constrain geometric matching and localize the robot within the stored map. Together, these designs enable efficient navigation across session and successive object goals. Experiments show that our method outperforms baselines on single-object, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in path efficiency. Multi-session evaluation demonstrates that the constructed memory can be reused, while deployment on a real quadruped robot further shows the system's applicability.
authors: Jiarui Guo, Jinkai Zhang, Yuanhong Yu, Yongchen Zai, Futang Zhu, Ruizhen Hu, Sida Peng, Xiaowei Zhou
bullets: Addresses the overhead of dense scene graphs and the non-executable nature of image–text scene records.

Introduces agent-guided relocalization to match current observations against stored memory and localize within prior maps.
Outperforms baselines across several navigation settings, with especially strong path-efficiency gains, and transfers to a real quadruped robot.

papers.abstract: A home robot that helps with chores needs to know where objects are, but people move objects according to routines that change and later change back. The robot's memory must adapt to the new routine without erasing experience that may become useful again. One approach is to have a language model maintain written summaries of the home from the robot's own observations, but existing evaluations of such memories use static worlds. We explore simulated households where a resident gets sick, recovers, and later gets sick again. We compare a rule that keeps every room an object has been seen in, language-model memories that store only written summaries, and language-model memories that can also read the raw history of sightings. The rule outperforms every summary-only memory, and giving language models the sighting history closes the gap. Surprisingly, writing summaries on top of the history adds nothing we can measure. When the illness returns, methods that keep the history search better than they did the first time, while summary-only methods show no consistent improvement. Deleting the first illness from memory removes all of the rule's gain and part of theirs. The summaries recorded where objects went during the illness but rarely distinguished sick-day patterns from normal routines. Our findings suggest that common approaches to summarizing robot memories struggle to remember facts about a routine that might return, highlighting the need for future benchmarks to evaluate this aspect of long-term robot deployment.
bullets: The study examines simulated homes where a resident becomes sick, recovers, and later becomes sick again.
It compares a room-history rule, language-model summaries, and language models with access to raw sighting histories.
The room-history rule outperforms summary-only memories; adding sighting history closes the gap.
Summarizing on top of the history provides no measurable benefit, while history-based methods improve when illness recurs.
Deleting the first illness removes the rule’s advantage and part of the history-based methods’ gains.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving systems must not only interpret the current scene but also anticipate perceptual challenges such as occlusions, sparse observations, and recurring failure patterns. However, most existing LiDAR semantic segmentation methods operate in a frame-centric manner, processing each scan independently and discarding past contextual experience, which limits robustness under dynamic scene changes. We propose DREAM, a Dual-memory REAsoning framework for continual LiDAR seMantic segmentation that reframes perception as an experience-driven and anticipatory process. DREAM maintains two complementary memory banks in a strictly online setting: a latent memory that stores compact semantic abstractions of previously observed scenes, and an error memory that records representations associated with uncertain predictions. At each timestep, relevant memory entries are retrieved via cosine similarity and integrated into the feature space through a lightweight modulation mechanism, enabling the model to reinforce consistent semantic patterns while suppressing recurring failure modes. The backbone remains frozen and no past scans are replayed, ensuring computational efficiency and bounded memory growth. Extensive experiments on multiple large-scale LiDAR benchmarks demonstrate that DREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance, with consistent improvements on dynamic and small-scale objects, highlighting the effectiveness of persistent and error-aware memory for robust long-horizon perception.
bullets: Targets frame-by-frame LiDAR segmentation methods that discard contextual experience and struggle with dynamic changes, occlusions, and sparse observations.
Maintains a latent memory of compact semantic scene abstractions and an error memory of uncertain-prediction representations.
Retrieves relevant memories via cosine similarity and applies lightweight feature modulation to reinforce consistent patterns and reduce recurring failures.
Operates online with a frozen backbone, no past-scan replay, and bounded memory growth.
Experiments on multiple large-scale LiDAR benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance, especially for dynamic and small-scale objects.

papers.abstract: Video world models generate plausible novel views but often lack persistent memory, failing to preserve a place's geometry and appearance when an agent revisits a scene. A central challenge is how previous views should be effectively used for creating memory. Reconstructing them independently underutilizes geometric constraints between nearby views, while repeatedly reconstructing a growing history can propagate later prediction errors into earlier geometry. We introduce RecallWorld, a persistent embodied video world model that jointly reconstructs short multi-view episodes into Scenelets while keeping geometry independent across episodes. Starting from a single source image, camera-aware ray lifting places perspective and native fisheye images in a common world frame, retaining wide-field content for perspective generation. Each generated segment extends the Scenelet memory and conditions subsequent generation. Coverage-based retrieval selects complementary Scenelets from the full history, while target-view visibility is resolved geometrically before appearance fusion, providing consistent memory conditioning for guiding subsequent generation. Across four datasets, RecallWorld improves revisit PSNR over the strongest evaluated baseline by 2.6 dB on partial revisits and 3.9 dB on full cycles, demonstrating substantially stronger preservation of scene identity across exploration and return.
authors: Sarosij Bose, Gitika Karumuri, Chenqi Li, Allen Tu, Srikumar Sastry, Mellon Zhang, Avinash Ravichandran, Alexander Schwing, Konstantinos Karydis, Amit K. Roy Chowdhury
bullets: Addresses the problem of world models forgetting scene geometry and appearance across revisits.

Retrieves complementary Scenelets by coverage and resolves target-view visibility geometrically before fusing appearance.
Improves revisit PSNR by 2.6 dB on partial revisits and 3.9 dB on full cycles across four datasets.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.
authors: Xinyu Cao, Tianjie Ju, Zhuosheng Zhang
bullets: Targets tasks where agents must preserve visual evidence before knowing which details will later be queried.

Improves average held-out performance over AutoMem by 31.3–47.6 points; programs written only from initial instructions perform substantially worse.

papers.abstract: Dynamic and continuously evolving environments present significant challenges for robotic mapping and scene understanding, particularly on construction sites where moving agents, temporary obstacles, and persistent structural changes coexist. While dynamic and long-term SLAM methods can detect motion and environmental changes, their outputs are predominantly metric representations that provide limited structure for higher-level spatial and temporal reasoning. This paper presents a LiDAR-based real-time temporal construction scene graph (T-ConSG) that jointly represents free-space regions, static objects, dynamic objects, and environmental events with spatial-relational and event-participation edges. The proposed framework incrementally constructs the graph from LiDAR-derived geometric evidence, maintaining persistent free-space and static-object information while tracking dynamic objects. Changes in accumulated spatial evidence are further represented as explicit installation and removal events, allowing the graph to capture both transient dynamics and persistent environmental evolution. We demonstrate the proposed representation through three complementary application studies: dynamics-aware navigation in a bricklaying testbed, construction progress monitoring on the ConSLAM dataset, and online change detection in a simulated construction environment. The results demonstrate that the proposed T-ConSG provides a unified representation for organizing spatial and temporal information and supports robotic reasoning across environments containing both short-term dynamics and persistent changes.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of metric-only mapping for reasoning about dynamic agents, temporary obstacles, and evolving structures.
Incrementally represents free-space regions, static and dynamic objects, spatial relations, and event participation.
Tracks dynamic objects while preserving persistent spatial information from static objects and free space.
Models environmental changes explicitly as installation and removal events.
Demonstrated for dynamics-aware navigation, construction progress monitoring, and online change detection.

papers.abstract: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.
authors: Zhenxuan Fan, Zhuoya Wang, Yuqian Yuan, Wenqiao Zhang, Juncheng Li, Jun Xiao, Siliang Tang, Yueting Zhuang
bullets: Addresses weak memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience in VLM-based manipulation agents.
Uses an Actor–Reflector framework: the Actor executes tasks, while the Reflector turns interaction evidence into reusable operational guidance.
Combines hierarchical short- and long-term memory with evidence-based failure reflection and recursive harness self-improvement.
Achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench, plus 96.7% average success across three real-world tasks.
Evaluates generalization, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation under environmental variation.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables embodied agents to reuse past observations across tasks. However, existing cross-episode vision-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks often leave it unclear whether successful navigation relies on historical memory or current exploration. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark designed to evaluate memory-dependent cross-episode VLN. Mem-X organizes episodes into sessions in which subsequent instructions refer to objects or routes encountered in earlier episodes. Its three levels evaluate historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization and historical-route reproduction. For the latter two levels, agents receive episode-local poses but no transformations between episode frames, requiring them to establish spatial correspondence with historical memory. Mem-X comprises 2,071 episodes across 710 sessions in 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We also provide MemBridge, a modular baseline that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval to support existing VLN agents. Experiments with state-of-the-art VLN methods demonstrate the benefits of MemBridge while revealing substantial room for improvement on memory-dependent navigation. The benchmark and baseline code are available at https://github.com/NJU-R-L-Group-Embodied-Lab/Mem-X.
authors: Zhikang Shi, Yuk Tung Samuel Fang, Hongyu Ding, Zixuan Chen, Yujin Wang, Junhui Guo, You Wu, Jieqi Shi, Jing Huo, Yang Gao
bullets: Organizes 2,071 episodes into 710 sessions across 34 scenes, with later instructions referring to earlier objects or routes.

The latter two levels require agents to align historical memory with current episode frames without cross-episode frame transformations.
Introduces MemBridge, combining semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval.
Experiments show MemBridge benefits existing VLN agents, while memory-dependent navigation remains challenging.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement through three views on the same run: what it knows, whether its own evidence supports that knowledge, and how far it gets in the world. It is built on the game Outer Wilds, where each episode is a 22-minute loop after which the world resets, only the agent's knowledge carries over, and progress is gated by knowledge. After every episode, we measure the places reached and ship-log rumor facts revealed, the correctness of answers to 164 questions about the world, and whether each answer is supported by the frames and position the agent cites from its own recorded play. Two LLM judges from different model families check every answer. In eight-episode baselines with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners, which act through a learned controller or their own gamepad inputs, the three views do not move together, so any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture of whether the agent is improving. The GPT-6.1 Sol agent's correct answers grow from 14.6% to 26.8% of all questions, but at episode 8 only 59 to 68% of them are supported by its cited evidence. It reveals no new rumor facts after episode 3, while the places it reaches and its memory keep growing. More than half of the answers that become correct after episode 3 cite only evidence from earlier episodes.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of judging self-improvement using only task progress, QA accuracy, or episodic memory.
Evaluates agents in Outer Wilds, where each 22-minute episode resets the world but preserves the agent’s knowledge.
Measures reached locations, revealed rumor facts, correctness on 164 world-knowledge questions, and whether answers are supported by cited frames and positions.
In eight-episode baselines, the three measures did not consistently improve together; GPT-6.1 Sol’s correct answers rose from 14.6% to 26.8%, but only 59–68% were evidence-supported by episode 8.
After episode 3, GPT-6.1 Sol revealed no new rumor facts while exploration and memory continued growing; over half of later newly correct answers cited earlier-episode evidence.

papers.abstract: An embodied agent cannot afford a large vision-language model (VLM) at every step of a long video, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only uncertain decisions to a large one. Each escalation, however, forces the large model to re-encode a history the small model has already perceived, and this dominates its cost. We present Baton, which hands the large model the small model's visual memory, its key-value (KV) cache over the history. Baton rests on one finding: the large model needs a usable memory, not a faithful copy of its own. A map trained to reproduce the large model's cache matches it most closely, yet brings no gain over the small model alone. Baton instead distills a per-layer linear map, without labels, from the large model's own answers, with the large model encoding only the current frame. Interventions on the map trace the gain to one direction, carried by the middle third of the large model's layers. On RoboMME, Baton beats the small model alone, a pruned or shortened re-watch, and a text memory; as the escalation channel of a cascade it matches re-watching to within about one point at 28-47% less compute, and 8x less per escalation at 64 frames. Its gain grows with the large model, from 8B to 32B, tracks the large model's headroom across eight model pairs from four families, and transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA.
authors: Qiang Zhou, Jianing Deng, Siyan Dong, Jingxian Chen, Han-Yi Lin, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Targets the high cost of re-encoding long video histories when escalating from a continuously running small VLM to a large VLM.
Distills a label-free, per-layer linear map from the large model’s answers, using only the current frame to transform the small model’s KV cache.
The useful transfer is concentrated in one direction across the middle third of the large model’s layers; faithfully reproducing the large model’s cache does not improve performance.
On RoboMME, Baton outperforms the small model alone, pruned or shortened re-watching, and text memory, while matching re-watching with 28–47% less compute.
The approach transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA and scales with the large model’s capability across eight model pairs from four families.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object. Existing approaches typically rely on full observation histories, which become redundant over long horizons, or text summaries, which may omit precise visual details. We study visual moment memory, the ability to retain such details from key moments for subsequent manipulation. To support this study, we introduce VMBench, a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring memory of spatial locations, visual appearances, and their associations. We further propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture in which a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on the selected memories. This separation enables us to evaluate memory selection alongside closed-loop task success and to study memorizer generalization independently of the executor. On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. Moreover, we find that the memorizer transfers well to unseen appearances zero-shot. It can also adapt to an unseen task with only a few memory annotations, reaching 43.7% success, close to the 44.3% obtained with full memory supervision. Further experiments show competitive performance on RMBench and improvements in real-robot manipulation. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory-dependent manipulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem.
authors: Guangyu Zhao, Yongchang Zhang, Ruizhang Jiang, Zhihong Yu, Yuhao Zhang, Tao Wu, Qimin Zhou, Kunsong Shi, Haoran Wen, Zeyu Zhang, Yin Li, Kun Zhan, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: Introduces VMBench, a benchmark for manipulation tasks requiring memory of locations, appearances, and their associations.
Uses a hierarchical design: a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes, while an executor predicts actions from selected memories.
Achieves 49.9% average success on VMBench, 31.7 percentage points above the strongest evaluated baseline.
Transfers zero-shot to unseen appearances and reaches 43.7% success on an unseen task with a few memory annotations, near 44.3% with full supervision.
Also reports competitive RMBench results and improvements in real-robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Large multimodal models can support long-horizon robot manipulation, but frequent model calls incur substantial latency and token costs. The central challenge is determining when agent assistance or intervention is needed and whether errors require correcting robot execution, subtask planning, or both. To address this problem, we propose RoC (Reasoning on Call), an efficient framework that coordinates a low-level policy and a high-level reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor combines temporal visual observations with ordered interaction memory to jointly estimate progress within the active subtask and predict its successor. These predictions guide event-triggered agent review for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. Verified outcomes govern memory updates and subtask transitions, allowing routine execution to remain with the policy while reasoning focuses on decisions requiring additional assessment. On RMBench, RoC improves task success rate by 24.0 percentage points and reduces token consumption by 65.3% compared with the strongest agent-based baseline. It also outperforms the strongest policy-based baseline by 15.1 percentage points in task success rate. Real-world experiments further validate its effectiveness across three long-horizon manipulation tasks. Overall, RoC supports efficient agent intervention and coordinated recovery across execution and planning for long-horizon robot manipulation.
authors: Zilang Cen, Chao Tang, Fangcheng Liu, Weishi Mi, Wei Hao, JiaYu Xu, Dehao Huang, Yehui Tang, Xiaohui Cui, Tingguang Li, Xiaoyuan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the latency and token costs of frequent multimodal-model calls during long-horizon manipulation.
Coordinates a low-level policy with a high-level reasoning agent using an online monitor of visual progress and interaction history.
Triggers agent review to repair execution, revise subtasks, or coordinate both, while verified outcomes update memory and transitions.
On RMBench, improves task success by 24.0 percentage points over the strongest agent-based baseline while reducing token use by 65.3%.
Improves task success by 15.1 percentage points over the strongest policy-based baseline and is validated on three real-world tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Qualitative comparison on RMBench without eventtriggered agent intervention (top) and with the full RoC framework (bottom).

papers.selection_reason: Proposes RoC, a framework for efficient long-horizon robot manipulation that coordinates a low-level policy with a high-level reasoning agent using a task-state monitor and interaction memory to trigger intervention only when necessary, significantly reducing token costs while improving task success rates.

papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in qualitative spatial reasoning, but remain limited in quantitative spatial reasoning. Current work leverages the VLM agent to invoke external vision tools to perform computation. However, these methods usually bind each functional requirement to a single predefined vision specialist, implicitly resulting in fixed and rigid tool pipelines. In practice, addressing diverse spatial scenarios and tasks demands a broader diversity in pipeline orchestration and vision specialist selection to achieve robust spatial reasoning. However, such diversity leads to a combinatorial execution space, making it challenging for the agent to orchestrate the optimal pipelines and specialists for different scenarios. In this work, we propose SpatialMem, a memory framework that enables a VLM agent to accumulate tool-use experience and leverage that memory to orchestrate vision specialists to solve the spatial reasoning problem. SpatialMem builds a two-level memory structure, with task memory capturing tool orchestration and scene memory capturing tool selection. It further introduces a dual-state trajectory optimization process to preserve successful tool experiences and refine suboptimal ones. Moreover, existing spatial reasoning benchmarks suffer from quality issues and limited coverage of scene types and tasks. To address these gap, we propose MetricBench, a benchmark covering both indoor and outdoor scenes and three quantitative spatial reasoning tasks. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on MetricBench, Q-Spatial, and SpatilRGPT-Bench, outperforming best VLM baselines by 32% on MetricBench. Additionally, the memory design yields a 9.1% absolute gain over a memory-free agent on MetricBench.
authors: Zinan Zheng, Nuo Chen, Jia Li
bullets: Targets VLMs’ limitations in quantitative, rather than qualitative, spatial reasoning.
Uses task memory for tool orchestration and scene memory for selecting vision specialists.
Applies dual-state trajectory optimization to retain successful tool-use experiences and refine weaker ones.
Introduces MetricBench, covering indoor and outdoor scenes across three quantitative spatial reasoning tasks.
Reports state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks, with a 32% improvement over the best VLM baseline on MetricBench and a 9.1-point gain over a memory-free agent.

papers.abstract: Recalling where and when an object was last seen and who saw it requires recognizing it across days and people. Existing long-video benchmarks focus on events, object categories, or relative locations, leaving instance-level spatial memory largely untested in multimodal models. To address this gap, we present EgoWitness, a benchmark for instance-level spatial memory and reasoning in egocentric video. Its 8,453 human-verified questions span approximately 324 hours of week-long and short-horizon recordings and test seven abilities, from recognizing an object or room to recalling who saw it and reasoning about room visits. Over one million reviewed masks of 34 registered landmarks and 21 movable-object labels are linked through room timelines. Among twelve direct vision-language models (VLMs), open-weight models reach at most 46.97% accuracy, and none exceeds 35% on identifying who saw an object last. We therefore propose EgoClue, a spatial-memory agent that retrieves candidate intervals, verifies instance identity, and computes spatial and temporal relations with five tools. Two-stage training with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises its 4B controller from 23.64% to 72.65% accuracy on 1,320 held-out questions. Evidence-trace synthesis matches the best direct VLM at 74.85% on week-long questions and achieves 80.56% in environments excluded from training.
authors: Zhengru Fang, Zehao Liu, Mingyu Tsoi, Yaoyu Zhu, Junlong Li, Fengmao Lv, Sijie Cheng, Yuanliang Sun, Fang Yang, Jun Zhang
bullets: Benchmarks recalling where and when specific objects were last seen, who saw them, and room-visit relationships.
Includes 8,453 human-verified questions across about 324 hours of recordings, with linked masks for landmarks and movable objects.
Direct VLMs achieve limited performance, with none exceeding 35% on identifying who last saw an object.
EgoClue retrieves candidate intervals, verifies instance identity, and computes spatial-temporal relations using five tools.
Two-stage SFT and GRPO training raises a 4B controller from 23.64% to 72.65%; evidence traces reach 80.56% in unseen environments.

papers.abstract: A collision-free detour can still bring a legged robot to the next stair or ledge a few centimetres or degrees off, and a fixed locomotion skill, factory or learned, can stall or fall. Existing methods prevent this with a robot model or extensive trial and error, but on a new site with unknown skills neither is available, so they cannot be used. We find that a single 27-minute teaching session already supplies what these methods have to derive or learn: for every stair and ledge, one crossing the skill has completed. Our method, passage-conditioned navigation, makes the route remember how each transition was entered, not only where the path went. It stores each taught crossing as an event and, without training or a robot model, enforces it after every local replan: before each ledge, an entry gate makes the robot turn or back up and retry if it is more than 10 cm or 10{\deg} off the taught crossing. Under localization noise, with path, gait schedule, and sensing unchanged, this raises the share of disturbed ledge crossings that stay within these limits from 24.1% to 88.6%. In contact simulation with our learned policies, a robot pushed off course before stairs never falls in 180 climbs, against 9 falls when the stored direction is ignored; pushed 1.2 m away, it rejoins the route, ending on average 0.14 m from it (1.10 m without rejoining), and finishes as often as an undisturbed robot. This suits any robot with fixed skills that repeats a route over terrain transitions, as in inspection and patrol, where one wrong entry can end the task. We deployed it in competition on a real wheeled-legged robot: over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain spanning 7.0 m of elevation, it completed all six runs, won third place at the 2026 Global Open-source AI Challenge, which drew 2,999 submissions, and was the only finalist in its task to finish fully autonomously.
authors: Wai Ka Sun, Waiyiu Pong, Bowen Wang
bullets: A collision-free route can still fail when the robot approaches a stair or ledge with the wrong position or heading.
A 27-minute teaching session records one successful crossing for each terrain transition as reusable route events.
Before each transition, an entry gate triggers turning or backing up when the robot is more than 10 cm or 10° from the taught approach.
Under localization noise, compliant crossings increased from 24.1% to 88.6%; simulation and real-robot tests also showed improved recovery and reliable completion.
The method was demonstrated over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain, with six autonomous successful runs in competition.

papers.selection_reason: Passage-conditioned navigation with taught crossing memory for wheeled-legged robots; fits embodied robot navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: Collision-Free Is Not Enough: Passage-Conditioned Navigation for Wheeled-Legged Robots
papers.tldr: Passage-conditioned navigation helps wheeled-legged robots reliably enter stairs and ledges by remembering and enforcing successful crossing directions, without a robot model or additional training.

papers.abstract: Revising every answer from a long-term memory can consume substantial inference budget and damage facts that were already correct. We introduce MemMend, a modular selective revision framework that routes potentially incomplete answers to an editor, represents corrections as bounded exact-text replacements, and accepts only edits with resolvable source coordinates and valid edit operations. The editor preserves the current answer when no legal repair is proposed; accepted edits require no additional semantic-verification call. On 1,986 LoCoMo development questions, MemMend achieves 67.17 conversation-macro F1 and 88.35 mean Judge score, improving over a verified revision chain by 0.82 and 1.24 points while using 62.37% fewer revision calls. Routing uses 54.15% fewer revision calls than ungated local review, with similar F1 but a 0.67-point lower Judge score. Applied directly to native PropMem, Mem0, and SimpleMem answers, the editing interface raises F1 by 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 points. It outperforms same-gate rewriting and saves 49.85-83.72% of editing calls relative to ungated editing, which retains higher F1 in this adaptation. A source-by-editing factorial supports local editing for F1 but leaves an independent quality benefit from source obligations unresolved. Transfer to 451 LongMemEval-V2 Small questions also favors revision efficiency, while an external PerLTQA dialogue subset reveals a completeness gap. These results support selective editing as a reusable quality-cost operating point.
bullets: Targets the cost and risk of revising every answer, which can damage already-correct facts.
Routes uncertain answers to an editor that performs bounded exact-text replacements with valid source coordinates and legal edit operations.
On 1,986 LoCoMo development questions, it improves over a verified revision chain by 0.82 F1 and 1.24 Judge points while using 62.37% fewer revision calls.
Direct editing improves native PropMem, Mem0, and SimpleMem answers, with gains of 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 F1 points, respectively.
Results support selective editing as an efficient quality–cost tradeoff, but show a completeness gap on an external PerLTQA subset and unresolved source-obligation effects.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces MemMend, a selective revision framework for memory QA that reduces inference cost by only revising potentially incomplete answers.
papers.title: MemMend: A Selective Revision Framework for Memory Question Answering
papers.tldr: MemMend selectively revises only potentially incomplete memory-based answers, improving quality while substantially reducing editing calls.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) offer a foundation for predictive decision-making by modeling the consequences of actions in representation space. Yet evaluating local reachability in latent space does not by itself provide a task-level execution interface: intermediate targets must be generated, local inference has finite budgets, and execution requires spatial feedback and persistent interaction state. We introduce LeCompass, a state-indexed execution framework built around a frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM). A proposer supplies intermediate latent targets, while CompassFlow searches the source space of a learned trajectory prior to obtain effective action candidates under limited predictive-evaluation budgets. Patch-token readouts provide spatial feedback, while observation-based memory supports phase transitions and bounded recovery. State-indexed targets support cross-episode context-goal composition. On 1,000 official TEST full-episode Cube trials, the complete LeCompass execution system achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach. Separate matched analyses show that predictive ranking raises success from 4.7% to 44.9% on TEST PushT and from 33.8% to 77.7% on TEST TwoRoom. These results demonstrate task-level execution with task-dependent roles for latent target proposal, predictive search, and observation-grounded control.
authors: Kai Shi, Shiqi Zhao, Zimo Li, Hairong Qu, Hongyu Ma, Yongsong Yang, Jiahao Ai, Ziran Yin, Peng Yin
bullets: Addresses the gap between local latent reachability and persistent, task-level execution.
Uses a frozen LeWorldModel with a proposer for intermediate targets and CompassFlow to search trajectory-prior actions under limited evaluation budgets.
Adds patch-token spatial feedback and observation-based memory for phase transitions and bounded recovery.
State-indexed targets enable cross-episode context-goal composition.
Achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach on 1,000 TEST Cube trials; predictive ranking improves matched PushT success from 4.7% to 44.9% and TwoRoom from 33.8% to 77.7%.

papers.tldr: LeCompass turns latent-space predictions into task-level execution by combining state-indexed targets, predictive action search, spatial feedback, and memory.

papers.abstract: As language-model agents are applied to increasingly extended tasks, their working context continuously accumulates interaction history, tool observations, intermediate decisions, and task progress. Context compaction offers a practical way to reduce this growing history while allowing execution to continue, yet the compaction ability of modern LLMs remains insufficiently understood. We introduce CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction through its downstream effect on agent task completion. Starting from successful agent trajectories, we insert compaction boundaries at different stages of execution, compress the preceding working context with the model under evaluation, and let the same executor continue the original task. To enable fair comparison across compactors, we evaluate them under controlled retention ratios using a lightweight iterative ratio-adjustment procedure. CompAct-Bench covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks through BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and an internal CompanyBench evaluation. Our experiments show that working-context compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models: Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, yet substantial degradation in downstream task accuracy persists under aggressive compaction. Further analysis reveals that failures are often caused not only by omitted information, but also by distorted task state, such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions or forgetting previously established results, which can lead to incorrect decisions or redundant execution. These findings highlight working-context compaction as a distinct and still challenging ability for LLMs operating in extended agent tasks.
authors: Jiayi Chen, Lizhe Chen, Yujia Chen, Shihan Dou, Ming Zhang, Chendi Ge, Shiguang Ni, Tao Gui, Qi Zhang, Xuanjing Huang, Maxm Pan
bullets: Measures compaction by inserting compression points into successful agent trajectories and evaluating continued task completion.
Uses controlled retention ratios with an iterative adjustment procedure for fair comparison across compactors.
Covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks.
Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, but aggressive compaction still causes substantial accuracy degradation.
Failures stem from both omitted information and distorted task state, including false conclusions and forgotten results.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction in long-horizon agent tasks, a form of memory management at inference time.
papers.title: CompAct-Bench: A Benchmark for Working-Context Compaction in Long-Horizon Agent Tasks
papers.tldr: CompAct-Bench evaluates how well LLM agents compress working context without harming completion of long-horizon tasks, finding that compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon world modeling in partially observable environments requires compact memories that preserve spatial structure despite accumulated localization drift. Inspired by hippocampal episodic and spatial memory and the multi-periodic coding of entorhinal grid cells, we propose HiSTFormer, a hierarchical spatiotemporal world model, which adopts a layer-wise organization of local temporal RoPE and multi-periodic spatial RoPE, together with content-conditioned address offsets, to capture recent temporal context and long-range spatial structure. A fixed-capacity memory keeps KV storage and per-step attention cost bounded as the sequence grows. On MemoryMaze and HM3D, HiSTFormer outperforms strong world-model baselines within the training sequence length and generalizes substantially better to prediction horizons far beyond those seen during training, while using a compact model. The hierarchical spatiotemporal design remains effective across deeper Transformer stacks, with consistent gains as depth increases. These results show that hierarchical spatiotemporal organization and content-adaptive spatial addressing provide effective inductive biases for efficient long-horizon world modeling.
authors: Tiantian Li, Junfeng Lu, Yifei Wang, Zhaoyang Zhang, Lei Wang, Tianyi Qian
bullets: Targets spatial-structure loss caused by localization drift in partially observable, long-horizon environments.
Combines layer-wise local temporal RoPE, multi-periodic spatial RoPE, and content-conditioned address offsets.
Maintains fixed-capacity KV memory, keeping storage and per-step attention cost bounded as sequences grow.
Outperforms strong baselines on MemoryMaze and HM3D, with stronger generalization to horizons beyond training.
The approach remains effective across deeper Transformer stacks, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of HiSTFormer. Observation frames are encoded into compact visual representations, while the motion encoder and coordinate transformation update a path-integrated grid-like spatial state. The temporal Transformer first extracts local context using temporal RoPE. Contentconditioned per-head offsets then adjust the grid-like spatial addresses used by the spatial Transformer to retrieve historical experience. The resulting latent representations are decoded autoregressively into future frames.

Figure 3: Analysis of hierarchical temporal–spatial encoding. A: Comparison of positional encodings in two-layer models. B: Temporal–spatial layer arrangements at depths of 2, 4, and 6 layers. C: Effects of exchanging the default cache organizations of temporal and spatial layers. D: Combined comparison of positional encoding, hierarchy, and cache-organization variants. E: Zero-shot generalization of different spatial encodings from the 9 × 9 training environment to larger environments under the 256→64 and 500→500 protocols.

Figure 4: Analysis of content-conditioned learnable address offsets. A: LPIPS of the full HiSTFormer, a model trained without address offsets, and three test-time interventions applied after normal training: replacing the learned offsets with their mean, shuffling them, or setting them to zero. B: Distance from the base and offset-adjusted spatial addresses to the wall intersected by the current viewing direction. C: A qualitative example showing the ground-truth target, high-attention memories retrieved by spatial heads H0 and H2, the full prediction, and predictions obtained after shuffling the retrieval results of either head.

Figure 2: Analysis of long-horizon visual prediction in Memory Maze. A: Qualitative predictions at selected rollout horizons under the 256→64 protocol. B: Per-step LPIPS over the 64-frame prediction horizon. C: LPIPS for the next 64 predicted frames as the available context length increases. D: MSE and LPIPS on spatially novel and revisited prediction frames.

Blue and orange lines indicate the observed 500-frame trajectories and the subsequent 500-frame ground-truth trajectories, respectively. Green circles, black diamonds, and red crosses mark the start, observation endpoint, and prediction endpoint. Each panel reports the position and pose matching rates against observed history, using thresholds of 0.5 m and 30◦.

The 32- and 64-frame predictions extend beyond the 16-frame training horizon; frozen-VAE reconstructions are shown as a reference for representation quality.

Position is decoded from the largest-period component of the grid-like representation and compared with the ground-truth position over the first 500 observed frames. The larger error on our collected trajectories indicates more severe localization drift and a more challenging setting for long-horizon visual prediction.

On HM3D, predicted frames are grouped by the number of historical pose-matching visits: 0, 1, 2–3, and 4 or more visits, using thresholds of 0.5 m in position and 30◦ in heading. (A–B) LPIPS and MSE under the 256→ 64 protocol; (C–D) the corresponding metrics under 500→ 500. Both models are evaluated using the same training seed (Seed 42). Metrics are first averaged within each revisit group per test window, then averaged equally across windows containing that group. Prediction errors generally decrease with increasing revisit frequency for both models.

Under the 256-to-64 protocol, the horizontal axis shows the spatial distance from each predicted position to the last observed position. The vertical axis reports the error difference (Singleperiod minus HiSTFormer) in (A) MSE and (B) LPIPS. papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models are advancing embodied navigation, but frequent inference incurs substantial computational cost. We present Cognitive-Horizon Action Chunking (CHAC), a training-free framework for memory-guided adaptive reasoning with a frozen navigation policy. Retained visual context, completion cues, and controller feedback determine the cognitive horizon, or how many cached waypoints the robot executes before refreshing its prediction. At the policy's stop request, local visitation history guides a bounded correction with at most one extra movement and no additional model calls. CHAC reduces vision-language model calls by 33.4% on HM3D-OVON and 64.7% on R2R-CE, with success-rate decreases of 0.63 and 10.82 percentage points, respectively. Success rate and success weighted by path length improve per model call on both benchmarks. Across four physical navigation tasks with 40 runs per method, CHAC achieves 18 successes versus 14 for native execution, reducing model calls by 54.9% and GPU inference time by 49.7%.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for complex robotic tasks, leveraging Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) to generate actions through Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based iterative denoising. However, existing models often struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. We observe that retrieving successful experiences and using them to warm-start denoising enables agents to better adapt to unfamiliar situations while reducing computational overhead. This creates a new opportunity to improve task accuracy and inference efficiency simultaneously, in contrast to conventional acceleration techniques that trade accuracy for computation. However, realizing this opportunity requires scaling experience banks, introducing substantial storage and search overhead that challenges the capacity, bandwidth, and power constraints of edge systems. We propose FlashX, a CMOS Directly Bonded to Array (CBA)-based NAND flash architecture for scalable experience reuse in embodied agents. FlashX exploits CBA's high internal bandwidth for parallel pSLC key search, employing interleaved Compute-in-Flash (CIF) engines to sustain sensing throughput while retaining dense TLC latent storage. Proprioception-aware clustering further reduces search overhead and enables incremental experience acquisition without global reclustering. Evaluations across VLA and WAM workloads demonstrate up to 12.24\%p and 7.43\%p improvements in task success under dense and compute-efficient configurations, respectively. FlashX achieves 2.57$\times$ higher search throughput than the strongest prior NAND search architecture under pSLC sensing, with a further 9.7$\times$ search reduction through clustering. This delivers 1.29--3.95$\times$ end-to-end speedup and 1.12--2.34$\times$ energy efficiency improvement over SSD-based retrieval.

Compared with SSD-based retrieval, it provides 1.29–3.95× end-to-end speedup and 1.12–2.34× energy-efficiency improvement.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in real-world long-horizon manipulation, where memory plays a crucial role. However, existing memory-augmented VLAs either retrieve past observations without reasoning about what they imply, or reason over the full history in a shared context where it crowds out current perception. Cognitive science treats them as distinct systems: memory reconstructs past experience to decide what to do, while perception guides how to act. We therefore propose ActMem, an in-context memory framework that decouples memory reasoning from perceptual grounding within a single vision-language backbone. Built on a vision-language model with native video understanding, ActMem infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history and keeps the hidden states formed during this inference as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT), which conditions a flow-matching action expert. Perception Attention further lets the expert attend directly to the current view. To keep inference fast under long histories, Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation across consecutive decisions without changing the output. ActMem achieves 71.1% task success and 80.8% completion success on RoboMemArena, surpassing the strongest baseline by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, and 73.8% average success on MIKASA-Robo, the best among all compared methods. In the real world, it reaches 68.8% average success on exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory tasks, 10.0 percentage points above the strongest memory-augmented VLA. Code and checkpoints will be released at https://github.com/LigphiDonk/ActMem and https://huggingface.co/donk111/ActMem.
authors: Linfeng Dong, Jianwei Niu, Jiuyi Zhao, Ruibing Feng, Xinghao Wu, Wu Yang, Shuai Tao, Wulong Liu, Mu Li
bullets: Addresses memory-augmented VLA models that either retrieve past observations without reasoning or let long histories interfere with current perception.

A flow-matching action expert uses the latent memory while Perception Attention directly grounds actions in the current view.
Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation across consecutive decisions to reduce inference cost for long histories.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ActMem. (b) Inside the backbone, the subtask tokens that form Memory CoT follow the history and the current view in the sequence, so under the causal mask they read both, and their hidden states become Ct; the action expert receives only Ct, not the history tokens. (c) Efficient Memory CoT Inference. Consecutive decisions usually share the same subtask, so the previous subtask is reused as a draft and verified against the updated context in a single parallel pass. If it is accepted, its hidden states are recomputed to give the new Ct, with no token-by-token decoding.

papers.abstract: Visual world models enable effective short-horizon goal-conditioned planning, such as reaching nearby targets and pushing objects over short distances, by predicting candidate action outcomes and comparing their representations with a goal representation. However, extending this approach to long-horizon tasks is challenging: prediction errors accumulate over extended rollouts, while latent-space similarity to distant goals provides limited guidance for ranking candidate outcomes. Existing methods address these limitations by introducing intermediate subgoals, either generated by learned models or selected from experience memory. Generated subgoals can contain hallucinations or be inaccurate in aspects such as object positions and timing. Memory-based approaches are constrained by experience coverage and may lack precise guidance for selecting appropriate intermediate states from stored observations. We introduce GEMS, which generates temporally structured subgoals to guide action search and state selection from Latent Experience Memory (LEM). A distance gate determines whether predicted outcomes are evaluated against the generated subgoal or the selected memory state. Experiments across six tasks and task suites spanning manipulation, navigation, and reaching demonstrate the effectiveness of GEMS for long-horizon planning. GEMS outperforms state-of-the-art world-model planning baselines across different manipulation settings, achieving success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World. It improves over the strongest evaluated baseline on these tasks by 24.0, 7.3, and 22.2 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate that generated subgoals and experience memory can jointly strengthen long-horizon planning with a frozen world model.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents accumulate extensive interaction histories when solving complex, long-horizon tasks, making efficient memory management critical to their performance and scalability. While existing memory management methods primarily focus on what to retain or retrieve, they often overlook how much perceptual detail should be allocated to individual past interactions. We posit that effective agent memory depends not only on the information preserved, but also on the granularity at which each past interaction is perceived. Motivated by this insight, we propose Resolution as Attention (RAA), a memory perception mechanism that uses visual resolution as a means of attention allocation across interaction histories. RAA renders past interactions as images and dynamically adjusts their resolution at every step according to their relevance to the agent's upcoming decision, preserving fine-grained information for critical interactions while reducing visual-token consumption for less relevant ones. To adaptively determine the perceptual fidelity of each interaction, we train a lightweight relevance estimator with teacher-model guidance and further optimize it to preserve the agent's decision consistency at a reduced visual-token cost. Experiments across multiple tasks and backbones show that RAA reduces token consumption by over 50% without compromising task performance. Moreover, RAA can be integrated as a plug-in perception layer with existing memory management methods, yielding further token savings and revealing adaptive perception as a complementary dimension of agent memory.

papers.abstract: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.
authors: Wenhao Yuan, Longhui Yuan, Zexi Jia, Ningzhe Shi, Jingwei Li, Shipeng Cen, Pengcheng Luo, Jie Zhou, Jinchao Zhang
bullets: Targets lifelong learning beyond fixed tasks, curricula, and objectives.

papers.abstract: Language-goal aerial navigation requires a UAV to reach a destination specified in natural language using observations collected during flight. A key challenge is linking changing egocentric perception with spatial evidence anchored to stable locations for long-range navigation. We propose CityNav-VLA, a dual-frame vision-language-action model for urban navigation integrating dynamic egocentric context with persistent allocentric spatial memory. The UAV incrementally accumulates visual observations on a fixed north-up map initialized with geographic and landmark priors, preserving evidence across viewpoint changes. A dynamic query conditioned on the instruction, current observations, UAV state, and motion history retrieves relevant memory evidence to predict a map-frame target. A deterministic controller converts this target into body-frame commands using the UAV's current pose, connecting global reasoning with egocentric execution. To reduce target fluctuations over long horizons, early goal commitment (EGC) fixes the execution target to the coordinate-wise median of the first $K$ predictions without extra trainable parameters. On Test Unseen, CityNav-VLA reduces NE by 21.2% and improves SR and SPL by 15.8% and 30.9%, respectively. It also reduces NE by 6.2% and improves SR and SPL by 5.6% and 23.2%, respectively, relative to the former SOTA after dataset refinement. Cumulative ablations show that navigation-map features yield the largest gains, while metric coordinates further improve endpoint accuracy. With a 4B-scale backbone, inference averages 0.68 s per decision with 8.6 GB peak memory on a single A100, presenting remarkable model efficiency.
authors: Haotian Xu, Yue Hu, Zhengqiu Zhu, Tuo Feng, Wenguan Wang, Quanjun Yin

On Test Unseen, it improves navigation error, success rate, and success-weighted path length, with efficient 0.68-second inference and 8.6 GB peak memory on one A100.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon visual agents must do more than inspect images: they must turn observations into evidence that remains usable as a task unfolds. Existing active-perception methods teach agents where and how to look, while a final-answer reward gives little structure for deciding which observations satisfy dependent subgoals or should be retained for later use. We present ViStep-RL (Visual Stepwise Reinforcement Learning), which models execution as a dependency-linked graph of evidence-bearing subgoals. A verifier tracks which subgoals are supported by valid evidence, and changes in graph potential provide a net-progress learning signal; an active memory protocol preserves evidence across turns and links retrieval to downstream use. On ViInteract, ViStep-RL reaches 60.0% strict completion with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, compared with 10.0% for the base model and 46.5% after supervised fine-tuning. Controlled studies show that incremental task-state rewards outperform cumulative rewards by 3.2 points, while active evidence writing improves strict completion by 7.75 points over automatic writing. Under a common interaction framework, the task-trained ViStep-RL policy achieves 59.5% answer accuracy, 24.0 points above the strongest of six general-purpose reference models. Held-out episodes confirm the gain at both Qwen scales, and gains extend to three external visual reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: In precision manipulation, small errors in alignment or force can cause jamming or deformation, making contact feedback essential for adapting pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models to these tasks. A single tactile observation leaves the response to recent actions ambiguous. Direct tactile fusion during post-training can also disperse the action expert's visual attention and reduce the share it allocates to contact regions. To address these challenges, CoRA-VTLA augments pretrained VLAs with lightweight tactile modules. A queryable action-response memory retrieves recent contact responses so that the action expert can combine them with immediate tactile feedback. Contact-guided gaze supervision concentrates the visual attention of the tactile semantic token on image regions corresponding to fingertip contact. CoRA-VTLA achieves 73.33% mean success across three MuJoCo tasks, compared with 50% for direct tactile fusion with the same sensor inputs. It also achieves 67% success on an optical-tactile task from the public UniVTAC benchmark and 66.7% mean success across three real-robot tasks. These results show that tactile post-training helps pretrained VLAs adjust to changing contact.
authors: Chengye Song, Rui Song, Shengqi Wang, Jiawei Zhang, Hongzhou Wang, Xueyang Guo, Yang Liu
bullets: Addresses ambiguous single-frame tactile feedback and attention dilution during tactile post-training.
Uses a queryable action-response memory to retrieve recent contact responses alongside current tactile input.
Applies contact-guided gaze supervision to focus tactile-related visual attention on fingertip contact regions.
Reports 73.33% mean success across three MuJoCo tasks, versus 50% for direct tactile fusion with the same sensors.
Also reaches 67% on a public optical-tactile benchmark and 66.7% across three real-robot tasks.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become a standard choice for visuomotor imitation learning, owing to their ability to model multimodal action distributions. In memory-dependent manipulation, the robot must act on information that is no longer visible. Existing methods feed the observation history to the policy as an additional condition, while action generation still starts from Gaussian noise. However, the policy must then pick out the relevant target from a long and redundant history, leading to spurious correlations and unreliable decisions as the memory load grows. Additionally, the initial noise carries no information about what the robot has seen, leaving generation without guidance toward the remembered target. To address these issues, we propose RecallFlow, a flow-policy framework that builds the source distribution from episodic memory. Recall-Relocalization relates the memory to the current view through a few recall slots, so that the source reflects where the remembered targets are now. Recall Anchors then turns each slot into a Gaussian component of the source, enabling generation to start close to the intended action instead of from noise. The transport network then completes the action from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy. We further build a suite of memory-dependent tasks grouped by memory load and compare all policies under a matched protocol. Extensive experiments show that RecallFlow achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate of 80.4% on the public MIKASA-Robo memory benchmark, and outperforms the strongest baseline by 20.3 points on our suite and by 18.8 points on four real-robot tasks.
authors: Xuji Zhang, Qilin Zhong, Zichen Zhang, Wei Zhai, Jian Di, Kun Li, Yang Cao, Wenjun Lv
bullets: Addresses unreliable decisions when policies must retrieve relevant information from long, redundant observation histories.
Uses Recall-Relocalization to connect episodic memories to the current view through a small number of recall slots.
Converts recall slots into Gaussian source components via Recall Anchors, guiding flow-policy generation toward intended actions.
The transport network completes actions from the current observation alone, keeping inference nearly as cheap as a memoryless policy.
Reports 80.4% average success on MIKASA-Robo, with gains of 20.3 and 18.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline on simulated and real-robot task suites, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of RecallFlow. The present observation is encoded into tokens Zt. Recall Anchors turns each slot into a Gaussian anchor in action space; with a standard Gaussian, the anchors form the source p0. A transport network conditioned only on Zt carries x0 ∼ p0 to the action chunk, so memory reaches the action solely through the source.
