papers.abstract: Counting distinct objects in a video is hard when the camera returns to places it has seen. A vision-language model that reads the whole video answers with a few small numbers, and one that reads it in parts counts an object again in every part that shows it. Object trackers need the category before the video is read, or a fixed vocabulary. We observe that a memory for counting does not need to know what it is looking for, only where it has been: objects rarely leave a room between visits, so parts of a video grouped by place share almost no objects, and a place can be recognised before any question is asked. Building on this, we introduce PlaceTally, a question-blind test-time memory model that constructs a place graph for each video. Each video fragment joins the place of its best earlier match or opens a new place, because a strong match is rarely wrong while a true return often matches weakly. A frozen vision-language model counts each place once from at most 128 of its frames, so every read has a bounded input and the memory grows with the number of places; the graph is built 15 times faster than real time. On RevisitCount, our benchmark of real room re-recordings, it scores 62.5% mean relative accuracy on test rooms and 61.2% on held-out rooms, against 51.2% and 44.3% for the same model reading the whole video. It stays level as rooms return more or less often, while a fixed correction of summed visits moves from 38.5% to 61.4%.
bullets: Motivation: Whole-video vision-language models struggle with long videos, while chunk-wise counting repeats objects and trackers require predefined categories.
Method: Group video fragments by their best visual match to earlier fragments or create a new place, then count each place once with a frozen vision-language model.
Design: Each place is read from at most 128 frames, bounding input size while memory scales with the number of places.
Results: On RevisitCount, it achieves 62.5% accuracy on test rooms and 61.2% on held-out rooms, versus 51.2% and 44.3% for whole-video reading.
Scope: The approach is designed for videos involving revisits to physical places and assumes objects generally remain within rooms between visits.

figures.caption: Figure 2. A PlaceTally memory is constructed per video instance before the question and read after it, shown on one real ARKit-Revisit test stream. (a) The detector cuts the stream into fragments. (b) Continuation and return evidence between fragments, which Eq. 2 would sum. papers.abstract: Latent world models plan towards a goal image by minimising the distance between predicted and goal latents. This distance is not geodesic: it has local minima, latent traps, behind walls, at corners and in dead ends, and memoryless receding-horizon replanning keeps the agent in them, revisiting states far from the goal. We propose Episodic Kernel Repulsion (EKR), a training-free cost term that penalises candidate plans by a top-$k$ Gaussian kernel to a novelty-gated memory of the latents the agent has actually visited, rescaled by the current base cost so that its strength is comparable across models. Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR raises average success from 31.8% to 46.7% (LeWM) and from 54.7% to 64.0% (H-JEPA) with the same model, planner and budget. Same-memory counterfactuals show that, in most settings, EKR pushes plans away from visited states, in navigation, often at a higher base cost; stuck episodes and revisits drop accordingly. In seven of eight settings it matches or exceeds $4\times$ samples at $0.8$--$1.5\times$ compute. Without tuning, it transfers to DINO-WM with CEM: $+6.7$ and $+19.3$ points on official and longer-goal Wall tasks, and from 44.7% to 100.0% and from 21.0% to 32.0% on long-horizon PointMaze and Push-T.
authors: Yican Zhao, Bolin Yang, Ruizhe Wang, Haiyang Guo, Fuji Yang, Bingo Wing-Kuen Ling, Zelin Zang
bullets: Latent distance-to-goal objectives can create local minima, especially near walls, corners, and dead ends.
EKR penalizes candidate plans near a novelty-gated memory of visited latents using a top-k Gaussian kernel.
Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR improves reported average success while using the same planning budget.
It reduces stuck episodes and revisits, often steering plans away from visited states even at higher base cost.
The method transfers without tuning to DINO-WM with CEM and improves performance on Wall, PointMaze, and Push-T tasks.

papers.abstract: Lifelong embodied navigation requires agents to accumulate experience through continuous interaction and reuse it for subsequent goal searches. Existing memory-enhanced methods typically retain historical observations or construct structured scene representations. However, storing observations or high-dimensional semantic embeddings incurs growing storage costs. Meanwhile, structured representations support retrieval and semantic reasoning but do not explicitly evolve accumulated experience into environment-specific knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose Experience-Evolving Memory (EvoNav), a novel two-timescale memory framework. It organizes semantic observations, spatial relations, and task-feedback cues into sparse experience atoms. During online operation, experience atoms continually consolidate repeated observations and form dynamic links based on transitions. At the slower timescale, EvoNav distills accumulated category co-occurrences and feedback signals into environment-specific structural knowledge without relying on predefined object--room relations. For each new goal, EvoNav combines direct goal evidence from experience atoms with learned structural knowledge to guide goal-directed search on the current traversability map. Experiments on single-goal, sequential multi-floor, and multimodal navigation demonstrate effective experience reuse and improved path efficiency with compact persistent memory, together with successful transfer to a real robot.
authors: Weitao An, Chenghao Xu, Xu Yang, Cheng Deng
bullets: Addresses the growing storage costs and limited knowledge evolution of observation- and embedding-based navigation memories.
Uses a two-timescale memory that stores sparse experience atoms and continually consolidates repeated observations, transitions, and task feedback.
Distills category co-occurrences and feedback into structural knowledge without predefined object–room relations.
Combines direct goal evidence with learned structural knowledge to guide search on the current traversability map.
Demonstrates experience reuse, improved path efficiency, compact persistent memory, and real-robot transfer across multiple navigation settings.

papers.abstract: Physical agents must use what they previously saw or touched after visibility or contact is lost. Their actions change the implications of these remembered facts. We introduce executable perceptual memory (EPM), a world-model framework that advances explicit perceptual state alongside neural latent dynamics during imagination. Its evolving read-out informs reward prediction, value estimation and policy learning. We align reward inputs with the transitions that produced them and supervise the reward head on open-loop rollouts of recorded actions. On Memory Maze $13\times13$, EPM reaches 30.37 return at 1M interactions, compared with 23.37 when the same evolving read-out informs only policy and value on a common perceptual front end: a gain of 7.00 [3.80, 10.21]. The complete method also improves control on $9\times9$ and in MiniWorld. Probes of remembered, out-of-view arrivals show stronger reward anticipation in both visual implementations. Concentration, tactile recovery and real tactile frames demonstrate complementary roles of remembered facts in imagined-policy training, motion-dependent decisions and sensory-content retention. EPM connects persistent perception to the predicted consequences and learning signals of a world model for Physical AI.
authors: Xianyao Li, Ruitong Tian, Rui Min, Fang Xu, Jing Du
bullets: Addresses how physical agents can use visual or tactile information after it is no longer observable.
Advances an explicit perceptual state alongside neural latent dynamics during imagined rollouts.
Aligns rewards with the transitions that produced them and trains reward prediction on open-loop recorded-action rollouts.
On 13×13 Memory Maze, reaches 30.37 return at 1M interactions versus 23.37 for a policy/value-only readout.
Additional tests show benefits across maze sizes and MiniWorld, with improved reward anticipation for remembered out-of-view events.

papers.abstract: Persistent spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents to operate reliably in environments they repeatedly encounter. It requires recognizing revisited places despite viewpoint changes, distinguishing them from similar-looking rooms, and updating memories as environments change. Yet existing evaluations often leave physical place identity across separated visits implicit. We introduce ReSpaceBench, a benchmark comprising 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes, organized into 9 tasks spanning room association, persistent state tracking, and downstream reasoning. Controlled walkthroughs define visits by physical room entry and deliberately include same-type room distractors and cross-session object changes. Our evaluation of 32 models and 3 agentic video-understanding frameworks reveals substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated zero-shot model achieves 50.5% overall accuracy and 52.2% on a 450-question subset, compared with 90.1% for human annotators. The evaluated agentic frameworks offer no overall improvement over direct inference with the same base model. Analysis of agent execution traces reveals evidence omissions and incorrect cross-visit room associations as major failure modes, suggesting that iterative evidence seeking alone does not ensure consistent spatial memory. Further analyses expose a gap between recognizing familiar rooms and identifying the correct visited room, while annotation-guided sampling highlights the importance of preserving intervening visits and transitions. We also provide RS-30K, a separate training dataset from synthetic sources with no template, scene, route, or video overlap with the benchmark. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B raises overall accuracy from 35.5% to 60.4%, with the largest gains in association and improvements extending to real-life scenes.
bullets: Benchmarks persistent spatial memory with 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes and 9 tasks.
Tests room association, state tracking, and downstream reasoning under viewpoint changes, distractor rooms, and changing objects.
The best evaluated zero-shot model reaches 50.5% accuracy versus 90.1% for human annotators; agentic frameworks do not improve overall results.
Key failures include omitted evidence and incorrect associations between rooms visited at different times.
Training on the separate RS-30K dataset improves Qwen3-VL-8B from 35.5% to 60.4%, especially on room association and real-life scenes.

papers.abstract: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams
bullets: Frames memory systems as custodians of users’ persistent information with explicit behavioral responsibilities.
Introduces an open-source benchmark suite covering performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty, while identifying remaining gaps.
Provides MilaMem and a governance layer for controlled study of memory-system design choices.
Finds that no system dominates all performance benchmarks, and strong task performance can coexist with weak privacy, sovereignty, and security.
Shows that recall and retention policies can improve privacy and poisoning resistance, though recall may reduce helpfulness.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving visual agents keep what they learn as skills: key frames with step notes on a task's steps and their order. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is now a popular way to train such skills into a vision-language model that matches, on its own answers, a teacher that also reads the written order. At deployment, frames often go missing or show an unusual order, as when a person or a website reorders the steps. Existing internalization methods keep any order they store in the frame-reading weights: trained on full frames, the model guesses when they are missing, and trained with frames withheld, it stores the order, so memory can override what it sees. We propose PriorSplit, which fills in missing frames from an order kept outside the model, with no training beyond OPSD. It counts which of two neighboring steps comes first in training episodes, and the model checks if both asked steps are in view: if so, it answers from the frames, and otherwise the counts answer. Extensive experiments on synthetic skills with five models and on step-tagged order questions in new episodes of seen web, cooking and egocentric tasks demonstrate that, with frames missing, PriorSplit outperforms every compared method at OPSD's training cost. With Qwen3-VL-4B on synthetic skills, it also stays close to OPSD on unusual orders, where methods that gain most by storing the order fall behind.
bullets: Addresses a key failure mode of OPSD-trained skills: memorized step order can override what the model actually sees.
Stores pairwise step-order counts outside the VLM and uses them only when one or both queried frames are unavailable.
When both relevant steps are visible, the agent answers from the frames; otherwise, it consults the external prior.
Requires no training beyond standard on-policy self-distillation.
Experiments across synthetic skills and web, cooking, and egocentric tasks show the best performance under missing frames, while remaining close to OPSD on unusual orders.

papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is entering the home. Cloud-based assistants face governance limitations in data transmission, continuous availability, and the reliability of physical actions, which are especially salient in households where devices remain online, data accumulate over time, and commands trigger real-world actions. Using the home local server as a unifying organizing axis, this article develops a design-oriented review framework. Sources from arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official documentation were searched through November 2026 and coded into five evidence categories: reviews, system prototypes, benchmarks, HCI and eldercare studies, and official documentation. System designs were mapped onto shared architectural modules, identifying nine recurrent responsibilities of the home local server. Generative models support perceptual interpretation, intent understanding, and candidate planning, while deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases confine candidate actions to an inspectable space. Home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding can be compared within a common framework: they share state and memory but differ in latency, false positive and negative rates, proactivity, and permissions. Existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments and cannot substitute for real-deployment evaluation. Local deployment is not inherently safer, and technical continuity alone does not establish the social or medical effects of companionship and guarding. The article proposes a five-dimensional evaluation framework covering architectural capability, system resources, privacy, safety and reliability, and human experience, together with six design principles and a future research agenda for local-first intelligent home systems.
bullets: Cloud assistants face challenges involving data governance, continuous availability, and reliable physical actions in homes.
The home local server is used to organize nine recurring architectural responsibilities across whole-home systems.
Generative models handle perception, intent understanding, and planning, while deterministic checks, knowledge graphs, and authorization leases constrain actions.
Home control, companionship, and guarding share state and memory but differ in latency, error trade-offs, proactivity, and permissions.
Current benchmarks rely mainly on virtual environments; local deployment is not automatically safer, and social or medical effects remain insufficiently established.

papers.abstract: Robots that work alongside people should be able to use what they have seen when new requests arise. The same experience may later support identifying an object or returning it to its original location, although these uses were unknown during observation. ReuseMem learns to use one visual memory for multiple later manipulation goals. It records visual features independently of future goals, retrieves complementary evidence for each request, and combines it with the current scene through a lightweight action interface. Retrieval is supervised by how well candidate evidence supports expert-action prediction across different current states, linking memory selection to its use in manipulation. Repeated visual features are stored once, and memory computations that remain unchanged during action generation are reused. Experiments on four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios demonstrate reuse of a common recording across different requests. With matched action adaptation, ReuseMem improves joint goal completion on the benchmark tasks by 24.5 percentage points over uniform memory. These findings show that one memory can support multiple later manipulation goals as the scene changes.
authors: Yoonseok Kang, Dayeon Jung, Seunghoon Jeon, Wonjib Kim, Dongchul Park
bullets: Addresses how robots can repurpose past observations for requests that were unknown when the observations were recorded.
Stores visual features independently of future goals and retrieves complementary evidence suited to each request and current scene.
Supervises retrieval using expert-action prediction, connecting memory selection to manipulation performance.
Uses a lightweight action interface and reuses repeated features and unchanged computations for efficiency.
Evaluated across four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios, demonstrating reuse across changing goals and scenes.

papers.abstract: Modern multi-camera 3D detectors increasingly rely on large Vision Transformer (ViT) image encoders, making repeated full-depth encoding a dominant inference cost even though adjacent driving frames are highly redundant. We present EvoMem3D, an adaptive-depth temporal framework that caches the most recent full-depth detector-interface appearance representation as a read-only anchor and combines it with policy-selected partial features from the current frame. A lightweight pre-encoding controller chooses among semantic encoder exits before image processing, allocating shallow computation to stable frames and deeper computation when the visual state changes. To reuse appearance without carrying stale geometry, we decouple temporal appearance from geometric alignment: current-frame calibration defines the decoder geometry at every timestamp, while a motion-conditioned positional adapter accounts for anchor-to-current ego motion. On nuScenes, EvoMem3D achieves 61.50 NDS and 52.76 mAP while reducing end-to-end latency from 364.4 to 168.7 ms (x2.16) relative to standard dense DETR3D. With StreamPETR, it reaches 61.36 NDS and 52.55 mAP at a x1.92 speedup. Controlled studies isolate the effects of current evidence, temporal reuse, memory correction, and adaptive routing, while our audit confirms that the policy learns to distinguish semantic driving regimes.
authors: Moshe Kimhi, Idan Kligvasser, Yotam Intrator, Regev Cohen, Ehud Rivlin
bullets: Caches a full-depth appearance representation as a read-only temporal anchor and combines it with selected partial features from the current frame.
A lightweight controller selects encoder exits before processing, using shallow computation for stable scenes and deeper computation when visual conditions change.
Separates temporal appearance reuse from geometric alignment: current calibration defines geometry, while a motion-conditioned adapter handles ego motion.
On nuScenes, achieves 61.50 NDS and 52.76 mAP with 2.16× lower latency than dense DETR3D; StreamPETR sees a 1.92× speedup with similar accuracy.
Scope: the method targets temporally redundant driving sequences and relies on policy-based recognition of semantic driving regimes.

papers.tldr: EvoMem3D accelerates multi-camera 3D detection by adaptively reducing image-encoder depth and reusing temporally stable appearance features while preserving current-frame geometry.

papers.abstract: A robot may know how to move an object yet still need to learn where it belongs. When a person rejects a placement, the robot must decide whether the correction applies only to that situation or expresses a broader rule. We study this problem in CRAFT (Contextual Requirement Adaptation with Frozen Tools), a framework for learning local requirements without retraining robot skills. It records physical success separately from whether an action meets the requirement. Our scope ladder uses memory when an action has already been judged in a nearly identical situation. Elsewhere, it combines memory, explicit rules and a learner for requirements beyond those rules, weighting their predictions by how well they predicted earlier feedback. Controlled studies show gains over correction memory alone in utility, which rewards acceptable actions and charges for mistakes and questions. In camera-grounded robot simulations, the ladder asks fewer questions than language-model agents with persistent memory, but some of those agents take fewer wrong actions and succeed more often after requirements change. All execution failures and timeouts remain in the evaluation. These results support combining specific memories with broader rules, while leaving reliable adaptation to changing requirements unresolved. All evidence comes from simulation with generated requirements and simulated feedback.

papers.abstract: Agentic navigation must maintain goals and adapt actions from incomplete evidence despite execution failures and delayed inference. We present AgenticJevNav, which links goal-directed planning, evidence memory, event-triggered verification, and bounded execution. The Agent plans from RGB, odometry, memory, and feedback, retaining goal ownership while authorizing a bounded action set. Jev reviews structured evidence after blocked/failed execution or two consecutive low-progress segments. Version, freshness, and once-only checks govern decision application. A single executor and independent RGB reflex constrain motion. Goal revisions revoke obsolete requests and actions before replanning. Across six simulated task families, AgenticJevNav achieves 73.33% SR over 60 trials, 21.67 percentage points above the next-best Agent-only aggregate control under differing historical protocols. A real-world GENISOM L1 quadruped deployment achieves 70.0% success over 30 trials, including bounded search reporting. Together, the simulation and physical-robot results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed architecture, while remaining failures highlight opportunities to improve grounding, approach planning, and runtime.

papers.abstract: Existing feedback-based methods for online vision-and-language navigation (VLN) primarily learn from current episode outcomes, leaving previously acquired feedback underutilized. Inspired by human episodic memory, we propose R2A, an online VLN adaptation framework that continually reuses successful and failed navigation experiences for policy learning. Specifically, Success-Failure Memory (SFM) retains successful and failed navigation episodes with acquired feedback and retrieves task-relevant experiences based on incoming instructions, enabling historical feedback to guide subsequent navigation. Prior-Anchored Adaptation (PAA) learns from these experiences by reinforcing successful trajectories and suppressing failed ones relative to a frozen pretrained policy, while regularizing behavioral drift. Together, these modules enable continual feedback reuse and stable policy adaptation without source-domain data or expert supervision. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks, REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE, and five navigation backbones demonstrate consistent performance gains. On the REVERIE validation unseen split, R2A improves DUET's SR from 46.98% to 69.84% and SPL from 33.73% to 50.98%.

Evaluated on REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE with five navigation backbones, showing consistent gains.

papers.abstract: Task configurations in factories, warehouses, and everyday physical environments change over time. Physical AI systems therefore need to incorporate new facts into scene memory while preserving valid information about equipment, objects, and operating constraints. We study updates to this parametric semantic-memory layer and present a joint evaluation of correction and preservation under finite update budgets. At fixed current fact count and memory parameter count, the protocol combines independent single-fact updates, budget trajectories, old-to-new answer diagnostics, and first stable success. Using a frozen 4B language model with late-layer LoRA, we evaluate seven preparation conditions and six update budgets on four-field synthetic semantic configurations. In two exposure-matched history conditions, increasing the budget from eight to 32 updates raises joint success from 6.25% to 94.79% and 91.15%, respectively, while exact obsolete-value outputs fall from 174/192 and 166/192 to zero. Constant32, which matches preparation steps but repeatedly trains on unchanged content during the first 32 events, achieves higher early joint success at eight steps (53.65%); at 32 steps, it reaches 85.42%, below both changing-history conditions. These results distinguish rapid correction under a small budget from simultaneous correctness of the new fact and the other three facts after further training. For both changing histories, most cases remain jointly correct at all subsequent measured points from step 16 onward. Output analysis shows that short-budget failures primarily retain the old value; repeated training on the new fact together with the other current facts progressively replaces these obsolete answers.
bullets: Studies correction and preservation of semantic scene memory under finite update budgets.

Repeated training on unchanged content improves early correction but underperforms changing-history training at 32 updates.

papers.abstract: Agents that work beyond a single context window, or in teams, hand their work to a successor as a short written summary. Evaluation has focused on whether an agent can solve a task, and relatively little is known about how much of what an agent has learned survives being written down. We study this in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, where an agent that is told nothing fails and an agent given a 300-character statement of the rules succeeds. We compare one agent that plays eight lives and keeps its whole history with a chain of eight agents that each play one life and inherit a 300-character note. All six models we test learn less in the chain: after eight generations it stands where the single agent stood after about four lives. Controlled variants of the chain decompose this handoff loss into three components: none from changing the agent, a smaller loss from compressing to 300 characters, and a larger loss from compressing repeatedly. When each note is written from the full record of earlier lives instead of from the previous note, the same 300 characters recover 70% to 82% of the loss. The loss is robust across model sizes and is not alleviated by instructing the writer to record evidence, to revise the inherited note, or to keep a structured ledger. In simpler terms, an agent cannot hand over what it has not yet understood: a note holds what its writer has worked out, and a rule that takes several lives to see is lost with the lives that were not passed on.
bullets: Studies knowledge transfer in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules.
Compares one agent retaining eight lives of history with eight one-life agents linked by 300-character notes.

papers.abstract: An embodied brain, or System 2, must turn an abstract goal into actions while discovering relevant scene conditions and checking whether executed skills achieved their intended effects. Open-loop evaluations cannot test observations shaped by an agent's decisions, while some closed-loop evaluations provide limited evidence during execution or assume idealized skill outcomes. We introduce SCOPER, a suite for studying observation-grounded planning, execution, and recovery. SCOPER-bench combines high-level goals, ongoing visual observations, a shared rule-based System 1 for low-level actions, and controlled execution failures. Its construction and validation pipeline yields 870 tasks across BEHAVIOR and ProcTHOR, complemented by about 3,500 situated questions tied to the evaluated agent's execution. Benchmark results reveal difficulties in retaining scene evidence, monitoring progress, and recovering from unexpected outcomes. To address these difficulties, SCOPER-harness combines Evidence Memory and Progress Verification with a dynamic task agenda and bounded exploration, without additional model training. Across two evaluated open-source backbones and two simulators, the harness improves task success by 11.1-28.6%; a harnessed 9B model outperforms a directly executed 27B model on both simulators. In an offline next-action evaluation using observations from 200 real-robot demonstrations, the harness also improves full-call accuracy by 14.7% and 15.3%. SCOPER provides a setting for diagnosing and improving embodied reasoning throughout a complete task execution cycle.

The harness improves task success by 11.1–28.6% across two backbones and two simulators, and improves offline next-action accuracy by 14.7% and 15.3%.
Findings highlight persistent challenges in retaining scene evidence, monitoring progress, and recovering from unexpected outcomes.

papers.abstract: Long-term spacecraft autonomy requires embodied agents to use operational history under communication delays, time-critical operations, environmental uncertainty, complex physical interactions, power and computational constraints, and safety and reliability requirements. We introduce AstroMemBench and a Scenario-Challenge-Capability design method that maps these requirements to executable memory tests. The benchmark covers 16 memory subchallenges through 140 templates and 2240 instances across nine tasks in planetary surface operations, on-orbit servicing, and deep-space exploration. A deterministic environment scores actions for task completion, state changes, safety, and resource use. Ablations under nine conditions show that the benchmark is sensitive to how accurately agents recover and use historical information and to differences in memory-system design. Main experiments compare six configurations. Mem0, Chain-of-Memory, LightMem, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improve same-session mean scores over native Pi Agent, with no clear advantage of the three memory systems over RAG. After a session restart, Mem0 outperforms RAG by 12.25 points. Benefits favor instruction retention and result reuse over ongoing state tracking and energy reservation. AstroMemBench supports the design, development, and selection of memory systems for embodied spacecraft agents. AstroMemBench 1.0 and its evaluation code are publicly available: https://github.com/flyingView/AstroMemBench-v1.
authors: You Wu, Guhong Zhang, Hongwei Li, Xinyue Hong, Yuan Jia

Tests six configurations and nine ablation conditions to assess memory recovery, use, and design differences.
Memory systems and RAG improve same-session performance over native Pi Agent, while no memory system clearly beats RAG overall.
After session restart, Mem0 outperforms RAG by 12.25 points; gains are stronger for instruction retention and result reuse than for state tracking or energy reservation.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires both spatial scene understanding and task history. However, many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely primarily on current observations, without explicitly integrating spatial structure and task history. Appearance-based memories can be sensitive to occlusion and viewpoint changes, while spatial representations of the current scene alone do not preserve how the scene has changed during task execution. We introduce STVLA, a framework that incorporates features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model into temporal memory alongside visual representations. This allows the policy to recall past scene structure as context for current action decisions. To select informative history, STVLA uses a mathematically grounded scoring rule that balances relevance to the current observation with complementary evidence from memory. Across evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge, STVLA achieves the highest average success rate among the compared methods on each benchmark. On real-world block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, it improves success over $\pi_{0.5}$ by $58.33$, $30.00$, and $35.00$ percentage points, respectively. These results support integrating scene geometry into temporal memory to improve manipulation requiring both spatial precision and task history. Project website: \href{https://stvla.github.io/}{https://stvla.github.io/}

Achieves the highest average success rate among compared methods across LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge.
Improves real-world success over π₀.₅ by 58.33, 30.00, and 35.00 percentage points on block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, respectively.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents make decisions by combining information from heterogeneous memory modules, including declarative memory for explicit knowledge, procedural memory for learned routines, and working memory for current observations. During interaction, the memory contents required for decision making change with the agent's state, goal, and task progress, while many contents remain shared across consecutive decisions. However, existing memory modules are typically accessed through separate interfaces, so each updated memory context is often processed as a new input to the foundation model. This prevents selective key-value (KV) cache reuse for unchanged memory contents and forces full KV cache recomputation even when much of the memory context remains valid. We introduce HeMeR, an inference framework that performs KV reconciliation between dynamically updated memory contexts and reusable KV states. HeMeR tracks declarative, procedural, and working memory contents across action decisions, preserves KV states for unchanged contents, and reconciles only the KV states affected by memory-content updates. This enables efficient and stable inference as memory contents evolve during interaction. We evaluate HeMeR on ALFWorld, Habitat, and real-world robotic deployments requiring coordinated use of heterogeneous memory contents. In the real-world setting, HeMeR achieves 83.20% task success and reduces per-step inference time from 2.94 to 1.87 seconds compared with MemRL, while preserving compatible KV states as task progress updates the memory context.

papers.abstract: In long-horizon manipulation, a robot may need to take different actions under identical observations, depending on task progress and the outcomes of earlier attempts. We refer to this ambiguity as decision aliasing. Resolving it requires the policy to maintain memory of its execution history. To reduce the cost of processing full observation histories, recent methods build compact event memories using perceptual, semantic, or kinematic cues. However, these criteria may miss events that matter for task success. We instead propose an outcome-grounded principle: remember events that substantially change the predicted probability of eventual success. Following this principle, we introduce CGEM, a critic-gated event memory that uses a critic to select events with large estimated changes in success probability. Positive and negative changes are encoded as progress and failure records, respectively. Failure records are discarded once the corresponding subtask is completed. In a ten-subtask diagnostic environment with exactly computed success probabilities, CGEM achieves 88.0% success, compared with 0.0% for both a 36-step observation window and a kinematic event memory. Removing failure records reduces success to 1.7%.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation under uncertainty remains a challenging problem in robotics. We present \ourmethod{}, an algorithm for Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning. \ourmethod{} extends existing deterministic task and motion planning solvers to partially observable object rearrangement tasks, while still being able to take advantage of the efficiency and compositional generalization over long horizons of the base solver. This extension interleaves sensing actions into a plan skeleton that assumed full observability, and uses a novel persistent object-based memory to fuse observations into object mesh hypotheses and an observed occupancy map. We evaluate \ourmethod{} on real-world tabletop rearrangement tasks which feature heavy occlusion and partial visibility and demonstrate that it outperforms baselines that do not perform active perception or have persistent memory.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding aims to continuously process incoming visual observations, making the retention and retrieval of relevant information increasingly important as the video history grows. Although existing benchmarks include memory-related questions, question-answering accuracy alone does not reliably measure memory capabilities. Incorrect predictions may arise from failures in visual understanding rather than forgetting, whereas correct predictions may rely on linguistic priors or recent observations without requiring historical memory. To address these ambiguities, we introduce MemInStream, a benchmark dedicated to evaluating memory capabilities in streaming video understanding. We develop an evidence-controlled validation protocol that associates each question with temporally localized evidence intervals. The protocol validates evidence solvability and memory necessity by retaining questions that models can answer from the annotated evidence but cannot resolve using recent observations, post-evidence observations, or textual input alone. This helps disentangle memory limitations from understanding failures while reducing memory-independent shortcuts. MemInStream provides a systematic evaluation of memory capabilities through four major categories, covering Episodic Retrieval, State Tracking \& Updating, Multi-Evidence Integration, and Contextual Memory across diverse video scenarios. Overall, \textsc{MemInStream} provides a comprehensive and reliable benchmark for systematically evaluating memory capabilities in streaming video understanding.

papers.abstract: Memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies are meant to remember what happened. Many of them, however, fill memory by time: they sample frames uniformly across the episode and stamp each frame with its time step. Because time passes even when nothing happens, such a memory may not tell waiting from working. We show that it does not. On the counting tasks of RoboMME, we make the robot briefly pause or fidget its wrist. Such a null event changes nothing the task depends on, yet a released memory VLA counts the interval as work done and stops early. We call this failure phantom progress. It cuts success from 47 to 16 of 50 on one task and from 44 to 10 on the other. When the same frames are withheld from memory, success returns, so the cause lies in memory rather than in the interruption itself. We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut: because demonstrations proceed at a steady pace, elapsed time predicts progress. Indeed, rescaling the time stamps alone makes the policy stop early when the clock runs fast and repeat when it runs slow. Surprisingly, removing the time encoding does not cure the failure, because the frames of a null event still occupy slots of the time-sampled memory. Across RoboMME's released designs, vulnerability follows how memory is indexed. Of the fixes the diagnosis suggests, training with injected pauses does not remove the failure and impairs counting, whereas indexing memory by events recovers half or more of the loss without retraining. A memory meant to remember what happened should count events rather than clock ticks.
bullets: On RoboMME counting tasks, brief pauses or wrist fidgets trigger phantom progress and sharply reduce success.
The failure comes from a temporal shortcut: steady-paced demonstrations make timestamps predictive of progress.
Changing timestamps alone induces early stopping with fast clocks and repetition with slow clocks.
Removing time encodings is insufficient because null-event frames still occupy sampled memory slots.
Event-based memory indexing restores at least half the lost performance without retraining; pause-injection training fails to fix the issue and harms counting.

papers.abstract: Three-dimensional scene graphs (3DSGs) can provide robots with persistent metric-semantic representations for spatial reasoning, but the existing methods have primarily been developed for indoor and terrestrial environments. In this paper we investigate how a representative outdoor open-vocabulary method transfers to maritime environments and which adaptations are needed. Our experiments show that zero-shot representative outdoor 3DSG descriptions agree with our labeled ground truth for a majority of geometry-supported objects on our data, but the resulting map exhibits considerable physical-entity fragmentation, and its terrestrial higher-level assumptions don't capture maritime spatial organization needs. We therefore keep the underlying mapping method and post-process its accumulated evidence. We show a metric-semantic consolidation method followed by geometry-grounded multi-view vision-language model (VLM) reasoning that reconciles remaining fragments into physical entities and groups entities through observations into local places. In parallel, we construct maritime macro regions using map priors and onboard water and structure observations, and associate them with the local places. The resulting representation reduces physical-entity fragmentation beyond both the baseline and our geometry-semantic consolidation component alone, supports correspondence of fixed local places across repeated maritime traversals, and improves contextual retrieval on our reviewed queries over tested baselines. These results show how an outdoor open-vocabulary map can be adapted into persistent maritime scene memory with our methods for object/place identity and spatial abstractions.
authors: Kim Alexander Christensen, Dina Zimmermann, Martin Steinert, Eleni Kelasidi
bullets: A representative outdoor 3D scene-graph method transfers reasonably to maritime environments for many geometry-supported objects, but produces substantial physical-entity fragmentation.
The method preserves the underlying mapper and post-processes accumulated evidence to consolidate fragments using metric-semantic cues and geometry-grounded multi-view VLM reasoning.
Consolidated entities are grouped into local places, while maritime macro regions are built from map priors and onboard water and structure observations.
The resulting representation reduces fragmentation, supports matching fixed local places across repeated traversals, and improves contextual retrieval on reviewed queries over tested baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the maritime scene-memory pipeline. It first accumulates persistent map fragments and their observation histories, followed by a conservative geometricsemantic consolidation. Selected geometrically grounded multi-view observations are then processed by a visionlanguage model (VLM) at two abstraction levels: physicalentity reconciliation decides which fragments belong to the same object, while place formation groups persistent entities and observations into meaningful local places. In parallel, coarse maritime regions are derived from geographic topology and onboard water/structure evidence. Local places are associated with these regions and corresponding places are related across repeated traversals, forming a persistent scene memory for contextual retrieval.
Fig. 3: Macro regions compared. The first is defined by [39] while P00 and P03 are from our method. The regions are largely consistent, with one small extra region in P03.

Fig. 4: Place persistence and retrieval at the Northern port quay. The same fixed setting is matched despite different vessel occupancy and reconstructed geometry. Place relations retrieve 6/6 reviewed vessel records across P00 and P03, compared with 3/6 for the 50m radius baseline centered at the P00 anchor location in both surveys.

papers.abstract: Remote sensing disaster assessment is moving from simple damage classification toward comprehensive report-level analysis. In this setting, responders need not only damage descriptions but also verifiable evidence to guide response and recovery. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) and tool-augmented agents offer strong multimodal reasoning and perception, but they struggle to provide the evidence required for high-stakes verification. To address these limitations, we propose DisasterAgent, an evidence-driven agent that uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow to generate verifiable disaster reports from bitemporal optical imagery. DisasterAgent first invokes a specialized vision expert toolkit in the perception phase to build a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph (STPG), serving as a structured memory to store and organize disaster-induced changes across space and time. Evidence-based Augmentation (EA) then extracts evidence from the STPG, attaching inline citations that form a closed evidence loop from each statement to the supporting visual evidence. Extensive experiments on the DisasterM3 and RSCC benchmarks demonstrate that DisasterAgent consistently outperforms general-domain VLMs, remote sensing-specialized models, and existing remote sensing agents. Notably, compared with the original model, it improves the average score for disaster report generation on DisasterM3 by 13.5\% and ST5-SCS on RSCC by 15.34\%, providing a more accurate and verifiable solution for disaster emergency response. The code will be available at https://github.com/ZhijianLi2003/DisasterAgent.
authors: Zhijian Li, Jiawei Song, Chao Ren, Yidan Zhang, Peijin Wang, Xian Sun, Kun Fu
bullets: Addresses the lack of verifiable evidence in report-level disaster assessment using vision-language models and agents.
Uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow over bitemporal optical imagery.
Builds a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph to organize disaster-related changes across space and time.
Extracts graph evidence and attaches inline citations, creating a link from each report statement to supporting imagery.
Outperforms compared baselines on DisasterM3 and RSCC, with reported gains of 13.5% and 15.34% on the respective metrics.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. The overall architecture of DisasterAgent. The framework processes multimodal inputs through two primary stages. (1) Skill Routing: Driven by the VLM’s interpretation of the query, the system dynamically routes to appropriate skills within a pre-defined repository and seamlessly registers the required functional tools. (2) Skill-Guided Workflow: Guided by the registered skills, the framework sequentially executes a three-step pipeline comprising Perception, Evidence-based Augmentation, and Generation.

Fig. 4. Illustration of the SCE extraction pipeline. The VLM first reasons over the STPG to generate atomic factual claims. Each claim is then independently verified against the raw bitemporal images to obtain a confidence score. Finally, claims with scores above the threshold are filtered to form the robust SCE set.

(c) Caption produced by DisasterAgent, which identifies a localized explosion, notes that surrounding roads and water bodies remain intact, and links each claim to a numbered visual evidence reference (scores: DAP 4, DDR 4, FC 5). (d) Ground truth caption.

(c) Caption produced by DisasterAgent, which describes buildings as largely intact, acknowledges limited structural disturbances, and identifies intact roads, with selected claims linked to numbered evidence references (scores: DAP 5, DDR 4, FC 5). (d) Ground truth caption.

Fig. 13. Qualitative DisasterM3 captioning case for a flood scene. (a) The input query with the corresponding pre- and post-disaster images. (b) Caption produced by Qwen3.5-27B, which identifies the flood but overstates its impact on buildings, including unsupported claims that some buildings are submerged with only their rooftops visible (scores: DAP 3, DDR 2, FC 2). (c) Caption produced by DisasterAgent, which distinguishes inundated roads and farmland from buildings assessed as intact and retains uncertainty for some structures, with selected claims linked to numbered evidence references (scores: DAP 5, DDR 4, FC 5). (d) Ground truth caption.

Fig. 14. Qualitative DisasterM3 captioning case for a wildfire scene. (a) The input query with the corresponding pre- and post-disaster images. (b) Caption produced by Qwen3.5-27B, which misclassifies the event as a mudslide or debris flow and introduces unsupported claims of sediment deposition, altered drainage channels, and restricted road access (scores: DAP 1, DDR 0, FC 1). (c) Caption produced by DisasterAgent, which identifies the fire, describes extensive vegetation loss, and recognizes that the road network remains intact, with selected claims linked to numbered evidence references (scores: DAP 5, DDR 5, FC 5). (d) Ground truth caption.

Fig. 1. Comparison between standard VLM inference and the evidencegrounded reasoning of DisasterAgent. (a) A user query for a disaster impact caption from a bitemporal optical image pair. (b) An existing VLM generates an unverified report and misidentifies the disaster type. (c) DisasterAgent invokes perception tools and attaches inline citations to pixel-level visual evidence, mitigating hallucinations and producing more accurate captions.

Fig. 3. Illustration of the STPG. (a) The Spatial Perception Graph constructs the spatial relationships between diverse geographical targets (e.g., buildings, roads, forests, farmland, and water) within a single phase. (b) The Temporal Evolution Edges establish the cross-phase mappings, explicitly capturing state transitions such as “maintained”, “shrunk”, “expanded”, “transitioned to”, “disappeared”, and “appeared”, while integrating domain-specific damage level assessments (e.g., building damage, road damage).

Fig. 10. Design of the perception tools. (a) Disaster type recognition encodes the pre- and post-disaster images with a shared DINOv3 ViT-L/16, fuses their patch tokens, and predicts one of ten disaster categories together with a confidence score. (b) Building damage assessment segments building instances with SAM3, consolidates them across the two dates, and assigns an instance-level damage label by coverage-aware voting over the masks from ChangeOS or ChangeMamba.

Fig. 11. Qualitative DisasterM3 captioning case for a tsunami scene. (a) The input query with the corresponding pre- and post-disaster images. (b) Caption produced by Qwen3.5-27B, which misclassifies the event as a landslide and introduces unsupported descriptions of slope-related soil and rock movement (scores: DAP 2, DDR 2, FC 1). (c) Caption produced by DisasterAgent, which identifies the tsunami and describes damage to buildings, roads, vegetation, and farmland, with selected claims linked to numbered evidence references (scores: DAP 5, DDR 4, FC 5). (d) Ground truth caption.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems provide a convenient framework for the massive deployment of agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs). It provides a sound framework where agents can interact with existing software to perform actions in an autonomous way. Agentic AI is the new term to denote these AI-based autonomous systems. In real multi-agent systems, agents need to deal with malicious agents some of which can exploit security vulnerabilities to do harm. A memory poisoning attack is an example of exploiting a vulnerability to modify agents knowledge and, thus, affect its behavior. In an agent, there are different types of memory systems (semantic, episodic, and short-term) which have their own characteristics and for which different memory poisoning attacks may be developed. In this paper we focus on semantic memory, we discuss its attack, and mitigation strategies. We introduce private knowledge retrieval and private inference. We propose a signature system in the knowledge base to prevent from undesired manipulation. This should avoid memory poisoning attacks by introducing security by design in the construction of the semantic memory. In our architecture, an agent contains a local Prolog-like inference system (i.e., using Horn clauses to represent knowledge) which accesses an external knowledge base to get the required knowledge. This externally signed knowledge base is accessed privately. We provide different implementations in Python using different privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy (IT-PIR).
bullets: Focuses on attacks that manipulate agents’ semantic memory and alter their behavior.
Uses signed knowledge-base entries to prevent unauthorized or malicious knowledge manipulation.
Combines a local Prolog-like Horn-clause inference system with private access to an external knowledge base.
Describes Python implementations offering privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy via IT-PIR.
Scope is semantic memory; episodic and short-term memory attacks are not addressed.

papers.abstract: Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions in large-scale physical environments. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of the consequences of actions and future conditions, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, an agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with anticipatory reasoning for robust urban navigation. Our central idea is to anchor local decisions in persistent medium-horizon subgoals, assess the consequences of predicted actions before execution, and continually update the reasoning context using actual outcomes. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. We further introduce a predictive world sandbox that uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to forecast world dynamics conditioned on candidate movements. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions under the current subgoal to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.
bullets: Targets the difficulty of translating distant navigation goals into coherent local decisions in large, complex environments.
Maintains persistent medium-horizon subgoals and relevant experience through a navigation memory module.
Uses an action-conditioned world model to predict candidate movement outcomes in a visual sandbox.
A vision-language reasoner evaluates predictions, while real observations update memory and revise actions or subgoals.
Evaluations report stronger gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PreAct-Nav. A shared VLM coordinates Navigation Memory and the Predictive Sandbox through Action Preview, Action Review, Action Execute, and Memory Update. papers.abstract: As multimodal agents accumulate increasingly long interaction histories, effectively retrieving and utilizing past information becomes critical for long-term interaction. Existing memory systems typically rely on semantic retrieval over compressed memories and expose predefined representations, which may miss relevant memories and overlook heterogeneous evidence needs across queries. We introduce \textbf{\hivemem}, a multimodal memory framework that interleaves \textbf{\textsc{H}}or\textbf{\textsc{i}}zontal Memory Expansion with \textbf{\textsc{Ve}}rtical Evidence Composition. For horizontal memory expansion, \hivemem organizes memory episodes into a relational graph using textual and visual anchors, expanding semantically retrieved seeds with related neighbors to recover complementary information. For vertical evidence composition, each retrieved memory retains multiple evidence forms, including compact summaries, captions, grounded visual views, raw images, and interaction history. A lightweight trainable selector independently composes an evidence subset for each retrieved memory, enabling query-adaptive utilization of heterogeneous multimodal information. This two-dimensional design jointly broadens memory coverage and adapts the evidence contributed by individual memories. Experiments across three multimodal memory benchmarks show that \hivemem consistently improves task performance across base models while reducing token consumption by about 90\% compared with the most efficient competing multimodal baselines.
bullets: Addresses missed relevant memories and fixed representations in semantic-retrieval memory systems.
Builds a relational graph of memory episodes using textual and visual anchors, then expands retrieved seeds with neighbors.
For each memory, selects among summaries, captions, grounded views, raw images, and interaction history based on the query.
Across three multimodal memory benchmarks, improves task performance across base models while reducing token consumption by about 90% versus efficient multimodal baselines.

papers.abstract: To address unreliable cross-view association in long-sequence feed-forward dense SLAM, this letter presents V3DSAM, an open-vocabulary semantic dense SLAM system that establishes physical correspondences at both the scene and object levels. The system combines feed-forward geometric estimates from VGGT-SLAM 2.0 with open-vocabulary semantic observations from SAM3. We introduce semantic-geometric dual-scale loop verification, which identifies false loop closures using pixel-level bidirectional reprojection and object-level 3D spatial correspondences, without accessing backbone-internal features. We further propose geometry-anchored persistent instance mapping, which defines physical instances through class-constrained 3D connectivity in an optimized global coordinate system and assigns global IDs without inter-frame identity propagation. The proposed verifier rejects all four false loop candidates in our TUM RGB-D evaluation, while long-sequence ScanNet experiments show improved instance identity consistency. Thus, V3DSAM reduces dependence on internal backbone features and temporal ID propagation for robust long-term cross-view association.
bullets: Targets unreliable cross-view association in long-sequence dense SLAM.
Combines VGGT-SLAM 2.0 geometric estimates with SAM3 open-vocabulary semantic observations.
Uses pixel-level bidirectional reprojection and object-level 3D correspondences to reject false loop closures.
Maps persistent instances via class-constrained 3D connectivity in a globally optimized coordinate system, avoiding temporal ID propagation.
Rejected all four false loop candidates in TUM RGB-D evaluation and improved instance identity consistency on long-sequence ScanNet experiments.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly in mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions. However, reliable manipulation in open-world environments requires robust spatial understanding: the ability to identify targets in complex layouts (spatial reasoning) and adapt to scenes that continuously evolve through interaction (spatial memory). Yet existing embodied benchmarks fall short in evaluating spatial understanding: they often introduce strong visual cues that bypass spatial reasoning, and focus on static scenes that offer little insight into an agent's capacity for spatial memory. To address this gap, we introduce GeoMind, a systematic benchmark for structured spatial understanding through tabletop manipulation. GeoMind comprises 54 evaluated task variants organized around spatial reasoning and spatial memory. It also incorporates a scalable pipeline that automates the generation and annotation of task instances with verified targets and executable interactions. Extensive evaluations across diverse embodied agents reveal their consistent weaknesses in spatial understanding. Our findings highlight that these agents struggle to track identities after spatial changes and convert relational or geometric constraints into executable actions. We release the GeoMind benchmark at https://github.com/Notfound-JH/GEOMIND-benchmark.git.
bullets: Targets gaps in existing benchmarks, including shortcut visual cues and predominantly static scenes.
Covers 54 task variants spanning spatial reasoning and spatial memory.
Uses an automated pipeline to generate and annotate tasks with verified targets and executable interactions.
Evaluations show consistent weaknesses in tracking object identities after spatial changes and translating relational or geometric constraints into actions.
The benchmark is publicly released on GitHub.

papers.abstract: Connected physical systems fuse observations from robots, IoT sensors, and edge-AI modules into a shared account of the world, yet most evaluations score only the final answer or action and cannot tell whether a method attributed the evidence, updated its belief, handled contradictions, and justified its decision. We argue that shared reasoning in Connected Robotics should be evaluated as an evidence-to-belief trajectory, and introduce the Connected Robotics Evidence Graph (CREG) Benchmark to make that trajectory measurable. CREG comprises 350 deterministically generated scenarios across seven regimes (justified revision, belief preservation, relation association, contradiction onset and resolution, stale/delayed evidence, and source reliability), each exposing a normative posterior reference at every evidence prefix, validated by an independent log-odds checker and screened by a blinded expert audit. Nine representation conditions separate relation content from serialization, ordering, and metadata. Evaluating four open-weight instruction models and six transparent fusion baselines yields three findings. First, entity grounding accounts for a substantial part of the weak-model deficit. Second, deleting semantic relations costs 15.3 points of strict belief-state accuracy on relation-dependent scenarios (Holm-corrected p<0.001), but an information-matched structured list outperforms the full graph and shuffling the graph does not hurt: relation content matters where required, while graph serialization confers no consistent advantage. Third, belief accuracy is strongly non-monotonic along the evidence sequence, with mid-trajectory failures that endpoint-only evaluation cannot detect. All scenarios, references, prompts, metrics, and analysis code are released for offline, hardware-free reproduction.
bullets: Introduces 350 deterministic scenarios across seven evidence-update regimes, each with normative posterior references at every evidence prefix.
Tests nine representation conditions to separate relation content from serialization, ordering, and metadata effects.
Finds entity grounding is a major source of weak-model errors, while removing semantic relations reduces strict belief-state accuracy by 15.3 points on relation-dependent cases.
Structured lists can outperform full graphs, and graph shuffling causes no consistent harm, suggesting graph serialization alone provides no reliable benefit.
Belief accuracy is strongly non-monotonic, revealing mid-trajectory failures missed by endpoint-only evaluation; resources support offline, hardware-free reproduction.

papers.abstract: Quadrotors inspecting buildings and tunnels must navigate unknown clutter with a forward-facing depth camera whose limited field of view constrains scene understanding and collision-avoiding navigation. Recent world-model agents learn navigation through imagined experience (e.g., AirDreamer), but remain data-intensive and often lack explicit geometric memory and awareness of what the camera can observe. We propose ScanDreamer, a map-grounded world model that constructs an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose. Our world model, actor, and critic are conditioned on this map, which also defines a geodesic progress reward. Moreover, a forward-cone penalty discourages horizontal motion outside the camera's viewing direction. During imagination, ScanDreamer propagates the quadrotor pose over a frozen map and derives progress and wall-contact signals from the mapped geometry. We train ScanDreamer for 0.8 million environment steps (5.5 h on one GPU) and evaluate it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim over 1560 episodes spanning unseen layouts and parameter ranges. Across three seeds (mean $\pm$ SD), ScanDreamer achieves 96.3 $\pm$ 0.3% success with 3.6 $\pm$ 0.3% collision, compared with 59.6 $\pm$ 3.0% success and 28.8 $\pm$ 2.8% collision for AirDreamer at the same online-interaction budget. Removing the forward-cone penalty increases collisions to 9.9 $\pm$ 3.1%. These results show that combining explicit map memory, map-grounded imagination, and perception-aware motion substantially improves navigation performance and data efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/WANGSHUAIzzzz/ScanDreamer.
bullets: Builds an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose to provide explicit geometric memory.
Conditions the world model, actor, and critic on the map and uses mapped geometry for geodesic progress and wall-contact signals.
Adds a forward-cone penalty to discourage motion outside the forward-facing camera’s view.
In Isaac Sim, it achieves 96.3% success and 3.6% collision across 1,560 episodes, outperforming AirDreamer under the same interaction budget.
Removing the forward-cone penalty raises collisions to 9.9%, highlighting its role in perception-aware navigation.

papers.abstract: Surgical video understanding is an important foundation for intelligent assistance in robot-assisted surgery. Similar surgical views can reflect different actions or procedural stages. Interpreting these views requires access to earlier observations, yet frame-centric prompting leaves this history unavailable. We introduce MemSurg, a framework that remembers surgical observations before reasoning over them. Its structured memory graph stores timestamped entity categories, locations, motion cues, and interaction summaries. Chronological links preserve recent context, while entity-associated links connect recurring observations across the procedure. Task-adaptive retrieval then supplies evidence-grounded prompts for scene and workflow reasoning, supporting both frozen inference and memory-conditioned supervised fine-tuning. Evaluation on robot-assisted prostatectomy and two complementary surgical benchmarks shows a 10.43-percentage-point gain over SurgRAW with GPT-4o. Memory conditioning adds 6.52 points under matched Qwen3-VL-8B fine-tuning, and an inference-time plug-in adds 7.04 points to EndoChat. These results support structured memory as a reusable source of procedural evidence for surgical video understanding. Our code will be publicly released.
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity of similar surgical views that correspond to different actions or procedural stages.
Builds a memory graph containing timestamped entities, locations, motion cues, interaction summaries, and chronological or entity-linked context.
Uses task-adaptive retrieval to generate evidence-grounded prompts for frozen inference or memory-conditioned fine-tuning.
Improves performance by 10.43 points over SurgRAW with GPT-4o, by 6.52 points with matched Qwen3-VL-8B fine-tuning, and by 7.04 points as an EndoChat plug-in.
Evaluated on robot-assisted prostatectomy and two additional surgical benchmarks; code is planned for public release.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses -- runtime scaffolds that wrap an LLM's reasoning loop with tool dispatch, verification, and persistent memory -- have become the standard substrate for deploying LLMs as autonomous agents, as demonstrated by Claude Code and Codex in software engineering. In trajectory planning, however, this paradigm has not taken hold: existing LLM-based trajectory planning methods either keep the LLM in the decision loop, exceeding the millisecond-level control budget, or offload it to offline rules or training-time supervision -- leaving the runtime planner non-evolving. Intermediate hybrids still lack the verification-and-consolidation loop that makes harnesses reliable. We ask: what runtime harness would let an LLM planner meet real-time constraints while self-evolving into a deployable one? We propose REINS, a harness built on three LLM-planner couplings: LLM outputs are (i) grounded to a learned variable-level dynamics model, (ii) verified via calibrated predicates and forward rollout, and (iii) consolidated into an indexed rule memory that serves future scenes in O(log n) without re-invoking the LLM. The harness closes a self-evolution loop: familiar scenes resolve by memory lookup; novel scenes invoke the LLM, whose verified outputs enrich the memory. Without modifying LLM weights, REINS attains 98%+ compliance, nearly 50% collision reduction, and 1.9-4.6 ms latency on simulated and real-world benchmarks at the tactical decision layer, with LLM invocation rate monotonically declining as memory matures. Code: https://github.com/ZhihongCui/REINS
bullets: Targets the tension between LLM reasoning flexibility and millisecond-level trajectory-planning requirements.
Grounds LLM outputs in a learned variable-level dynamics model, then verifies them with calibrated predicates and forward rollout.
Consolidates verified decisions into indexed rule memory, enabling O(log n) lookup without repeated LLM calls.
Reported results include 98%+ compliance, nearly 50% collision reduction, and 1.9–4.6 ms latency on simulated and real-world benchmarks.
As memory matures, familiar scenes increasingly bypass the LLM, reducing invocation frequency.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon forecasting of neural population activity tests whether a model has captured dynamics that remain predictive well beyond the observed history. Prediction quality typically declines as the horizon grows, yet neither short-horizon accuracy nor teacher-forced evaluation, which supplies the true activity preceding each predicted step, reveals how well models sustain predictions from an initial history alone. We compare direct multi-step prediction and autoregressive rollout on spiking recordings across horizons and introduce NeuroHorizon, which pairs event-based spike encoding with a causal decoder for population firing rates. Its hierarchical prediction memory keeps recent predictions at full temporal resolution and compresses earlier ones into segment summaries, giving the decoder both local detail and longer-range context. Under teacher-forced training this memory holds ground-truth activity, whereas during rollout it holds the model's own predictions. To reduce this mismatch, we train with scheduled sampling, progressively exposing the decoder to its own predictions. From 500 ms of macaque motor-cortex activity, NeuroHorizon achieves the highest forward-prediction score among the evaluated autonomous models at all four horizons from 100 to 1000 ms, and its per-bin predictions remain above a mean-firing-rate baseline across nearly the full 1 s window. Complementary experiments on macaque sensorimotor and mouse multi-region recordings show that performance generally increases with model and data size, alongside improved prediction after cross-subject pretraining and fine-tuning. Together, these results clarify how forecasting performance changes across horizons and offer an effective approach to long-horizon forecasting of neural population activity.
bullets: Addresses the gap between short-horizon or teacher-forced accuracy and sustained forecasting from an initial history alone.
Uses event-based spike encoding, a causal firing-rate decoder, and memory that preserves recent predictions while compressing older context.
Scheduled sampling reduces the mismatch between training with ground-truth activity and rollout using the model’s own predictions.
On 500 ms of macaque motor-cortex activity, it achieved the highest forward-prediction score among evaluated autonomous models from 100–1000 ms.
Additional macaque sensorimotor and mouse multi-region experiments indicate gains with larger models/data and cross-subject pretraining plus fine-tuning.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the NEUROHORIZON architecture. A POYO+ event encoder maps observed spike events to history latents. A causal decoder predicts future firing rates bin by bin, attending to both history latents and a hierarchical prediction memory. Figure 2: Per-bin temporal decay of forecasting performance. Panels (a–d) show per-bin fp-bps for prediction horizons of 100, 240, 500, and 1000 ms, respectively, using a 500 ms observation window. All panels report session means with ±1 SEM for TF and RO fp-bps, using 500 ms observation and prediction windows. Parameter counts are shown in millions and exclude neuron and session embeddings.

papers.abstract: SLAM failures remain difficult to avoid in autonomous robotic systems, and undetected failures can propagate to unsafe planning, control, and mission-level decisions. Existing monitoring strategies often depend on prior maps, estimator-internal variables, or redundant sensing, which limits their applicability to deployed and resource-constrained robots. This paper presents a scene-geometry consistency monitor for detecting geometry-manifested SLAM failures using only the geometric output of the SLAM backend. The targeted failures include cumulative drift-induced failures, abrupt misregistration failures, and backend map corruption when they become observable as inconsistency in reconstructed scene geometry. The proposed method represents revisited local regions with recursive latent voxel geometry and evaluates each current observation against a trusted continuation explanation and a weak non-propagated reference explanation. The resulting voxel-wise evidence contrasts are aggregated into a fixed-boundary monitoring signal for online failure declaration and downstream safety response. Experiments on self-collected sequences, GEODE benchmark sequences, multiple robotic platforms, and different SLAM backends show that the monitor responds to failures when they are manifested in backend scene geometry. It achieves 4/4 valid post-onset declarations with no pre-onset alarms on four self-collected sequences, detects geometry-manifested failures in all five corrupted GEODE runs while remaining alarm-free in five geometrically consistent runs, adds only 0.1--0.2\% absolute CPU load, and supports a closed-loop UAV detect--isolate--recover workflow.
bullets: Targets cumulative drift, abrupt misregistration, and backend map corruption that become geometrically observable.
Uses recursive latent voxel representations of revisited regions and contrasts trusted continuation evidence with a weak non-propagated reference.
Aggregates voxel-level evidence into a fixed-boundary online signal for failure declaration and safety response.

Reported experiments achieved 4/4 post-onset declarations without pre-onset alarms on self-collected sequences and detected all five corrupted GEODE runs while staying alarm-free on five consistent runs.
Adds only 0.1–0.2% absolute CPU load and supports a closed-loop UAV detect–isolate–recover workflow.
