papers.abstract: In real homes, assistive robots must repeatedly locate targets from large furniture to tiny tabletop items, as people move objects between household surfaces. Uniformly instantiating detections at different scales as 3D objects can be brittle for small on-surface items; without explicit object-state validation, stale entries may persist after scene changes. Our key insight is to separate persistent 3D furniture entities from revisable surface-object hypotheses, retaining their visual evidence without requiring independent object geometry. We formalize this design as the Hypothesis Scene Graph (HSG), which preserves small-object evidence and supports local revision without rebuilding the stable entity topology. Building on HSG, HSGNav uses this separation for multi-scale lifelong navigation: retrieval selects entity or hypothesis evidence according to target scale, exploration acquires additional surface observations, and verification confirms target presence or invalidates contradicted hypothesis records. Because existing lifelong benchmarks such as GOAT-Bench rarely require mid-episode memory invalidation or multi-scale search, we introduce FAROS-Bench (Find And Re-find Objects across Scales) for mid-episode relocation of surface objects and multi-scale find goals. Experiments show that HSGNav performs competitively on GOAT-Bench while substantially outperforming prior methods on FAROS-Bench.
bullets: Addresses stale memories and brittle 3D representations when small objects move between household surfaces.
Introduces Hypothesis Scene Graphs, preserving visual evidence for surface objects while keeping persistent furniture topology stable.
Uses scale-aware retrieval, exploration for new surface observations, and verification to confirm or invalidate hypotheses.
Introduces FAROS-Bench for multi-scale search and mid-episode object relocation with memory invalidation.
Performs competitively on GOAT-Bench and substantially outperforms prior methods on FAROS-Bench.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of HSGNav. Streaming RGB-D observations build a two-level HSG: persistent 3D entities serve as anchors, while on-surface objects are represented as revisable hypotheses linked to them. SAMR retrieves scale-appropriate visual evidence for the target. When retrieval fails, OCE selects a new observation goal; CGN executes the selected goal, and BDV verifies retrieved targets using fresh views. New observations and SAMR add or enrich hypotheses, while BDV invalidates contradicted descriptions and removes hypotheses with no valid descriptions remaining. Dashed plus and trash icons denote hypothesis updates propagated to the HSG.

Figure 3. Overview of FAROS-Bench. Each episode interleaves static and dynamic find subtasks; the same movable target is queried at steps 1, 5, and 10 with two intervening relocations, while goals span tiny, small, and large scales.

Figure 4. Hypothesis effectiveness. (a) Evidence retention (ERR, ↑) and information omission. (b) Micro BDV confusion matrix and recovery (FRR); D counts erroneous invalidations. (c) Recheck revisit rate (RR) and wasted travel ratio (WTR).

papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts interleave model reasoning with tool calls in persistent workspaces. Scaling these rollouts incurs substantial memory costs for concurrent environments, while slow tool calls delay entire rollout batches. We present BunshinRL, an agentic RL rollout system that exploits shared environment state and recurring tool calls through three techniques: memory sharing across environments, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution. These techniques build on BunshinFork, a novel live whole-workspace forking mechanism for containers. BunshinFork reconstructs process trees, shares memory copy-on-write, and preserves file, communication, and GUI state, enabling cached-state reuse and rollback after incorrect speculation. We implement BunshinRL and BunshinFork through Linux kernel module and CRIU modifications. BunshinRL reduces peak memory by up to 43%, total memory consumption by up to 51%, and end-to-end rollout latency by 23%.
bullets: Targets memory overhead from concurrent environments and delays from slow tool calls.
Combines shared environment state, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution.
Introduces BunshinFork, which supports live whole-workspace forks with copy-on-write memory, preserved state, and rollback.
Implemented via Linux kernel-module and CRIU modifications.
Reports up to 43% lower peak memory, 51% lower total memory, and 23% lower end-to-end rollout latency.

figures.caption: Figure 4. BunshinFork architecture. A brief freeze captures a consistent workspace state. The live fork path reconstructs isolated clones that share unchanged pages copy-on-write and allocate private pages on writes. Retained snapshot holders support asynchronous serialization, allowing the source to resume without waiting for disk writes.

Figure 3. Illustration of BunshinRL. Right shows two samples in a simplified rollout step; left shows the on-disk and in-memory workspace snapshot stores for tool call prefix. Reasoning steps’ generated tool call signatures are matched with the tool prefix tree. All initial matched tool calls are skipped until the first miss in tool signature (Tool 3 for R1 and Tool 4 for R2), at which point the corresponding snapshots are used to reconstruct the workspaces. As C3 is not cached in memory, Tool 3 is replayed for R2 and its delta write is added to the C0+C1+C2 snapshot. The samples execute actual Tool 3 for R1 and actual Tool 4 for R2, creating new delta CoW pages. After these calls finish, speculation starts from the resulting workspaces: Tool 4 for R1 and Tools 5 and 6 for R2. The Spec Tool Selector selects tool calls that are likely to happen from previous tool call history. When a reasoning step finishes, its output tool signature is compared with the speculative tool signature. For failed speculation, the system rolls back to the workspace snapshot before speculation.

Figure 5. Linux Process Fork vs. BunshinFork Process-Tree Fork. Left: native fork() duplicates one process as a child of the source process. Right: BunshinFork creates a sibling container and reconstructs the whole process tree inside an independent namespace.

Figure 1. Shareable Memory in Agentic RL Environments. Share of each environment’s memory that is identical in another environment, split into file cache, heap, and shared memory. The bars compare environments of different tasks with environments of the same GRPO group at step 0 and step 10.

Figure 2. Peak Memory as Rollouts Scale. Peak CPU memory of BunshinRL and CRIU as the number of concurrent rollouts grows. Each CRIU fork holds a private copy of memory, while BunshinRL forks share the memory they have not changed.
Figure 11. Training Reward. Average rollout reward in each OSWorld training epoch for the Base, Full, and Spec configurations of BunshinRL (§5.3).
Figure 10. Hit Rate over Training. Share of tool calls in each OSWorld training epoch served from a cached snapshot or a speculative fork, for the Full and Spec configurations of BunshinRL (§5.3).
Figure 6. Memory over an OSWorld Epoch. Working set of all environments on a node over one epoch of OSWorld rollouts with BunshinRL, CRIU, and AgentENV.

Figure 8. Rollout Completion over Time. Number of rollouts still running over one OSWorld epoch for the Base, Full, and Spec configurations of BunshinRL (§5.3). A batch that drains sooner means higher rollout throughput.
Figure 9. Memory Cost of Environment Reuse. Working set of all environments over one OSWorld epoch for the Base, Full, and Spec configurations of BunshinRL (§5.3).
Figure 7. Memory over a WebArena Epoch. Working set of all environments on a node over one epoch of WebArena rollouts with BunshinRL, CRIU, and AgentENV.
Figure 12. Memory of Forks. Total memory of a source environment and its forks as the number of forks grows, for BunshinFork, CRIU, and AgentENV.

papers.title: BunshinRL: Whole-Workspace Forking for Agentic Reinforcement Learning Rollouts
papers.tldr: BunshinRL accelerates agentic RL rollouts by forking and reusing live container workspaces, reducing memory use and rollout latency.

papers.abstract: LLM agents have made impressive progress in coding and mathematical reasoning, motivating growing interest in learning from long-horizon interaction. Memory supports this process, but plausible lessons can be redundant or reinforce inappropriate actions. Can a memory's source decision provide a practical test for whether to retain it? We localize consequential trajectory steps, extract candidate memories, and replay each source decision with and without its candidate under the same context. This reveals two properties: most candidates barely shift the probed distribution, and both successful and failed source actions can be reinforced or suppressed. These observations motivate Anchor, which tests shift magnitude and source-role alignment before retention. Admitted memories guide later trajectories, enabling experience-driven improvement under a frozen policy. On held-out ALFWorld and WebShop tasks, Anchor improves success rate and mean score by up to 19.9% and 17.2%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline for each backbone. With Qwen3.5-27B, it retains 41% fewer ALFWorld cards than unfiltered retention and outperforms all four WebShop cost-comparison baselines while using fewer tokens.
bullets: Memory candidates often have little effect on action distributions, and successful or failed source actions may both be reinforced or suppressed.
Anchor localizes consequential trajectory steps and replays source decisions with and without each candidate memory.
It retains memories based on both distribution-shift magnitude and alignment with the source action’s role.
On held-out ALFWorld and WebShop tasks, it improves success rate by up to 19.9% and mean score by up to 17.2% versus the strongest backbone-specific baselines.
With Qwen3.5-27B, it retains 41% fewer ALFWorld memory cards and outperforms four WebShop cost-comparison baselines while using fewer tokens.

papers.title: From Reflection to Co-Evolution: Self-Evolving Agents with Locally Verified Memory

papers.abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.
authors: Chen Chen, Omid Bagherieh, Naveen Nikamanth Appiah Balaji, Jesse T. Gonzalez, Negin Heravi, Fahad Islam, Xueting Li, Jean-Baptiste Regli, Kejia Ren, Petr \v{S}vec, David J. Yoon, Matthias M\"uller, Vladlen Koltun
bullets: AMPs adapt actions as tasks unfold and run across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation without task-specific training or demonstrations.
AMP1 achieves 85.6% zero-shot success on RoboLab-120, versus 49.2% for leading VLAs and 42.9% for WAMs.
It succeeds in 104 of 108 real-world trials across twelve tasks and three robot instances, with substantially lower failure rates than specialist baselines.
The agent independently develops behaviors such as searching for hidden objects, using tools, and calibrating cameras.
Persistent memory reduces failure rates on RoboDojo bimanual tasks by 4.6× compared with zero-shot deployment.

(B) Success rate with the basic and assistive harnesses, each model at its more-reasoning setting from A (Sec. 2D.2). The SDK’s functions fall into three groups: sensing, perception, and motion. The task instruction and all sensory input reach the model via the harness. In addition to the interpreter, the model has a number of auxiliary tools, such as viewing a saved image and terminating the episode (not shown for clarity). The memory (shown dashed) is used when learning from experience (Sec. 2C).

Fig. 4. Learning from experience. (A) Example RoboDojo simulation tasks. (B to E) Few-shot learning on the Mahjong task. (B) AMP1+ must push over the three tiles that match the opponent’s tile, take a tile from the stack and stand it at the right end of the row. Practice is run five times per task, and the run that succeeds most often is evaluated. (F) Success rate after k rounds of practice. (G) Number of model calls on successful episodes, relative to zero-shot deployment. (H) Success rate of AMP1+ and the top entries on the RoboDojo simulation leaderboard. (I to K) Continual learning across tasks, from a single run over one random permutation of the tasks. (I) Success rate through continual learning. (J) Number of model calls relative to zero-shot deployment. (K) Per-segment success rates at the end of each segment, colored by whether the segment has not yet been seen (green), was just seen (yellow), or was seen earlier (blue). In (F, G, I, J), shaded bands show 95% confidence intervals across tasks. All evaluations are on unseen layouts.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.
authors: Maxime Burchi, Fayaz Ali Dharejo, Radu Timofte
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of surpassing human performance on tasks requiring long-term memory and planning.
Learns a distinct world model for each episode by updating model parameters at test time, rather than relying only on contextual memory.
Validated across multiple world-model architectures in a simplified 2D Memory Maze setting.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on the 3D Memory Maze benchmark while retaining strong performance on DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

papers.abstract: Memory plays a crucial role in long-horizon task execution and cross-task generalization for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models operating in complex 3D scenes. However, existing VLA memory mechanisms suffer from memory noise, particularly in complex 3D scenes, as stored episodic memories contain extensive redundant details about scene layouts, object configurations, and robot-specific states, which obscure generalizable manipulation principles and hinder cross-task transfer. To address this challenge, we first introduce a hippocampus-inspired memory consolidation mechanism that synthesizes extensive episodic experiences into a compact set of essential semantic memories, enabling VLA models to derive generalizable principles from practical experience. Second, we propose an episodic memory pruning mechanism that removes redundant episodic memories whose contents are captured by consolidated semantic memories, thereby increasing effective memory capacity and improving long-horizon task execution. Finally, to handle complex task scenarios, we develop a flexible memory composition mechanism that jointly leverages multiple episodic and semantic memories to enhance cross-scenario generalization. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus demonstrate the effectiveness of HiMEM across different VLA backbones, improving the average success rate of pi_0 from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.
authors: Boran Zhao, Yanbin Hu, Jun Ye, Zhenxian Hu, Yuxin Zhai, Jin Cui, Pengju Ren
bullets: Addresses noisy, redundant episodic memories that obscure transferable manipulation principles in complex 3D scenes.
Consolidates detailed experiences into compact semantic memories capturing essential, generalizable knowledge.
Prunes episodic memories already represented by semantic memories to increase effective memory capacity.
Composes multiple episodic and semantic memories for more flexible cross-scenario task solving.
Evaluated on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus across VLA backbones; pi_0’s average success rate improves from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.

papers.abstract: Long-term object search requires learning where objects usually appear from repeated but uneven observations of a changing environment. We formulate retrospective open-vocabulary memory as probabilistic inference from censored observations, where the key idea is to reason with evidence per opportunity: a detection or non-detection should influence belief only in proportion to the robot's opportunity to observe the corresponding location. We introduce ECROM, which uses this principle to estimate long-term prevalence for concepts specified only at query time and converts the resulting belief directly into an active-search prior. To evaluate this problem, we introduce a controlled long-term benchmark in ten HM3D homes that independently varies object placement and observation opportunity across repeated traversals. ECROM improves support-level AP on held-out queries by 4.5 points and search SPL by 4.2 points over the strongest competing memory in each metric. The benchmark, dataset, and code will be open-sourced. Project page: https://jiaming.im/ecrom/
bullets: Addresses learning object-location prevalence from repeated, uneven observations.
Models detections and non-detections as censored evidence weighted by observation opportunity.
Supports concepts specified only at query time and converts beliefs into active-search priors.
Evaluated on a controlled benchmark spanning ten HM3D homes with varied placements and observation opportunities.
Improves support-level AP by 4.5 points and search SPL by 4.2 points over the strongest competing memory in each metric.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive driving world models systematically suffer from structural drift, identity drift, and quality decay over long rollout horizons due to transient conditioning signals that lack persistent state. We present WAM-Sim, a driving world model anchored by a persistent hierarchical memory and optimized via online flow-matching RL. WAM-Sim structures persistent context across three temporal and semantic scales: pose-aligned structural tokens encoding persistent road topology, read-only scene tokens supplying geolocated background appearance, and write-once instance tokens preserving individual traffic participant identities across occlusions and chunk boundaries. To restore visual sharpness and physical plausibility degraded by multi-scale conditioning, we introduce an online post-training framework that optimizes self-generated rollouts via flow-matching RL guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a vision-language model physical judge. The invariant memory empirically confines policy optimization within the anchored context, helping suppress semantic collapse and reward hacking, while online RL systematically enforces physical commonsense and fine-grained visual fidelity. On the nuScenes benchmark, WAM-Sim achieves a superior generation fidelity (FID=3.47, FVD=25.72) and strong downstream perception performance (24.16 mAP, 71.23 road mIoU). On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data, WAM-Sim substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, preserving high scene similarity and subject identity coherence across extended horizons. Project page: https://fudan-generative-vision.github.io/WAM-Sim.

papers.abstract: A child who learned to add small numbers adds numbers of any length. LSTMs and Transformers trained on short sequences fail on longer ones. We trace this to what learners read when deciding. A position, count or time takes new values as input grows: it is a coordinate, and a learner that reads one meets in every long input values its experience never covered. Whether two things are the same has the same two answers at every size: it is a coincidence, and a learner that reads only coincidences finds in a long input nothing that short inputs lacked, so finite experience fixes its rule for every size. The memory carries the size of the input and the rule stays finite, and this determines the memory a generalizing brain can have: a memory that grows while what the learner reads of it stays finite has to look the same from every place, so it is made of cycles, and the past is reached by asking what happened when the cycles last stood where they stand now. The cycles are the grid modules, the cells that detect their return the place cells, the records the hippocampal index; a prefrontal controller moves the cycles and never sees them. Reading only coincidences costs no power: what finite experience fixes in such a learner is what Turing machines compute in step with their input, which is why a circuit that evolved to find the way home can learn arithmetic and grammar. In a network of neurons this machine of cycles is the dynamics seen through its symmetry, and symbols are its invariants. Trained on strings up to 40 symbols, the machine solves five benchmark tasks that no LSTM or Transformer solves, among them duplication and binary addition, and beyond the reach of its cycles it fails on the curve the theory predicts. Given larger cycles after training, a machine that saw no string longer than five symbols reverses a string of a million without error. Its controllers run unchanged on neurons.
bullets: Coordinate-like inputs such as positions and counts can exceed training experience, while coincidence-based relations remain size-invariant.
The proposed memory uses cycles whose state grows with input size but is read through finite, symmetry-based observations, linked conceptually to grid cells, place cells, and hippocampal indexing.
Its computational power is characterized as equivalent to Turing-machine computation synchronized with input.
Trained on strings of at most 40 symbols, it solves five benchmark tasks that the abstract reports LSTMs and Transformers do not solve, including duplication and binary addition.
With larger cycles after training, it reverses a million-symbol string despite seeing no training string longer than five; performance fails beyond cycle capacity as theoretically predicted.

figures.caption: Figure 2. One system, three descriptions. (a) The parts of the machine in the brain. (b) The same computation described three times: a Turing machine’s tape is a clock whose cells are records and its head the reading (Theorem 3); a clock is a ring of neurons whose bump stands in one of p wells, read by Π and Q, and a place cell fires where the bump returns (Theorem 4); the finite table, the controller and the prefrontal circuit are one rule. (c) Two rings of Eq. (2), with 5 and 3 wells, under a sequence of moves, and the reading Q ◦Π after each. (d) Place cells recruited as a clock of rings 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 advances: recruitment stops at 2,310 cells when all rings must agree, at 210 or 30 when one or two may differ. (e) A clock released after 40 moves runs back through its last readings by itself (top); above τ/τv adaptation makes a bump travel (bottom). (f) A count is exact up to its clock’s range and then repeats; an estimate reads a graded magnitude. Brain outline adapted from Servier Medical Art, CC BY 3.0.

Figure 1. A learner that reads coincidences. papers.abstract: Lifelong object maps must estimate whether an object remains at its previously observed location after it leaves view. Existing persistence filters rely on class-based survival priors, making them difficult to apply reliably in open-vocabulary settings. We introduce HiPer, a hierarchical persistence filter that derives persistence beliefs directly from data rather than semantic categories. For a new object, HiPer retrieves visually and geometrically similar training instances and estimates an initial survival rate from their observed histories, without requiring class labels. This estimate initializes a conjugate Beta belief over the object's survival probability, which is updated in closed form using detections and missed observations under Rosen's persistence-filter framework. When an object is re-identified at a new location, its persistence belief is transferred with the object, enabling the map to learn object-specific mobility over time. Experiments on 120 held-out simulated sequences show that HiPer consistently achieves the best performance among competing methods. Retrieval-based priors outperform CLIP-derived label priors, and object-specific online learning provides further gains. Results on 47 held-out 3RScan environments demonstrate that the proposed retrieval-based prior also outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in real-world settings.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of predicting whether out-of-view objects remain at their mapped locations in open-vocabulary settings.
Retrieves similar training instances to initialize a Beta belief over each object’s survival probability.
Updates persistence beliefs in closed form from detections and missed observations.
Transfers beliefs when objects are re-identified, enabling object-specific mobility learning over time.
Outperforms competing methods in simulated sequences and held-out 3RScan environments; retrieval priors beat CLIP-based label priors.

papers.abstract: In the real world, mobile manipulation robots must perform complex object interactions and make multi-step decisions, often relying on task-relevant information that is no longer observable. However, existing benchmarks provide limited evaluation of such memory-dependent decision-making in mobile manipulation. To address this gap, we introduce RoboCasa-Mem, a new benchmark comprising nine mobile manipulation tasks that require agents to use interaction history at key decision points. Specifically, the tasks are grouped into two categories of memory: One is environment memory, which captures spatial locations, object attributes, and object relationships. The other is process memory, which captures single-task progress and multi-task scheduling. Particularly, we introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation. For tasks with multiple valid execution paths, instead of fixing a single target or trajectory, the evaluator derives later task constraints from the robot's earlier actions. This allows us to evaluate whether later behavior is consistent with the robot's own interaction history while reducing shortcuts based on fixed target assignments. We provide 1,800 successful demonstrations for policy training. We also develop a baseline on our benchmark, namely Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy(HMAP). Its high-level planner uses structured entity and process memories to generate subtasks. Its low-level VLA controller uses subgoal-conditioned queries to incorporate VGGT-Omega geometry into action generation. Together, RoboCasa-Mem and HMAP baseline support systematic evaluation of memory-dependent behavior and the development of memory-aware mobile manipulation policies.
authors: Sihang Chen, Chen Ye, Wei Chen, Xiaohan Lei, Zhipeng Tang, Sha Zhang, Yuan Zhang, Zixuan Chen, Jiajun Deng, Houqiang Li, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: Introduces nine tasks requiring interaction history at key decision points.
Covers environment memory—locations, attributes, and relationships—and process memory for task progress and scheduling.
Uses Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation to derive later constraints from the robot’s own earlier actions, reducing fixed-target shortcuts.
Provides 1,800 successful demonstrations for policy training and an HMAP baseline with structured memory and subgoal-conditioned control.
Scope: evaluates memory-dependent behavior in mobile manipulation rather than general-purpose memory.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering information that is no longer visible, such as an object's location before occlusion or the order of a demonstrated action sequence. A large vision-language planner can read this history, but calling it before every action chunk is slow and costly. We present a three-tier system for the RoboMME benchmark. GPT-6 Astra (System 2) selects a grounded subtask from stored visual history, a $\pi_{0.5}$ vision-language-action policy (System 1) executes it, and a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B monitor (System 1.5) checks after each action chunk whether the subtask is finished. The instruction is kept until the monitor reports completion or a task-specific event occurs, while the policy keeps acting on new observations. On RoboMME, the system succeeds in 79.13% of episodes with an average of 3.63 Astra calls and 80.84 seconds per episode. This is 34.62 points above the best published non-oracle baseline and 4.95 points below GroundSG+Oracle, which gives the low-level policy ground-truth subgoals.
authors: Bingao Chen, Haoquan Fang, C. Karen Liu
bullets: Addresses the need to remember occluded object locations and demonstrated action order without invoking a large planner before every action chunk.
Astra (System 2) selects grounded subtasks from visual history; π0.5 executes them; a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B monitor detects subtask completion.
The system retains instructions until completion or a task-specific event, while the policy acts continuously on new observations.
It averages 3.63 Astra calls and 80.84 seconds per episode, outperforming the best published non-oracle baseline by 34.62 points.
Performance remains 4.95 points below GroundSG+Oracle, which provides ground-truth subgoals.

papers.abstract: Coding agents powered by models such as GPT-6-Astra connect spatial reasoning with executable robot behavior, raising the question of how such agents can produce lasting improvements in robot capabilities from physical interaction. In this work, we study embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) through real-world exploration, code refinement, and deployment using PyRUA-REAL, a framework in which coding agents retain interaction experience as persistent memory and reusable executable skills that inform subsequent exploration and improvement. Our empirical study places physical manipulation at the center of the improvement process, examining how agents collaborate, what kinds of execution feedback support effective code refinement, and how task specifications and previously acquired skills influence robustness and task transfer. We further investigate the efficiency and capability of the resulting programs when deployed without involving an online agent for decision-making. Across eight real-world tasks, PyRUA-REAL achieves an average success rate of 91.1%. In complementary evaluation on 42 tasks from the RoboDojo benchmark, it achieves an average success rate of 84.4%. This study provides empirical guidance for turning physical exploration into reusable robot skills that support continued improvement and robust, efficient deployment.
authors: Qiang Wang, Jianxin Bi, Shulong Jiang, Ruiyang Si, Wenbo Huang, Kaiqi Chen, Jiaxin Li, Liyun Li, Xuanyi Li, Daquan Zhou
bullets: Studies embodied recursive self-improvement through real-world robot exploration, code refinement, and deployment.
Stores interaction experience as persistent memory and reusable skills to guide later exploration and improvement.
Examines agent collaboration, execution feedback, task specifications, and prior skills as factors in robustness and transfer.
Evaluates deployment efficiency and capability without an online decision-making agent.
Reports average success rates of 91.1% across eight real-world tasks and 84.4% across 42 RoboDojo tasks.

papers.abstract: As agents become more capable, they are moving beyond one-off tasks toward sustained assistance across successive user goals. Such assistance requires agents to discover how unfamiliar environments work, reuse what they learn across tasks, and keep that experience current as environments evolve. Existing benchmarks increasingly study experience reuse and adaptation, but provide limited insight into which parts of accumulated experience agents revise, retain, or lose. To address this gap, we introduce ReScopeBench, a benchmark for the experience lifecycle across 18 interactive environments. It distinguishes structural experience about how an environment is organized and accessed from rule experience about reusable principles and constraints that guide decisions across tasks. To study how experience is acquired, reused, and revised, we propose an experience-first construction approach. It builds task streams around shared experience and introduces silent environmental changes. We evaluate task performance and track changes in saved experience throughout each stream. Across 20 models, we find that retained experience improves task performance, but agents struggle to keep it current as environments change. Even when the required experience is correctly recorded, agents do not always complete tasks successfully. These findings identify selective maintenance and effective use as complementary challenges for long-lived agents.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon consistency is essential for video world models, yet it becomes difficult to maintain once observed content falls outside the context window. Existing memory mechanisms either retrieve history as implicit context, which remains constrained by context capacity and entangles static and dynamic information or consolidate history into explicit global representations, which struggle to model evolving dynamics and accumulate geometric errors. To overcome these limitations, we introduce GROME, a novel factorized memory framework that augments video world models for long-horizon coherence across both static scenes and dynamic entities. GROME operates via three synergistic components: 1) Static-Dynamic Factorization decouples historical evidence into static and dynamic components, preserving static scene geometry and dynamic entity states separately; 2) Local Memory Retrieval selects spatially aligned static history to eliminate geometric drift alongside the latest dynamic entity states to ensure temporal continuity; 3) Training-Free Memory Injection seamlessly grounds the factorized memory into video world models via their native conditioning pathways. Experiments on long-horizon revisit scenarios demonstrate that GROME substantially enhances scene persistence and dynamic entity fidelity over existing methods, all while preserving the visual quality and controllability of the frozen backbone without additional training. Beyond self-rollouts, GROME readily accommodates external observations as plug-and-play memory, unlocking flexible and controllable video continuation and scene exploration.
bullets: Addresses context-window limitations and errors from mixing static and evolving information in video-model memory.
Factorizes history into static scene components and dynamic entity states.
Retrieves spatially aligned static memories and the latest dynamic states to reduce geometric drift and preserve temporal continuity.
Uses training-free injection through the world model’s native conditioning pathways.

Long-horizon revisit experiments show improved scene persistence and dynamic-entity fidelity while preserving visual quality and controllability; it also supports external observations for video continuation and exploration.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of GROME. GROME factorizes historical evidence into static scene and dynamic entity components. Both are retained over extended rollouts as local spatial memories, with the dynamic component further organized by explicit temporal indexing. Given a target camera trajectory, relevant historical evidence is separately retrieved from the static and dynamic components to render references. These static-dynamic references are then injected into the model’s native history-conditioning pathway through a set of training-free injection strategies, conditioning generation together with the local context and user actions. This allows GROME to better preserve consistency over long rollouts while maintaining generation quality and controllability.
Figure 4: Qualitative comparison. GROME better preserves revisit scene structure and entity consistency simultaneously across diverse revisit trajectories compared with existing world models.

Figure 12: Static complex-memory revisit-case 2. The L-shaped explore–return trajectory distributes pose and scene evidence across several views, causing context-based methods to drift or omit content. GROME retrieves complementary static scene evidence through max-coverage retrieval, preserving the revisit scene structure. Red boxes mark representative failures.

Figure 11: Static complex-memory revisit-case 1. GROME retrieves and consolidates local memories to reconstruct comprehensive, high-fidelity static scene references. Red boxes highlight representative inconsistencies in the baselines.

Figure 20: Robustness to imperfect geometric projection. Although rendered historical memories often exhibit geometric artifacts such as disocclusion holes and blur, GROME leverages them as soft spatial guidance rather than rigid pixel-level targets via timestep-aware memory routing. Guided by pretrained world priors, the frozen model corrects moderate rendered distortions and plausibly synthesizes unobserved regions during finer denoising steps while maintaining scene consistency.

Figure 13: Static complex-memory revisit-case 3. Complex camera trajectories create multi-view spatial configurations where different parts of the target view are scattered across disparate historical references, exposing the limits of single-frame retrieval. While maintaining a monolithic global cache often suffers from accumulated drift and high overhead, GROME retains historical evidence as local point clouds and selectively retrieves them under target poses. This strategy synthesizes complementary scene evidence to generate the target view with high-fidelity revisit consistency. Red boxes mark representative baseline failures.
Figure 15: Dynamic complex-memory revisit-case 2.

Figure 14: Dynamic complex-memory revisit-case 1. Explicit-memory baselines overlook dynamic entities during memory construction, freezing them at outdated historical states, whereas context-only generation inevitably loses long-range environmental evidence. By factorizing static structure from dynamic entities, GROME simultaneously preserves background consistency and enables dynamic states to evolve. Red boxes mark representative failures.
Figure 16: Dynamic complex-memory revisit-case 3.

Figure 19: Spatially Grounded Exploration. Additional spatially grounded exploration cases. Each row shows the source evidence, the memory transformation or composition, and the resulting rollout under a novel camera trajectory. This arrangement exposes which visual content originates from each memory region.

Figure 21: Representative failure cases of GROME. (a) At long rollout horizons, appearance and color drift inherited from the frozen backbone can still accumulate despite Reference Value Adaptation. (b) Severe local geometry errors can produce sparse or corrupted warped evidence. Although the pretrained VWM usually tolerates moderate projection imperfections, extreme artifacts may be interpreted as plausible scene content and propagate into the generated frame.

Figure 2: Comparison of memory paradigms. Implicit memory suffers from substantial scenecontent overlap and ambiguous in dynamic states, while explicit memory consolidates historical frames into a global 3D scene but struggles with evolving dynamic entities and accumulated geometric drift. GROME instead factorizes historical frames into static-dynamic memory, preserving both persistent static scene structure and evolving dynamic entities over long-horizon generation.
Figure 5: Qualitative ablation of GROME. Static-dynamic factorization and three injection strategies demonstrate their complementary roles in maintaining static scene and evolving entity states.

Figure 17: Long-horizon qualitative comparison. When historical views leave the finite context, implicit memory and explicit memory-based baselines drift from the scene, while GROME preserves static structure beyond 1,400 frames. On dynamic scenes, factorized memory retains evolving dynamic entities without forcing them to remain in a stale state.

Figure 18: Video-to-Memory Continuation. Additional real-world video-continuation cases. Each row pairs an observed video with a GROME rollout generated along a new camera trajectory. Revisit frames assess retention of previously observed scene content, while novel-view frames show the continuation beyond the input.

Figure 9: DA3 inference scaling with input-frame count. Geometry-estimation cost increases with the active input-window size during initialization. GROME subsequently maintains a fixed sliding window instead of expanding the geometry input with rollout length.

papers.abstract: As embodied agents perform object-goal navigation across residential environments, they accumulate successful experiences whose semantic structure recurs across scenes even when geometric trajectories do not. Reusing such experience is challenging because differences in region naming and observation granularity produce distinct graph representations of similar approaches, while meaningful differences in anchors, branches, and endpoints must stay distinguishable. We introduce HTCE, a homeomorphism-inspired topological framework that canonicalizes and reuses navigation experience. Feature and topology subdivisions characterize representational variations, and their semantically constrained reductions produce comparable semantic sequences and structural signatures while preserving semantic anchors, branching relations, and navigation endpoints. HTCE then retrieves historical successful approaches through subdivision-aware matching as guidance for a frozen vision-language policy. Canonicalization compresses the experience index losslessly, merging 17.7--23.6\% of distinct stored route descriptions while retaining full task performance. Under a single frozen vision-language backbone shared by all compared systems, HTCE attains the best SR and SPL in every setting---59.9\%/31.8\% on HM3D v0.1, 71.0\%/31.5\% on HM3D v0.2, and 46.6\%/16.6\% on MP3D---with SR gains of up to 4.9 points and structured retrieval contributing up to 2.8 SPL points. The code is available in https://github.com/startracker0/htce.git
authors: Xiaoran Xu, Yupeng Wu, Tianyu Xue, Xuanran Dong, Yifan Xu, Xiaoshan Yang, Changsheng Xu

Losslessly merges 17.7–23.6% of distinct route descriptions while retaining full task performance.
Achieves the best reported SR and SPL across HM3D and MP3D settings, with gains of up to 4.9 SR points and 2.8 SPL points from structured retrieval.

papers.abstract: We present a spatial-memory system that enables optical see-through AR glasses to recall earlier physical encounters. The dual-camera prototype combines hierarchical visual acquisition with source-linked storage and staged retrieval. Quality screen-ing, global and regional appearance novelty, and temporal support select monochrome observations for detailed RGB cap-ture. Semantic observations retain links to their source images, allowing retrieval to answer indexed historical questions direct-ly or inspect visual details omitted from scene descriptions. The architecture separates capture acceptance, interpretation out-come, and support for a particular question. This distinction motivates two core control mechanisms: bounded reassessment of familiar views when earlier processing leaves an evidence gap, and retention guided by source dependencies. In a 131.35 s egocentric replay, the implemented acquisition policy selected six RGB views from 648 monitoring observations, while feature extraction ran on 97.7% of observations. These results demon-strate selective RGB acquisition and identify frequent local inference as a remaining cost. Exposure duration and cross-view timing further constrain the evidence preserved from se-lected encounters. The system provides a practical acquisition-to-recall architecture for persistent AR assistance, with explicit boundaries between captured evidence, indexed interpretations, and supported historical claims.
bullets: Addresses persistent AR assistance when historical questions require visual evidence from earlier encounters.
Uses hierarchical acquisition: quality, novelty, and temporal cues select monochrome observations for detailed RGB capture.
Links semantic observations to source images and separates capture acceptance, interpretation, and question-specific support.
Introduces bounded reassessment of familiar views and source-dependency-guided retention.
In replay, six RGB views were selected from 648 observations, while feature extraction covered 97.7%; frequent local inference remains costly.

papers.abstract: In groups, knowledge is distributed among individuals, and how it is brought together depends on social ties. Taking inspiration from how a single mind recalls and reacts to memories and current stimulus, we build a shared memory that does this for a community, prototyped as a social app, SEAM. Members post arbitrary moments; SEAM works out how fragments relate, distills knowledge about the group, and replies in a situated and associative way. Some of these memories act as instructions that can alter how the system behaves, making it programmable by its members. We deployed SEAM to 46 people in a co-located community for two weeks of open-ended use, and ran a follow-up workshop with 14. Members shared their days, interrogated the memory, and instructed it to track routines and run games; replies introduced them to people and subjects they had never encountered. SEAM points towards communities where knowledge finds people.
authors: Keru Wang, Michael Xu, Ken Perlin, Nebojsa Jojic, Andrzej Banburski-Fahey
bullets: Addresses how socially distributed knowledge can be combined and surfaced within a co-located community.
Members post arbitrary moments; SEAM connects fragments, distills group knowledge, and responds in context.
Some memories function as instructions, allowing members to modify the system’s behavior.
A two-week deployment with 46 people and a follow-up workshop with 14 explored open-ended use.
Members used it to share daily life, query the collective memory, track routines, play games, and discover unfamiliar people and topics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: How SEAM handles one post, with an illustrative example rather than a case from the deployment. A post (A) enters both retrieval layers. The relationship layer (B) and the executable layer (C) run the same three steps: plan, retrieve and reflect, looping until each judges it has enough, and both read the same shared memory: a knowledge wiki distilled from past posts, and the archive of posts as submitted. They output reflections on the memory related to this moment, as well as context resolved regarding what actions to carry out and how to carry them out; The reply (D) is composed from both outputs with every claim grounded in the posts backing it, and the post, its follow-ups and the connections learnt are written back (E). Members can also read the knowledge wiki directly and leave a comment on any page, which the consolidation agent acts on at its next pass.

Figure 3: Word clouds of the subjects in the 345 posts: (A) what the poster was focused on sharing, (B) what the system captured from the same post, and (C) what the knowledge wiki recorded. Text size follows the number of posts behind each subject, on a square-root scale within each panel.
Figure 2: The four kinds of post, distributed across each participant’s own posting period.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled fine manipulation capabilities, yet performing tasks that require working memory remains a key challenge. Most existing VLA architectures operate under a Markovian assumption, mapping only the current observation to an action, which leads to failure in non-Markovian environments. Inspired by the human 'inner monologue', we propose Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory (HeLM), a hierarchical VLA framework that maintains task-relevant history in explicit language through factorized event detection and event-triggered memory updates. We evaluate HeLM across 10 non-Markovian real-world tasks with 56 variants, including five newly formulated inter-episode tasks that require persistent context across task boundaries. HeLM improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and achieves 78% subtask success on compositional generalization tasks, while using up to 4.5x less memory and running 2.5x faster than the keyframe baseline at long horizons.
bullets: Addresses failures of Markovian VLA models on tasks requiring working memory and persistent context.
Uses factorized event detection with event-triggered updates to maintain task-relevant language history.
Evaluated on 10 real-world non-Markovian tasks with 56 variants, including five inter-episode tasks.
Improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and reaches 78% subtask success on compositional generalization.
Uses up to 4.5× less memory and runs 2.5× faster than a keyframe baseline at long horizons.

The Low Level Policy (LLP), a pretrained VLA, executes action commands generated by the HLP.

papers.tldr: HeLM enables VLA agents to handle non-Markovian manipulation by storing task-relevant history as hierarchical, explicit language memory.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents that answer questions about their route need a memory of what they saw, and scene graphs are a natural form for it. A vision-language model (VLM) can receive such a graph as text or through a graph encoder, but accuracy alone cannot show whether the graph holds the episode's facts, reaches the model, or is actually relied on. In this diagnostic study, we introduce a graph-swap test for the last of these: each episode is given another episode's graph, and we count how many answers change. On an embodied question-answering benchmark with routes through two to seven rooms, we use it to compare ways of delivering scene-graph memory to a fine-tuned VLM. As text, the memory is used strongly, adding 30 points on route questions. As a graph, it is not, and we trace why: the encoder preserves the information, but standard pooled and late fusion discard it. Giving each node its own input token recovers part of it, a gain of 8.3 points on route questions that the swap test confirms comes from the graph. The test also exposes a shortcut that accuracy hides: when the same facts appear in the text, the model ignores its graph. The test thus offers a cheap check of whether a VLM uses its scene-graph memory, and our analysis points to how that memory should be delivered.
bullets: The study tests whether scene-graph memory is represented, reaches the VLM, and actually influences answers.
It swaps each episode’s graph with another episode’s graph and counts answer changes to measure graph reliance.
Text-based graph memory is strongly used, improving route-question performance by 30 points.
Graph encoders preserve information, but standard pooled and late fusion discard its usefulness.

Giving each graph node its own input token recovers part of the benefit, with an 8.3-point route-question gain confirmed by the swap test; duplicated text facts can cause the model to ignore the graph.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a novel 'graph-swap test' to diagnose whether embodied VLMs actually utilize their scene-graph memory, finding that standard graph encoders often discard information via pooling and identifying a shortcut where models ignore graph memory when text is present.
papers.title: Do Embodied VLMs Actually Use Their Scene-Graph Memory?
papers.tldr: A graph-swap diagnostic shows that embodied VLMs often fail to use scene-graph memory unless graph information is delivered through node-level input tokens.

papers.abstract: AI agents often rely on persistent memory to retain user preferences and operational rules across sessions. However, this capability introduces a new safety risk: malicious instructions from messages, documents, or Web content can be retained in memory and influence future tasks even after the original attack content is removed. Existing attack success metrics, however, fail to capture who is affected and how attacks translate into downstream harm during otherwise normal task execution. We introduce MemHarmBench, a victim-centric benchmark for evaluating cross-session prompt injection in memory-persistent AI agents. MemHarmBench considers three categories of potential victims: users, workspace/project owners, and external stakeholders. Our evaluation first exposes an agent to malicious instructions and tests whether they are retained in memory. We then remove the attack content and initiate a new session with a legitimate task while preserving the agent's memory. We jointly evaluate whether the agent follows the attacker's intent, completes the legitimate task, and exhibits observable execution anomalies. Across multiple agent systems, we find that cross-session attacks can remain behaviorally stealthy: agents often complete tasks normally and exhibit no detectable anomalies while still making critical decisions aligned with the attacker's intent. By connecting malicious memory retention to downstream decisions and affected parties, MemHarmBench provides a systematic framework for exposing safety risks that conventional attack- and task-success metrics may overlook. We publicly release MemHarmBench at https://github.com/Kirito14IT/MemHarmBench.
bullets: Targets cross-session prompt injection in memory-persistent AI agents.
Tests whether malicious instructions persist after the original content is removed and affect a subsequent legitimate task.
Jointly measures attacker-intent adherence, legitimate-task completion, and observable execution anomalies.
Finds that attacks can remain behaviorally stealthy: agents may complete tasks normally without anomalies while making attacker-aligned decisions.
Provides a publicly released benchmark for connecting memory retention to downstream decisions and affected parties.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces MemHarmBench, a benchmark for evaluating cross-session prompt injection in memory-persistent AI agents. This directly addresses memory mechanisms for agents, a key subtopic of Adaptation and Memory, and highlights safety risks in long-term memory retention.
papers.title: MemHarmBench: Evaluating Cross-Session Prompt Injection in Memory-Persistent AI Agents
papers.tldr: MemHarmBench evaluates how malicious instructions retained in an agent’s memory can silently influence later tasks and harm users, project owners, or external stakeholders.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models draw each frame from a memory bank of earlier frames stamped with their capture times. With frames, weights and noise fixed, reversing the timestamps of two views flips the state that generators of two families draw: they take the newest timestamp as the truth. That reading is right as long as states never return. After an agent undoes an action, the newest view of a region is outdated and the only view of the present is older; memories for changing worlds delete that older view, and memories that keep it hand the generator the past. Temporal databases separate when a record is stored from when its content holds, its valid time. ReDate keeps every frame and dates each retrieved token by its valid time, read from the agent's action log. The frozen generator then reads a reverted region as one that has just reached a new state, so ReDate needs no training. We prove that trusting the newest timestamp is right exactly when every current view is dated after every outdated one, that without a view taken after the return only the action log tells a reverted region from an up-to-date one, and that a generator able to draw from its own prediction gains more from re-dating than from deletion when the moved tokens keep little weight. After an undo, ReDate raises the share of FAR's steps showing the current state from 0.36 to 0.62 and HY-WorldPlay's from 0.003 to 0.19. We also propose a calibrated state metric to test any memory after undos.
bullets: Problem: Using the newest capture timestamp as truth fails when an agent reverses an action and the current state is represented by an older frame.
Method: Retain all frames and re-date retrieved tokens using valid times inferred from the agent’s action log.
Theory: Newest-timestamp selection is correct only when all current views are newer than all outdated views; after a return, the action log may be essential.
Results: After undo, current-state coverage rises from 0.36 to 0.62 for FAR and from 0.003 to 0.19 for HY-WorldPlay.
Scope: Re-dating is especially beneficial when moved tokens receive little weight, and the paper introduces a calibrated metric for evaluating memory after undos.

papers.selection_reason: Valid-time memory mechanism for interactive video world models after action undos; directly targets action-conditioned world generation and embodied memory.
papers.title: Old Is Not False: Valid-Time Memory for Interactive Video World Models
papers.tldr: ReDate improves interactive video world models after undo actions by assigning memory tokens their valid state time rather than their capture time, requiring no retraining.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied manipulation requires policies to act on information that is no longer visible. Modified objects may leave the field of view, while completed subtasks continue to constrain future actions. Existing approaches extend temporal context through recurrent state updates, test-time training, or storage and retrieval of past observations. As horizons grow, these mechanisms can still leave the policy to infer task state from long, redundant, and viewpoint-dependent visual experience. We argue that long-horizon agents benefit not merely from remembering more, but from remembering task-relevant state changes and progress. We propose Memory of Object States and Task Progress (MOST), a policy-internal memory framework that compresses multi-view observations into temporal tokens. Historical and predictive future tokens are explicitly supervised with object states and subtask progress, structuring memory around what has changed in the world and what has already been accomplished. The resulting memory directly conditions action generation within a single end-to-end policy, without an external planner or retrieval stage. We further introduce RoboCasa-Long, a benchmark of multi-minute, multi-stage mobile manipulation tasks. Across RoboCasa365, RoboCasa-Long, and real-world robot experiments, MOST consistently outperforms Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (XR-1), the previous state-of-the-art model. It raises average success from 65.9% to 72.1% on RoboCasa365, average maximum task progress from 20.83% to 42.22% on RoboCasa-Long, and real-world success from 6.66% to 43.33%. MOST also outperforms a matched visual-history memory variant, showing that effective long-horizon memory depends not only on how much experience is retained, but on whether it preserves decision-relevant progress and world-state changes.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of acting on modified objects and completed subtasks that are no longer visible.
Compresses multi-view observations into temporal tokens representing historical object states and predicted future task progress.
Uses these tokens to condition action generation within a single end-to-end policy, without an external planner or retrieval stage.
Introduces RoboCasa-Long, a benchmark for multi-minute, multi-stage mobile manipulation.
Reports gains over XR-1 and a matched visual-history memory variant across simulation and real-world experiments.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Memory Expert architecture. Historical multi-view observations are encoded into history tokens, and future queries are appended to form the memory sequence. The sequence is processed with block-causal self-attention and conditioned on the instruction through cross-attention. During training, each token predicts its subtask and the state of every relevant object. The output of each Memory Expert layer conditions the corresponding Action Expert layer.

Figure 2: MOST overview. MOST integrates a Vision Language Model, a Memory Expert, and an Action Expert within one end-to-end policy. The Vision Language Model encodes the current observation and instruction. The Memory Expert represents sampled history as object states and task progress, and the Action Expert uses both contexts to generate continuous actions. Task-state supervision is training-only.

papers.tldr: MOST improves long-horizon mobile manipulation by remembering object-state changes and task progress rather than retaining redundant visual history.

papers.abstract: A robot's next action can depend on recent motion or earlier visual evidence absent from its current observation. A recurrent visual-memory architecture can retain this history in a visual state, but its usefulness depends on what the state represents and how it is updated with new observations. We introduce Prediction-Regulated Memory (PREM), a framework that uses action-conditioned future prediction to guide both memory learning and updating in vision-language-action policies. During training, predicting future visual features provides temporal supervision for memory learning. During execution, PREM compares current visual features with the prediction made at the preceding decision and uses the spatially normalized prediction discrepancy to regulate updates to the visual state at each spatial location. The updated visual state supplies temporal context for action generation alongside current observations. Built on $π_{0.5}$, PREM improves average success rate from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO dynamic manipulation tasks and from 14.4% to 83.8% on the RMBench M(1) memory-dependent setting. Further evaluations on LIBERO and LIBERO-Pro show improvements in general manipulation and robustness to spatial perturbations. PREM incurs a mean inference overhead of 7.7 ms on a single NVIDIA H800 GPU.
bullets: Addresses the need to retain motion history and earlier visual evidence missing from current observations.
Trains memory with temporal supervision from predicted future visual features.
At execution, uses spatially normalized prediction discrepancies to selectively update the visual state.
Improves success from 9.63% to 20.74% on DOMINO and 14.4% to 83.8% on RMBench M(1).
Also improves general manipulation and spatial-perturbation robustness, with 7.7 ms mean inference overhead on an NVIDIA H800.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Motivation and overview of PREM. (A) Current observations alone can miss recent motion and earlier task-relevant visual evidence. (B) PREM uses future prediction to supervise memory learning and prediction discrepancy to regulate visual-state updating. (C) PREM improves general manipulation, dynamic manipulation, and memory-dependent manipulation.

Figure 2: PREM architecture. (A) PREM compares the cached prediction with observed visual features at each spatial location to compute prediction discrepancy. (B) The spatially normalized discrepancy regulates how much of the candidate visual-state update is incorporated. (C) An actionconditioned predictor predicts the next visual features from the incoming visual state, observed visual features, and latent action representation. The prediction objective supervises memory learning. The cached prediction provides a reference for subsequent visual-state updating.

Figure 4: Prediction discrepancy and visual-state updating. A temporal prediction-discrepancy curve and visual-state update maps are shown for a successful LIBERO rollout. Spatial responses concentrate around the gripper and manipulated object near bowl grasp (c) and bowl placement (f).
Figure 5: Representative successful rollouts on LIBERO. The rows show LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, LIBERO-Goal, and LIBERO-10, respectively.
