papers.abstract: Before foraging, desert ants perform learning walks (LWs) to acquire visual memories around their nest. With experience, these walks expand, become straighter, and contain fewer visual scans. We previously proposed a model in which these behaviours emerge from the angular mismatch between path integration (PI) and a mushroom-body-inspired visual compass (VC). Here, we test whether this mechanism can generate learning walks on a physical robot, despite the sensory and motor noise inherent to real-world conditions. We implement the model on a four-wheeled robot equipped with a panoramic camera, an IMU and wheel encoders providing compass and stride information for PI, and test it outdoors using a replicated desert-ant experimental setup. The PI--VC mismatch regulates walking speed, turning, pirouettes, and returns to the nest, while PI provides a teaching signal for visual learning. The robot autonomously decides when to acquire visual memories, while its behaviour gradually shifts from exploration towards foraging as visual learning progresses. The robot reproduces desert-ant LW features, including expanding and straightening trajectories, decreasing pirouette frequency, and improved visual homing. These results demonstrate that a simple error-driven mechanism can generate key features of learning walks under real-world conditions, supporting its plausibility as an explanation for active visual learning in desert ants. More broadly, this work illustrates how physical robots can be used to test biological models.
bullets: Learning walks emerge from angular mismatch between path integration and a mushroom-body-inspired visual compass.
The mechanism controls speed, turning, pirouettes, nest returns, and visual-memory acquisition.
Implemented on an outdoor four-wheeled robot with a panoramic camera, IMU, and wheel encoders despite real-world noise.
The robot reproduced expanding and straightening paths, fewer pirouettes, and improved visual homing as learning progressed.
Results support the mechanism’s plausibility as an explanation for active visual learning in desert ants and demonstrate physical robots as tools for testing biological models.

figures.caption: Fig 2. Experimental reproduction of Fleischmann et al. [12]. Photograph of the robot in the foreground, with the three white cylinders reproducing a scaled-up version of the experimental layout of Fleischmann et al. [12], near the Library Square at the University of Sussex. The sky was cloudy. The grass is unusually yellow due to the summer 2026 drought. The buildings in the background provided prominent visual landmarks compared with the largely featureless Tunisian desert environment used by Fleischmann et al. [12].

Fig 3. Robot point of view through the Pixpro SP360. (A) Raw 100×100 px fisheye image. (B) Unwrapped panoramic view of the image in A. The upper 90◦, containing mostly sky, were excluded to reduce the influence of the sky and moving clouds on the visual-compass input. The three cylinders are visible but remain small relative to the surrounding landmarks such as trees and buildings. (C) Raw fisheye image acquired at the same orientation as A, but from a different position, twenty minutes after A. Distant background landmarks remain unchanged, whereas the nearby cylinders shift substantially. The clouds have also moved relative to A. (D) Unwrapped panoramic view of the image in C. Comparison of B and D also shows that the camera was not fully stabilized in pitch as the robot moved over uneven terrain. This can be seen as the yellow grassy ground is neither flat nor forming a similar horizon in B and D. Unfortunately, we did no record tilt and roll data (which the IMU had access to), so we could not plot camera pose data.

Fig 6. All consecutive LWs of two agents. (A) All consecutive LWs for agent 2. Eight walks were recorded, each shown in a different color (blue for the first walk, orange for the second, etc.). The 6 m radius around the nest is indicated by a grey dashed circle. The first two LWs remain close to the nest. Subsequent walks are more directed and extend beyond the 6 m radius, and are therefore labelled as foraging walks. The plotted area is a 24× 24 m square. (B) Another example of a series of consecutive LWs, for agent 4. Nine walks were recorded. Cylinders as white dots.

Fig 4. Top view of all 44 learning walks (A) and 54 zero-vector visual homing tests (B) conducted across the six trials. The plotted area spans 60 m in longitude and 40 m in latitude, with the longest LW reaching 27.32 m from the nest. Colours are used only to distinguish the trajectories and have no additional meaning.

Fig 5. (A) Example of two consecutive LWs performed by a single agent. First LW in blue and second in green. Each arrow represents the robot’s heading at 100 ms intervals. Red arrows indicate the robot’s heading during snapshots. Nest position as a white star. Cylinders as white circles. The background is a 50% whitened Google Earth image of the experimental site. (B) Example of two consecutive ZV visual homing trajectories from an experienced agent. Seventh test in blue, eighth in green. Tests started 12 meters south-east of the nest (red dot mark). Both visual searches are centered roughly on the nest. Scale differs between A and B.

Fig 10. Pirouette and snapshot statistics. (A) PI angular error relative to the ground-truth nest direction provided by GNSS. (B) Distribution of snapshot headings relative to North, showing an approximately uniform distribution. (C) Distribution of snapshot headings relative to the nest direction, also approximately uniform. (D) Angular interval between consecutive snapshots, with two peaks around −65◦ and +65◦. (E) Distance of snapshots from the nest. Most snapshots, and therefore most pirouettes, occurred within 5 m of the nest. (F) Inter-pirouette time interval averaged across LW1 and LW2, with a peak around 7 s.

Fig 7. Changes in LW behaviour with increasing experience. Measurements are shown for the first four LWs, with all subsequent walks grouped as 5+. (A) Maximum distance from the nest increased approximately threefold between the first LW and the 5+ group. (B) Total distance travelled increased across LWs. (C) LW duration remained broadly similar, with a slight increase across walks. (D) Path straightness doubled between the first LW and the 5+ group. (E) Pirouette frequency decreased two-fold. (F) Number of pirouettes performed within a 6 m radius of the nest, following the same criterion [33], decreased twofold. (G) PI–VC angular error, which control learning behaviours, decreased across LWs (H) Proportion of foraging walks (> 6 m from the nest), increased and reached a plateau by the third LW. (I) Forward driving speed of the robot during successive LWs in meters per seconds.

Fig 11. Comparison of scanning-bout timing in ants and robotic learning walks. (A, B) Distribution of interbout intervals during the first (A) and second (B) learning walks of ants, digitized from Deeti and Cheng [7], with mean intervals of approximately 2.15 and 2.45 s, respectively. (C) Mean time of successive scanning bouts in ants, with linear regression slopes of 2.16 and 3.87 s/bout for LW1 and LW2, respectively (R2 = 0.98 and 0.99). (D, E) Distribution of inter-pirouette intervals during the first (D) and second (E) learning walks of six robotic agents, with mean intervals of 6.31± 1.01 s (n = 70) and 7.16± 1.35 s (n = 71), respectively (mean ± SD). (F) Mean time of successive robotic pirouettes, with regression slopes of 6.29 and 7.13 s/bout for LW1 and LW2, respectively (R2 = 0.9998 and 0.9995). Error bars in (C) and (F) represent SD. Data in (A–C) were approximately digitized from Deeti and Cheng [7].

Fig 12. PI search error after LWs. (A) PI search locations after the 44 LWs. Red dots indicate the positions at which the PI search started, the black star indicates the true nest position, and the black cross indicates the centroid of the search locations. Grey lines show the trajectories produced when the robot was manually driven from the PI search position back to the nest. The background is a 50% whitened Google Earth image of the experimental site. The plotted area is 16× 16 m. (B) Percentage of snapshots for which the angular error between the PI-estimated nest direction and the GNSS-derived ground-truth exceeded 90◦, for four distance bins from the nest. (C) Absolute angular error between the PI-estimated and GNSS-derived nest directions for the same distance bins. Only measurements with GNSS horizontal accuracy below 10 cm were included in B and C. Average angular error decreased with higher distance to the nest.

Fig 15. Relationship between prediction variance and visual-compass accuracy on the robot. (A) Absolute angular error of the centroid of 10 consecutive raw visual-compass predictions (1 s of sampling), relative to the ground-truth nest direction derived from GNSS position. During these 1-s windows, the maximum angular spacing between headings was 54.31◦ ± 20.63◦ (mean ± SD), with a maximum of approximately 100◦, while the maximum linear spacing between sampled positions was 0.287± 0.212 m, with a maximum of approximately 0.8 m. Only LW3 and subsequent LWs were included, excluding LW1 and LW2. Mean centroid error increased monotonically with circular variance, from 20.42◦ in the lowest-variance bin (0–0.1) to 83.32◦ in the highest-variance bin (0.9–1.0). Prediction variance was positively correlated with centroid error (Spearman’s ρ = 0.358, p < 0.001), with a linear R2 = 0.167 and mutual information of 0.113 nats. Error bars show standard deviations, which increased with variance. The variability in all variance bin was quite high, hence the low correlation and low predictability despite a clear trend on average. (B) Frequency distribution across all the one-second prediction samples across circular-variance bins. Low-variance samples were more frequent. The positive correlation between prediction variance and angular error suggests that the variance of successive visual-compass predictions could serve as a proxy for prediction accuracy, providing a confidence or reliability signal. This could be used to weight visual-compass predictions against PI, or to distinguish familiar from unfamiliar locations. Unlike the visual familiarity or novelty signals commonly derived from MBON activation in visual-compass models [1, 34, 41, 48], this signal would reflect the consistency of successive directional predictions rather than the familiarity of the visual input itself.

Fig 1. Robot platform. Photograph of the custom-built robot used in the experiments. To give an indication of scale, the wheels are 27 cm in diameter and the top-mounted panoramic camera is positioned 29 cm above the ground. The two HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensors used for obstacle avoidance are visible at the front of the robot, on the right side of the image. See Section 6.1 for a full description of the platform.

Fig 8. Visual homing tests performance at different levels of experience. (A) Heatmap of all naive test trajectories. Cylinders as white dots, nest position as a white start. Grid size is 4 m by cell. Test start position as a red dot. (n = 6) (B) Heatmap of all homing tests from long-LW agents. Searches remain spread out, but are clearly centred on the nest. (n = 23) (C) Heatmap of all tests from foraging agents (n = 25). Trajectories are more directed and searches are more tightly centred on the nest. Long LWs data not shown. (D) Centroid distance to the nest during visual homing tests as a function of test ID. Search centroids were farther from the nest during early tests and became progressively closer after successive LWs, showing improved homing performance with experience.

Fig 9. Influence of the cylinders (A) Search behaviour was affected by the position of the cylinders. The agent was trained using cylinders positions shown in blue. Control tests shown in blue. All tests were conducted with an experienced agent which performed seven LWs prior to the tests. The orange trajectory shows the search after the cylinders were shifted 4 m to the northwest. The orange, shifted configuration was used only during tests. The search centre shifted in the same direction as the cylinders, showing that they strongly influenced visual homing. This is reminiscent of the classic landmark-displacement experiment of Tinbergen [42], in which shifting landmarks around a wasp nest displaced the subsequent search. (B) Nevertheless, the cylinders were not the only landmarks available to the agent. When they were removed, the agent was still able to perform a tight search centred near the true nest position, indicating that other visual landmarks, such as trees and buildings, could also support homing.

Fig 14. GNSS horizontal accuracy. (A) Horizontal accuracy over time for agents 1–4, tested on 15 August 2026. Each line corresponds to a LW (blue) or visual homing test (red). Most measurements were below 5 cm and nearly all below 20 cm; the worst was approximately 2 m. (B) Distribution of horizontal accuracy across the four GNSS statuses for agents 1–6. Blue (left flattened box): RTK fixed; orange: RTK float; green: no RTK; red: bad GNSS fix. Accuracy was high for RTK fixed and RTK float states, ranging from very precise in RTK fixed ( 1.4 cm) to unusable in bad GNSS fix (>10m). (C) Horizontal accuracy for agents 5 and 6, tested on 16 August 2026. Accuracy exceeded 2 m in four walks and even reached up to 33 m. One walk showed sustained poor accuracy above 2 m. (D) Proportion of recording time spent in each GNSS status. Agents 1–4 (left), tested on 15 August, spent almost all recording time in RTK fixed or RTK float states. Agents 5–6 (right), tested on 16 August, spent more time without RTK and nearly 1% of the data was completely unusable due to bad GNSS fix.

papers.title: Emergent Control of Ant Learning Walks in a Mobile Robot
papers.tldr: A physical robot using a path-integration–visual-compass mismatch autonomously reproduces key desert-ant learning-walk behaviors and transitions toward foraging.

papers.abstract: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.
authors: Shengguang Wu, Suning Huang, Cherie Ho, Ria Doshi, Hao Zhu, Serena Yeung-Levy
bullets: Addresses the costly, manual redesign of agent harnesses for new robots and benchmarks.
A coding model observes rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness over optimization episodes.
Evaluates evolved harnesses on held-out scenes and tasks, improving average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks.
Automatically discovers strategies such as clearing jammed arms, approaching obstacles horizontally, and reusing grasp-depth experience through persistent memory.
Benefits are strongest when the benchmark differs substantially from the policy’s training data; scope is demonstrated across multiple benchmarks and policies.

papers.title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
papers.tldr: RoboArchitect automatically improves frozen robot policies by evolving their control harness and persistent memory, substantially boosting manipulation success without updating model weights.

papers.abstract: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks present a challenging routing environment due to rapidly changing topology, traffic, and link conditions. Existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) routing methods typically rely on current observations and information encoded in network weights, limiting their ability to exploit successful past experiences. We propose RAMA, a retrieval-augmented multi-agent DRL framework with Approximate Information State (AIS), in which each satellite combines its local observation, recent routing history, neighboring state information, and retrieved entries from a per-satellite episodic memory. Retrieved experiences are integrated through a Transformer-based decision network trained with AIS-based auxiliary objectives. With weights frozen in a 140-satellite Kepler constellation, RAMA reduces mean end-to-end latency by 13.4% and 99th-percentile latency by 66.7% relative to the state-of-theart double deep Q-network (DDQN) routing method, mainly by avoiding long detours. Updated online, RAMA remains stable while DDQN degrades. On the 1,584-satellite Starlink shell 1, the reduction in mean latency grows to 93.2%, and updating RAMA online lowers its mean latency by a further 25.5%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented memory for scalable decentralized routing in LEO satellite networks.
bullets: Addresses rapidly changing topology, traffic, and link conditions that limit observation-only DRL routing.
Uses per-satellite episodic memory, local and neighboring state, recent routing history, and a Transformer-based decision network.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative foundation models have expanded the capabilities of embodied AI, enabling increasingly general navigation, manipulation, and long-horizon task execution. However, effective interaction with dynamic environments requires more than only strong perception and reasoning: agents must act with partial knowledge and retain, retrieve, and update information from past observations, actions, and experiences. This survey examines embodied memory as a mechanism for preserving decision-relevant information beyond the current observation. We organize existing approaches along two complementary dimensions: six fundamental memory requirements, spanning world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance, and experiential learning; and eight architectural categories, including recurrent states, fast weights, visual and symbolic representations, spatial memory, and experience-based systems. We analyze their capabilities and limitations, and examine how existing benchmarks evaluate memory-dependent behavior, distinguishing genuine use of historical information from general task performance. Finally, we identify open challenges in selecting relevant experiences, maintaining consistent beliefs in changing environments, and consolidating knowledge across episodes. Our analysis provides a framework for understanding memory as an essential component of reliable, adaptive, and lifelong-horizon embodied intelligence.
authors: Siqi Li, Ziyi Bai, Xinrun Xu, Tinglei Huang, B\"orje F. Karlsson
bullets: Defines six requirements for embodied memory, including world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance, and experiential learning.
Categorizes methods into eight architectural families, such as recurrent states, fast weights, visual/symbolic representations, spatial memory, and experience-based systems.
Reviews benchmark practices for distinguishing genuine use of historical information from general task-solving ability.
Highlights open challenges in retrieving relevant experiences, maintaining consistent beliefs, and consolidating knowledge across episodes.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal foundation models exhibit strong perception, reasoning, and in-context learning capabilities, but translating these capabilities into physical action remains challenging. Through real-world experiments across diverse manipulation tasks, we find that ChatGPT-6-Astra, a state-of-the-art general-purpose reasoner, can serve as a physically actionable, context-responsive manipulation policy, demonstrating effective fine manipulation and spatial reasoning. Building on these findings, we introduce LEXP, a harness for learning from physical experience through context-space adaptation. LEXP combines task-level planning with an experience module that interprets execution evidence, extracts and retains lessons with applicability conditions, and reuses relevant lessons to generate contextual feedback for subsequent actions. Model weights and the action interface remain fixed throughout. Across 12 real-world manipulation tasks, LEXP achieves $23/36$ successful trials (63.9\%), compared with $19/36$ (52.8\%) with memory alone and $2/36$ (5.6\%) for vanilla Astra. On three tasks, bread transfer, sort trash and toiletries, and retrieve drawer, removing planning reduces success from $7/9$ to $4/9$, while removing retained experience reduces it to $3/9$. Execution traces illustrate feedback-guided corrections and cross-episode reuse of an inspection strategy. Execution analyses illustrate how task structure and experience-derived feedback guide task progression, action correction, and experience reuse. These results support context-space adaptation as a practical mechanism for turning physical interaction into reusable guidance for robotic manipulation.
authors: Yihan Zeng, Yisu Li, Kaixin Huang, Marc WuDunn, Amelia Kovacs, Mikael Harseno, Kimmy Lin, Porter Hunley, Fred Shentu, Philipp Wu, Zhongyu Li, Zike Yan

Across 12 real-world tasks, LEXP succeeds in 23/36 trials, compared with 19/36 using memory alone and 2/36 with the unmodified policy.

papers.abstract: Giving embodied agents the freedom to act autonomously, initiate interactions, and understand their surroundings through experience is a step toward bringing them to life in the physical world. Realizing this vision requires action, interaction, and memory to work together, so that each encounter can inform current decisions and contribute experience for future tasks. We present EvoLife, a unified navigation harness that enables a multimodal embodied agent to choose how to move, when to ask, and what experience to carry forward. Its hybrid action space supports waypoint navigation, local discrete adjustments, pixel-based navigation, and object-directed navigation. Active interaction allows the agent to seek clarification or assistance when it encounters ambiguity or difficulty, while persistent spatial memory binds observations and dialogue to places, retaining useful experience to guide subsequent visits. We evaluate eight benchmarks across four task families: vision-language navigation, object navigation, interactive instance navigation, and continuous multi-task navigation. With an average of only 1.87 active interactions per episode, our method achieves a first-visit success rate (SR) of 100% across four 100-episode sets spanning vision-language navigation and object navigation. Complete-sequence SR reaches 98% on 50 LHPR-VLN sequences and 94% on 50 GOAT-Bench sequences. In the R2R revisit setting, success weighted by path length (SPL) increases from 82.23% to 93.31% with retained experience. Multi-day physical navigation further demonstrates exploration, proactive help-seeking, and revisiting remembered places. Together, these results advance the vision of bringing embodied agents to life through autonomous action, proactive interaction, and the accumulation and reuse of experience.
bullets: Supports waypoint, discrete local, pixel-based, and object-directed navigation actions.
Lets agents ask for clarification or assistance when facing ambiguity or difficulty.
Stores observations and dialogue by location to improve future visits.
Evaluated across eight benchmarks spanning four navigation task families and multi-day physical navigation.
Reports strong performance, including 100% first-visit SR across four 100-episode sets and improved R2R revisit SPL from 82.23% to 93.31%.

The navigation agent actively generates a question, while an independent multimodal guide generates a natural-language response based on the navigation instruction, current observations, target information, and reference route. The figure illustrates the current and target views, reference route, and spatial relationships between the agent and the destination. Only the generated natural-language response is returned to the navigation agent, which independently makes subsequent decisions. This process simulates natural human-to-human interaction, providing navigation guidance through directions, landmarks, and spatial relationships.

In Task 1, the robot navigates from room 625 to the elevator on the opposite side of the floor, recording key locations along the route. In Task 2, the robot returns to room 625 using persistent memory and actively requests human assistance when encountering a closed door. In Task 3, the robot identifies and restores the matching saved map on the following morning and navigates to the glass office visited the previous day. The three trajectories are visualized in a shared coordinate frame, demonstrating active interaction, adaptation to environmental changes, and cross-day memory reuse.

papers.abstract: An agent deployed in a single body cannot learn how fast that body wears, because every trial that would reveal its wear resistance wears the body it would protect. We study this \emph{epoch-one} setting, in which the parameters of a fixed-weight policy are set before the body is drawn and never updated in life. The agent carries a load-gated nociceptive channel and a memory that retains what was felt. We prove that felt cost moves the allocation to the best-\emph{paid} work not yet felt rather than the gentlest, that an agent without retention never sees the felt-cost constraint bind, and that the channel pays only where the threat is individually unpredictable, cheap to avoid and expensive to ignore. We measure per body, setting the agent with channel and memory against the same individual without them, where neither carries a schedule learned across lives. On $2{,}000$ simulated floor-layer knees, with wear anchored to published loss rates, feeling, retaining and substituting extends the working life from age $55.2$ to $59.6$ and raises career output from $33.7$ to $36.1$. $69.3\%$ of bodies gain and \textbf{none lose}. A body that feels but retains nothing past the day gains one of the $+4.4$ years, and retention carries the rest. A population-trained agent gains $+0.65$ years from the same channel at $-0.54$ output. The difference is what a species prior already supplies, and a single body has none. The two are related by an identity, the ablation mean reporting $(1-χ)$ of the per-body value with $χ$ the share a blind schedule already captures, so we report both. Where the regime map predicts value, a care robot sextuples its certified service life and a field-anchored fleet writes off $0.15$ of its machines instead of $0.55$. Where it predicts none, a rover gains little over blind caution, so the map holds in both directions.
bullets: Studies the “epoch-one” setting: policy parameters are fixed before deployment and cannot be updated across life.
Combines a load-gated nociceptive channel with memory of experienced costs to guide work allocation and avoidance.
Across 2,000 simulated floor-layer knees, the full agent extends working life from 55.2 to 59.6 and career output from 33.7 to 36.1; 69.3% of bodies benefit and none lose.
Memory provides most of the benefit: feeling without retaining adds 1 of the 4.4 years gained, while retention supplies the remainder.
A regime map predicts where nociception helps, with reported gains in care robots and field fleets but little benefit for rovers in regimes favoring blind caution.

papers.abstract: Long-context models repeatedly solve closely related retrieval problems. Attention or global retrieval can retain large stores, but each forward pass again searches for what matters. Recurrent compression avoids this search only by deciding earlier what information to preserve. Neither mechanism directly exploits that useful memories at neighbouring retrieval steps may substantially overlap. We propose an alternative in which retrieval is a persistent local traversal through an address space. We separate a memory's content from its address. Utility is defined by the information revealed by retrieving the content, while geometry determines only how cheaply that information can be reached. This leads to a cost-regularised indexing objective that preserves information value inside local neighbourhoods while charging for every memory made locally accessible. Its marginal-value form gives both attractive and exclusion pressures. Thus, complementary memories should be co-retrievable when the additional value exceeds retrieval cost, whereas redundant memories should not occupy the same retrieval set solely because they are individually useful. As a proof of principle, we test only the simplest fixed-geometry instance on MiniGrid Memory. A persistent local traversal head reaches $0.95$ mean return after $0.59$M training steps with a five-token context, compared with $0.94$M for Gaussian absolute addressing and more than $2$M for categorical absolute addressing. The experiment does not test learned geometry or repeated retrieval. Instead, it motivates the hypothesis that stateful retrieval may be easier to learn than stateless. To test the full proposed method further experimentation is necessary.
authors: Daniel Strau{\ss}, Zhenshan Bing, Alois Knoll
bullets: Motivation: Global retrieval repeatedly searches large stores, while recurrent compression risks discarding information too early.
Method: Separate memory content from address and optimize local neighborhoods using retrieval information value minus accessibility cost.
Key principle: Complementary memories should be co-retrievable when their added value exceeds cost; redundant memories should be excluded despite individual usefulness.
Proof of principle: On MiniGrid Memory, fixed-geometry traversal reached 0.95 mean return after 0.59M steps, versus 0.94M for Gaussian absolute addressing and over 2M for categorical addressing.
Scope: The experiment does not evaluate learned geometry or repeated retrieval, so the full method remains unvalidated.

papers.abstract: Mobile robots must open doors and drawers, yet their scene maps record what each object is and whether it has moved, not how it will respond to a pull. This paper proposes PhysVLMM, a method that maintains a physical belief for every articulated part of a Vision-Language-Motion Map and answers a planner's queries about it, with two algorithms: a map update and a query. Watching a part move provably cannot identify its dynamics, and a measured pull identifies only the pulled part, up to one direction. PhysVLMM therefore (i) keeps that direction as a posterior instead of a point estimate, (ii) passes the evidence of each pull in closed form to the untouched look-alike parts of the map, and (iii) answers whether an action will succeed at a stated risk, or abstains. On real doors and drawers in 18 homes, it identifies the joint type in 86% of held-out pulls (48% for a learned single-view method) and predicts the response to a pull with 41% lower error than differentiable simulation (CRPS 0.323 vs. 0.544), four orders of magnitude faster (13 ms vs. 230 s per case). The posterior lowers the final-position error from 0.460 to 0.270, sharing lowers the force error of untouched parts from 56% to 42%, and at every stated risk from 0.02 to 0.30 the false-safe answers stay within it. Pooling all measured parts of a home does as well as the look-alike groups, and simpler variants predict where a pulled part stops at least as well.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents now do long, multi-step and multi-session software work with little supervision. When a developer comes back to that work, the useful question is not what the model said but what was actually done, by whom, and whether it is finished. We study this in three parts. First, we verify Agenttrail, an open-source local observability tool for coding agents, against its source at commit e4ba2da: nine documented constants and mechanisms hold at file-and-line level, two event pipelines are never unified, and its Map service has an unauthenticated local mutation surface. Second, we run a prototype of our system on 45 real coding-agent sessions (102,233 records, 20,577 tool executions, 2,336 human-to-agent episodes). With a blind-audited classifier (precision 83.3% and 96.7%) we estimate that 23.4% (95% CI 17.1 to 35.7) of code-editing episodes end with no independent check after the last edit, and that 57.8% of to-dos the agent marked complete after editing had no proof in between. A 10-minute timing heuristic for session hand-offs recovers 6 of the 24 session pairs that content lineage links. 42% of sessions run longer than 24 hours, 48.1% of transcript bytes lie past a 2 MiB replay bound, and 1,326 records in 16 sessions contain credential-like strings. Third, we propose Soei (Structured Observability of Evidence and Intent): an acknowledgement-aware event schema, a hash-chained local ledger, a W3C PROV-aligned graph, calibrated inference for attribution and lineage, and a verification layer that keeps a claim of completion apart from proof. On the same corpus the ledger is 20% of raw size, holds no content or credentials, verifies at about 126k events/s, detects tampering and replays deterministically. We position the work against concurrent 2026 proposals and define autonomy levels with evidence gates and harness metrics baselined on our data.

Defines autonomy levels, evidence gates, and harness metrics grounded in the observed session data.

papers.abstract: Experience can help embodied agents turn high-level plans into grounded actions, but transferring it across tasks remains challenging: previously effective strategies may be inapplicable to the current state or fail to produce their intended outcomes. We present EmbodiExp, a framework for constructing transferable experiences and composing them online during embodied task execution. Our key observation is that tasks often share subgoals whose completion can be assessed independently of overall task success. We therefore introduce an outcome-grounded subgoal experience that specifies a subgoal, applicability conditions, an adaptable policy, and a verifiable outcome. During execution, applicable experiences guide action generation, while verified outcomes can establish the conditions required by subsequent experiences, enabling online composition. Subgoal-level outcome attribution further enables failure utilization: failed trajectories can still contribute verified local successes and condition-specific guidance on actions to avoid. Experiments on multiple embodied benchmarks under a fold-based protocol with frozen experience banks demonstrate the effectiveness of EmbodiExp.
authors: Zhifeng Gu, Ying Chen, Rui Jiang, Lei Yi, Bing Wang

papers.abstract: Embodied instruction following in interactive environments requires agents to interpret natural language commands and complete long-horizon tasks. Existing planners either rely on large labeled trajectories, or use few-shot and zero-shot LLM prompting that produces a whole plan in a single serial reasoning process. These approaches depend on linguistic common sense, commit to a plan from the initial instruction, and only update after failures, which weakens robustness and state awareness. We present AtomTree, a hierarchical framework for state-aware task planning with LLMs. AtomTree incrementally builds a tree of subgoals and actions, where the LLM decides at each step, from the current symbolic state, whether to further decompose or to output a grounded low-level action. A lightweight memory module summarizes past outcomes for reuse in later decisions. When a low-level action stalls, AtomTree triggers hierarchical backtracking replanning to return to the parent node and regenerate the subtree plan from the latest state, preventing continued drift along an incorrect trajectory. In zero-shot evaluation on the ALFRED benchmark, AtomTree outperforms prior LLM-based planners. Project page: https://zhaihaotian.github.io/atomtree-website/.
authors: Haotian Zhai, Tianming Sha, Junnan Li
bullets: Addresses the brittleness of one-shot, serial LLM plans for long-horizon interactive tasks.
Builds a hierarchical tree of subgoals and actions, deciding at each step whether to decompose further or issue a grounded low-level action.
Uses symbolic state updates and lightweight memory to inform subsequent planning decisions.
Performs hierarchical backtracking and replanning when an action stalls, regenerating plans from the latest state.
Outperforms prior LLM-based planners in zero-shot evaluation on ALFRED.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of our hierarchical planning framework for embodied instruction following. Given a task instruction and the current visual state, our method recursively decides whether to decompose the current goal into finer-grained subgoals or execute it directly. This process incrementally builds an explicit hierarchical goal tree, shown in the upper-right panel, where higher-level goals are progressively refined into executable actions. In contrast, we compare against two representative paradigms: (1) a fully supervised end-to-end EIF model trained on the full dataset, and (2) an LLM-based method using retrieved few-shot examples. While these baselines may produce incorrect action sequences, our method maintains a structured tree-based plan and performs step-by-step decomposition conditioned on the current state and memory, enabling more accurate long-horizon reasoning and execution.

Fig. 3: Overview of our state-aware decision prompt. The prompt summarizes the role and mission, decision options, input information, available atomic actions, global rules, output format, and a small set of decision-guiding examples. Given the current subgoal together with the current state and memory, the LLM predicts whether to decompose the goal into subtasks or execute it directly.

Fig. 4: Qualitative comparison with and without memory. Without memory, the model predicts an incorrect subgoal after picking up the cleaned lettuce, whereas AtomTree correctly predicts the next subgoal as navigating to the fridge.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training. We study what information an 8B-scale navigation system should retain and how it should be organized for subsequent decisions. Our agent combines instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation history anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry in complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories. An 8B observer summarizes observations, and an 8B reasoner uses the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, a geometric controller executes the selected targets. A semantic information perspective motivates the distinction between retaining evidence, making it accessible to the reasoner, and acquiring further observations. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the complete system achieves the highest among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and sharply increases average path length from 16.9 to 39.1m, removing the spatial-map and planning component reduces SR as well. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that our zero-shot method achieves higher success rates than the post-trained baseline in both corridor and office environments, suggesting better transfer to the evaluated real-world settings. As a complementary evaluation, LAW2 uses paired instruction interventions to examine behavioral responses, instruction following ability beyond endpoint success. These results support preserving task progress, observation history, and geometry in structured memory for zero-shot navigation with smaller open models.

papers.abstract: Embodied systems can update policies, world models, skills, and executable programs from deployment experience, allowing one interaction to benefit later tasks. When a system also revises and reuses its data-acquisition, feedback, or learning procedures, experience changes the process that produces capability, introducing recursive self-improvement. This paper surveys research in physical AI through the connection between persistent capability and its improvement process. We first explain the functional distinction between learner updates and improvers, then compare policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable harnesses. These approaches connect to revisions of curricula, rewards, and research programs in different ways. Contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs determine whether the resulting gains accumulate during continued deployment. An L0-L3 rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation, persistent capability gain, inherited process revision, and verified improver gain. Representative benchmarks and within-study contrasts relate these distinctions to existing results. We further propose common-data and interactive comparisons that evaluate reference and revised improvers from shared learner starts, separating the use of experience from its acquisition. This perspective connects the diverse methods, physical operating conditions, and evaluation evidence, underpinning embodied RSI. A comprehensive list of studies in this survey is available at https://github.com/nkd-lkz/physical-ai-rsi-survey.
authors: Xiaofeng Han, Kaize Luo, Zenghuang Fu, Zichong Zhu, Zhe Feng, Changwei Wang, Rongtao Xu, Weiliang Meng, Xiaopeng Zhang
bullets: Distinguishes ordinary learner updates from improvers that revise data collection, feedback, or learning procedures.
Reviews policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable learning harnesses.
Identifies contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs as factors governing whether gains persist during deployment.
Introduces an L0–L3 rubric spanning task-local adaptation to verified improvement of the improver itself.
Proposes common-data and interactive comparisons to separate learning from experience from improving how experience is acquired.

figures.caption: FIGURE 1. Overview of the review framework for recursive self-improvement in physical AI. (a) Conceptual distinctions among programmed robots, learned policies, persistent self-improvement, and recursive improvement. (b) Physical experience and feedback support capability updates, while system-generated process revisions are retained and reused to govern later learning. (c) Persistent artifacts can modify the learner, the improver, or both. (d) The evidence rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation (L0), persistent capability gain (L1), inherited process revision (L2), and verified improver gain (L3). L3 requires greater subsequent gains from shared learner starts under matched resource budgets and independent tests. The levels specify evidence requirements for individual claims. Comparisons are schematic, and robot scenes are illustrative renderings.

FIGURE 3. Evidence requirements across a declared reset boundary. Episode context c, retained learner state x, and improvement procedure ϕ have different persistence roles. L0 describes task-local changes that reset; L1 concerns retained capability gains in later independent attempts. L2 requires a system-generated process revision to be inherited and used in a later learner update. L3 requires greater subsequent gains under shared learner starts, matched resource budgets, and independent tests. The diagrams illustrate the criteria and corresponding evaluation conditions.

FIGURE 5. Four carriers of persistent physical experience. Policy and value updates change parameters and action selection; world models retain predictive structure learned from observed transitions; indexed memory and skill libraries support retrieval and composition; programs and harnesses retain changes to execution logic, illustrated by a recovery branch. Each panel exposes the retained representation and its later use. A program change is classified by its functional role in execution or in producing later updates.

FIGURE 6. Fixed-model planning and model–policy co-improvement. The fixed-model planner evaluates imagined action alternatives and executes a selected action while retaining model parameters. In the coupled loop, real transitions train the model, the updated model generates imagined trajectories for policy learning, and the updated policy collects further physical experience. Solid and dashed paths distinguish physical and model-generated experience. The observed–predicted offset is schematic; coupling alone does not establish inherited revision of the improvement procedure.

FIGURE 2. Information boundaries between physical interaction, learner updates, and improver revision. Observations supply experience for learner updates; system-generated procedure changes are retained and used in later update rounds. Development screening can inform these revisions. A concealed reporting audit evaluates frozen candidates on independent held-out outcomes and supplies no feedback to the updates being assessed. Grids, contact geometry, records, and program differences are schematic representations.

FIGURE 7. Four locations for inherited improver revision. Changes to acquisition alter the selected experience; changes to feedback alter the training signal; changes to learning or search alter the update routine; changes to a development gate alter which candidates are retained. Highlighted differences are accepted, inherited, and used in a later cycle. The rows describe alternative intervention locations. Development-gate revisions remain subject to declared external constraints, while independent reporting tests stay fixed for the comparison.

FIGURE 8. Physical continuity and learning-state retention are separate, coordinated processes. Contact changes or calibration drift can require physical recovery before redeployment. Candidate changes to retained state are checked on earlier and new tasks, then accepted or rolled back to the previous checkpoint. Recovery is not itself a learning update. The resource ledger spans collection, recovery, updating, and verification, including robot time, computation, human effort, and wear or repair.

papers.selection_reason: Survey connecting persistent capability, world-model updates, memory, and recursive self-improvement in embodied physical AI.
papers.title: Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Evaluation
papers.tldr: This survey frames embodied recursive self-improvement as systems that improve both their capabilities and the processes used to acquire those capabilities, and proposes ways to evaluate it.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in previously unseen environments requires effective perception, persistent environmental representation, and collision avoidance while maintaining progress toward a goal. Existing perception-based methods often rely on prior maps or short-horizon observations, limiting their ability to exploit previously observed structure. We propose a memory-aware multi-sensor navigation framework that integrates LiDAR and RGB perception, online distance-field representation learning, and a stage-adaptive Modulated Control Barrier Function Quadratic Program (MCBF-QP). The framework persistently represents static infrastructure while tracking dynamic obstacles, enabling the MCBF-QP controller to exploit previously observed geometry for obstacle circumvention and adapt its safety constraints and guidance to local conditions. Experiments in complex indoor and outdoor environments demonstrate improved navigation efficiency and goal-reaching performance while maintaining collision avoidance in narrow passages and around dynamic obstacles.
bullets: Targets limitations of prior-map dependence and short-horizon perception in unseen environments.
Fuses LiDAR and RGB data with online distance-field representation learning.
Separately preserves static infrastructure while tracking dynamic obstacles.
Uses a stage-adaptive Modulated Control Barrier Function Quadratic Program for safe, context-aware control.
Experiments in complex indoor and outdoor settings show improved efficiency and goal reaching while avoiding collisions in narrow and dynamic scenarios.

papers.title: Memory-Aware Multi-Sensor Perception for Efficient and Safe Navigation in Dynamic Environments
papers.tldr: A memory-aware LiDAR–RGB navigation framework persistently models environments and adapts safety control to navigate efficiently and collision-free around static and dynamic obstacles.

papers.abstract: Long video understanding requires reasoning over hours of content that far exceed the context window of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Existing approaches compress video into fixed-length clips, yet events are fragmented and unrelated content is merged, yielding noisy retrieval. To overcome this challenge, we propose EMMA, an Event-driven Multimodal Memory system with Multi-Agent retrieval, which organizes memory around semantic events in three stages: (1) Event segmentation: a dual-stream detector adaptively locates event boundaries by fusing visual semantic drift with spoken transitions, rather than fixed windows. (2) Memory construction: built on the detected events, a three-level hierarchy of raw video, clip-level memory, and event-level memory stores content at progressively higher semantic abstraction. (3) Memory retrieval: a multi-agent framework collaboratively queries this hierarchy through query decomposition, tiered search, evidence validation, and answer generation, narrowing evidence from coarse events to precise clips. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements, showing the effectiveness of our event-aligned memory system. Code, prompt templates, and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/BAI-LAB/EMMA.
bullets: Targets noisy retrieval caused by fixed-length video chunking, which can fragment events and merge unrelated content.
Detects event boundaries using visual semantic drift and spoken transitions.
Builds a three-level memory hierarchy spanning raw video, clip-level memory, and event-level memory.
Uses multi-agent query decomposition, tiered search, evidence validation, and answer generation.
Experiments on three challenging benchmarks show substantial improvements, though the abstract does not specify metrics or limitations.

papers.abstract: We present and tackle two problems associated with deploying Foundation Models (FMs) on Embodied Agents performing navigation: 1) Training bias in FMs leading to poor personalization in unseen environments, and 2) Limited FM context length hindering success, especially on long horizon tasks. Our solution for the former involves priming the FM with human-habit data mined from the scene and our solution for the latter involves active memory management via a novel `memory head' augmentation. We first present a taxonomy of existing literature on FM-based Embodied Navigation, and highlight these limitations. We then present our approaches, Transit-Aware Planning (TAP) and MemCtrl to address the limitations. With TAP, we present real-world results in a lab environment with a Turtlebot for personalized target finding that shows an average improvement of 18% over a non-TAP baseline. On MemCtrl, we report a 6% average improvement across various embodied tasks, with 20% on long instruction subsets, all while using nearly half the context used in the baseline model. Motivated by these result, we present our stance the deployability of FM-based embodied agents in real-world environments, and highlight open research directions.
bullets: Targets poor personalization in unseen environments and context-length limits on long-horizon navigation.
Transit-Aware Planning (TAP) primes models with human-habit data mined from the scene.
MemCtrl adds a memory head for active context management.
In a Turtlebot lab setting, TAP improves personalized target finding by 18% over its baseline.
MemCtrl improves embodied-task performance by 6% overall and 20% on long-instruction subsets while using nearly half the baseline context.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Taxonomy: We consider 3 classes of FM-based methods for Embodied Navigation. The gray boxes indicate the classical pipeline. 1) FM as a Perceiver (in red) takes the input observation and instruction and produces semantic groundings to be used by a planner. 2) FM as a Planner (in blue) uses the outputs of a perception module to produce subgoals or sequences. 3) FM as a policy goes directly from the input to action.

Fig. 3:Real-world Experiment: We create a simulation of our lab environment and define DOMs for priming FM-based TAP agents. The first phase involves gathering images from the scene and constructing a topological scene graph (in blue). The graph is then converted to a Dynamic Object Map (DOM) that models the object dynamics, which is then used to train a transit model T for the transit-aware agent (TAP). Finally, we transfer this to the real-world for personalized assistance. Please refer to the video attached for more visuals. Table 2 presents our results in this environment.

Fig. 7:Base Performance on EB-Habitat: Here, we compare the performance of GPT-4o vs Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Ins, with various memory augmentations. The green box around the image indicates successful task completion, while the red box indicates otherwise. The images are agent observations. Note GPT-4o takes more steps to complete the task. On the other hand, µ boosts the performance of a significantly weaker model, and in this scenario, even doing it quicker with µRL. Grayed out images indicate discarded memories.

Fig. 4: MemCtrl (µ): We present MemCtrl, a novel memory filtering scheme to improve decision making performance on small MLLMs tackling embodied tasks. Our approach proposes a trainable memory head (green box) that learns to actively filter out redundant observations on-the-go. This form of active filtering aims to alleviate issues inefficient retrieval from stored observations, while also enabling scalable deployment on FMs as a detachable memory head.

Fig. 6: Context Growth: MemCtrl (in blue) shows for lesser memory usage and better performance over a baseline Memo-style (in red) approach that stores the entire history as context. These results are on the EB-Habitat environment with Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Ins augmented with an offline supervised µ, using GPT-4o data.

Fig. 2: Finding Portable Objects: Objects at home move over time. Modelling these movements in simulation would help with personalized inference during deployment. In this figure, an embodied agent is tasked with finding a wallet that changes positions between 9:00 and 9:20. Pwallet represents the transit route of the wallet. The Transit-Aware Planner (TAP) is learns routines on ‘real2sim’ data which primes the FM-based navigation agents with these routines for temporally informed decision-making.

Fig. 8: Long Horizon performance on EB-Habitat: We notice that on long horizon tasks, the expert tends to end the task early by hastily assuming that it is done (finishing after placing one plate instead of all plates). Memory heads highlight unique performance improvements, with µRL exhibiting a more exploratory nature by continuing to place new objects at the right counter, and µExpert being more exploitative by repeating the same activity over and over, with a single plate. Investigating this is part of a future study. Note: Grayed out images indicate discarded memories.

Fig. 5:MemCtrl Variants: We experiment with 3 variants. The simple case acts as a non-trained baseline, where the MLLM is directly queried about storage. In the offline supervised case, µ is first pretrained using expert answers from a high performing, expert MLLM (GPT-4o here). This trained binary classifier then acts as a head on top of the MLLM backbone. In the Online RL case, we train the memory head online as a policy network. We use a sparse reward on task success and a dense reward on action success. Note that MemCtrl is trained as a detachable head that takes the latent MLLM embeddings as input.

Table 3: MemCtrl Results: We augment Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Ins with the 3 variations of MemCtrl on 5 subsets of EB-ALFRED and EB-Habitat [45] across 3 trials. Note the improve performance overall of adding the memory head µ. In particular, we note superior performance on long context and complex instructions, which tend to be long horizon where memory is particularly useful.

Table 1:Object Transit Scenarios: Portable targets transition in a topological graph under structured scenarios inspired by human habits. In the random case, the portable objects can move to any room at any time during each episode. In the routine cases, the rooms that the target objects can travel to are fixed.

Table 2: Real World SR: We report average success rates for finding portable objects in our lab environment over 50 episodes. Note the improved performance of the TAP-LLM approach over a vanilla LLM scheme ( [13]). Transit awareness helps improve performance in the routine cases, where paths have structure.

papers.abstract: GUI memory should preserve the results of past actions and learn reusable operations. This is difficult in long-horizon workflows, where agents must use information across applications and useful operations are interleaved with failed attempts. We introduce Task Advancement Memory (TAM), which defines task advancement as verified task progress, and supports ongoing task execution and learns reusable operations. During execution, Task Advancement State represents how verified task progress changes the remaining goals, allowing the agent to build on earlier achievements across applications. After each task, advancement supervision identifies and abstracts the interactions that produced a verified local result. The learned operations preserve the relation between required inputs, expected outcomes, and verification conditions. This retains locally successful operations from both successful and failed tasks. On MobileWorld GUI-only tasks, Advancement State alone raises success from 12.0% to 28.2%. Full TAM achieves a 17.6% relative gain in task success over the strongest evaluated baseline and reduces lifecycle tokens per solved task by 38.7%. On SPA-Bench, TAM achieves state-of-the-art task success in the single-app English Level 3 setting.
authors: Ziyang Chen, Qian Li, Chengwei Qin
bullets: Addresses failures in long-horizon, cross-application workflows where useful actions are mixed with failed attempts.
Represents verified progress as Task Advancement State to update remaining goals during execution.

On MobileWorld, Advancement State alone improves success from 12.0% to 28.2%; full TAM provides a 17.6% relative success gain and reduces lifecycle tokens per solved task by 38.7%.
Achieves state-of-the-art success on SPA-Bench’s single-app English Level 3 setting.

papers.selection_reason: Memory mechanism that preserves task advancement and reusable operations from agent interactions; directly relevant to embodied/environment-grounded memory.

papers.abstract: Humanoids and other legged robots operating in complex environments must remember information that leaves their field of view and only becomes relevant much later. Reinforcement learning policies address this using memory networks such as LSTMs that are trained end-to-end with the policy to memorize such task-relevant aspects. Yet, such architectures often fail to preserve sufficient information over long horizons. In this work, we propose a network architecture based on Hadamard memory that specifically targets robot navigation. Our Local Spatial Matrix Memory (LSMM) enables RL agents to store generic task-relevant information at specific, position-based memory cells, enabling flexible and spatially grounded memorization. We evaluate LSMM on the task of autonomous maze exploration, where it matches the maze coverage of strong recurrent and finite-history baselines while being the only architecture that remembers the maze layout, reducing the reconstruction error threefold.
authors: Leon Magnus, Nico Bohlinger, Jan Peters, Oleg Arenz
bullets: Long-horizon navigation requires remembering information beyond the robot’s current field of view.
The proposed Local Spatial Matrix Memory (LSMM) stores task-relevant information in position-based memory cells.
LSMM is evaluated for autonomous maze exploration against recurrent and finite-history baselines.
It matches baseline maze coverage and is the only evaluated architecture to remember maze layout, reducing reconstruction error threefold.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies and language-model agents provide complementary capabilities, but completing a task also requires adapting their use to the consequences of physical interaction. We study execution as a locus of adaptation: feedback guides the current action and supplies evidence for revising subsequent decisions under fixed model weights. We introduce RoboDoctor, a training-free framework that connects diagnosis, grounded action, and persistent experience across three revision targets. The harness allocates control between policy and agent; intervention determines when to assist while preserving useful policy behavior; and operation refines physical methods through observed effects. Linked experience records retain the reason for a decision, the attempted method, its outcome, and conditions for reuse. On a curated archive of 54 RoboDojo-Sim task entries, RoboDoctor achieves a five-dimension mean score of 57.10, with a native success rate of 49.44%. Recorded interactions illustrate strategy changes, selective correction, and grasp revision. These findings characterize execution-time adaptation in the evaluated system; controlled trials remain necessary to isolate the contribution of cross-episode experience.
authors: Heyang Yu, Haomin Li, Sihang Li, Jixin Yan, Shiyun Peng, Wanqi Zhong, Tianyu Xin, Yuan Yao, Xiaoyu Tian, Yiming Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting robot-policy and language-agent behavior to the consequences of physical interaction.
Uses three revision targets: control allocation between policy and agent, selective intervention, and refinement of physical methods.
Stores linked experience containing decision rationale, attempted method, outcome, and reuse conditions.
On 54 RoboDojo-Sim task entries, it reports a five-dimension mean score of 57.10 and a native success rate of 49.44%.
The results demonstrate execution-time adaptation, but controlled trials are still needed to isolate the value of cross-episode experience.

figures.caption: Figure 2: RoboDoctor architecture: experience-guided control and grounded execution. After three HYBRID Warmup episodes, Harness RSI selects HYBRID or DIRECT control and keeps this choice fixed. In HYBRID, the Doctor reviews a WAM proposal and its robot-only forwardkinematics preview, then retains up to 16 unchanged policy steps or issues a grounded correction of 1–5 physical steps. Corrections and DIRECT actions ground the current scene, execute a physical method, and verify its observed effect. The illustrated pouring episode separates a lateral alignment correction that preserves the grasp from subsequent policy-led pouring. Task experience links diagnostic cues, attempted operations, and observed outcomes to inform later decisions.

Figure 1: RoboDoctor: training-free adaptation across three levels of execution. Harness RSI allocates control between the policy and the Doctor; Intervention RSI decides when to retain or correct policy motion; Operation RSI revises physical methods and verifies their effects. External experience connects these decisions while both models remain frozen. The radar chart summarizes five capability scores for Warmup, Refinement, and the published GPT-6-Astra reference. Recorded examples illustrate alignment correction followed by pouring, and grasp revision followed by a test lift.

papers.abstract: Vision-language navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through 3D environments. Maintaining persistent episodic memory remains a challenge for VLM-based streaming agents in long-horizon navigation. We present MEMVLN, a streaming episodic memory framework that maintains a bounded bank of compressed perceptual features annotated with timesteps and action-derived relative poses, and produces compact memory tokens via cross-attention. We pair the proposed memory with a frozen pretrained geometry encoder. To learn the memory module, we design a masking-based trajectory summarization task with multi-granularity sub-trajectory decomposition, encouraging route reconstruction exclusively from episodic memory. Under navigation training restricted to the official R2R/RxR trajectories, MEMVLN achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics on standard VLN-CE benchmarks. Long-horizon analyses further characterize when episodic memory is useful. For physical evaluation, we collect 30 instruction-conditioned episodes in one physical scene, use 24 as demonstrations for post-training, and hold out six for testing. On the held-out episodes, MEMVLN improves success over the VLM baseline from 17% to 40%, and post-training further raises it to 47%.
authors: Yan Wang, Jiangyong Huang, Baoxiong Jia, Siyuan Huang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining useful past observations during long-horizon VLN.

papers.abstract: Running a language model and a dense 3D map on one device means the two share one memory, and exceeding its limit is an out-of-memory failure. Map systems that keep a bounded working set bound it by a count of keyframes, but the memory one keyframe occupies varies widely with what it carries, so a count does not control what the working set occupies. The unit of admission is as poorly matched, since a radius around the pose, a fixed cell, or the graph neighbors of the last matched keyframe all move parts of the map that are not needed. We therefore propose two decisions. First, the memory the resident map uses is bounded directly, and the cost of every admission is known before any data is read, from per-keyframe resident sizes computed offline and carried with the map. Second, keyframes are admitted and released at a semantic spatial unit, the rooms and corridors of the building, so that the robot holds the zone it occupies together with the zone it is about to enter while the zones it has passed are released. Every admission measures the resident total, makes room, and only then reads, so the budget is never overshot. On two NVIDIA Jetson boards the budget holds in every run and the model gives up at most 0.8 percent of its throughput, whereas without it the operating system kills the model or the map. Under that budget, and over the environments evaluated, admission by semantic zone localizes 6-9 points more of the query frames than a geometric partition of matched zone count and about twice as much as the retrieval of RTAB-Map, at a lower ATE. Bounding memory lets the map and the model coexist, and moving the map in semantic zones makes the bounded map usable.
authors: Huichang Yun, Jaeyeul Kim, Seungho Yoo
bullets: Keyframe-count limits are unreliable because keyframes vary substantially in memory usage.
The system predicts each keyframe’s resident size offline and enforces a strict memory budget before reading new data.
It admits and releases map content by rooms and corridors, retaining the current and next zones while removing passed zones.
On two NVIDIA Jetson boards, the budget held in every run with at most 0.8% model-throughput loss.
Semantic-zone admission localized 6–9 percentage points more query frames than geometric partitioning and about twice as much as RTAB-Map retrieval, with lower ATE in the evaluated environments.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-and-language navigation (VLN) policies act on their visual history, and an incorrect action can take them off the instructed route. Paired interventions on four VLN policies show that clearing the history doubles pooled success at the onset of a deviation but lowers it on route, while later in a deviation, removing only the off-route frames helps much less. After a deviation, the retained history keeps the policy from turning where a turn is needed, which we call behavioral inertia. We propose MOON, a framework that equips a frozen VLN policy with two lightweight modules, adding less than 1% of its parameters. A deviation judge decides when to forget, raising an alarm that clears the history when it predicts that the agent is off route. A recovery policy, trained with GRPO from alarm states, learns how to move on, turning more of the successes found only by sampling into a single greedy rollout. Experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE show that MOON reaches the highest R2R-CE success rate among the compared methods and raises the success rate of its frozen base by 5.2 and 6.0 points, and an ablation with a random trigger indicates that this gain depends on when the history is cleared. Without retraining, MOON also improves zero-shot object-goal navigation on HM3D-OVON. Together, these results suggest that deviation recovery depends on knowing when to forget, not only how to act. Code is available at https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/MOON.
authors: Jingmeng Zhou, Seson Sun, Binyao Xu, Lingming Zhang, Hanshi Wang, Fudong Ge, Weiming Hu, Jin Gao, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Incorrect actions can create behavioral inertia: retained off-route history prevents the agent from turning when needed.
MOON adds two lightweight modules to a frozen VLN policy: a deviation judge that triggers history clearing and a recovery policy trained from alarm states.
On R2R-CE and RxR-CE, MOON improves its frozen base success by 5.2 and 6.0 percentage points, respectively, and achieves the highest R2R-CE success among compared methods.
A random-trigger ablation shows that recovery depends on clearing history at the right time, not merely clearing it.
MOON also improves zero-shot object-goal navigation on HM3D-OVON without retraining.

papers.abstract: Robots can use historical observations to answer spatiotemporal queries in familiar environments, but the presence of relevant evidence does not imply that existing tools support the operations a task requires. We introduce ReSight, a task-driven self-improving memory system for embodied agents that expands the capabilities for processing and accessing historical observations as task demands arise. ReSight retains keyframes and their spatiotemporal associations, separating observation evidence from extensible derived fields so that stored observations can be reprocessed for new needs. An execution agent and a coding agent share this memory through different interfaces: the former calls registered tools within a bounded online budget, while the latter uses a programmable workspace and a larger exploration budget to inspect evidence, write programs, and acquire models as needed. To realize capability expansion in ReSight, we develop Explore-Distill-Mount (EDM), which identifies capability gaps from execution and exploration records without task reference answers and converts exploration-derived solutions into reusable memory builders, query tools, and skills, extending memory representations and access capabilities as needed. Experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate effective base memory access and capability expansion. With the execution model and online budget held fixed within each benchmark, EDM reduces mean position error on OC-NaVQA from 33.10 m to 24.72 m and improves high-level success on FindingDory from 38.3% to 63.8%. With the tools and skill frozen, success still improves by 28.3 percentage points on FindingDory episodes excluded from exploration and distillation. Experiments on real robot patrol memories further demonstrate reuse of these capabilities for subsequent queries and new memories, with fewer online tool calls on average.
authors: Lirong Che, Yang Chen, Yimeng Su, Daqi Liu, Zhenyu Huang, Jiong Wang, Yuzhe Yang, Xu Cao, Chuang Wang, Jian Su, Xueqian Wang
bullets: Addresses the gap between available historical evidence and tools capable of performing task-specific operations.
Stores keyframes and spatiotemporal links separately from extensible derived fields, allowing observations to be reprocessed.
Uses distinct execution and coding agents for bounded online querying versus broader exploration and program/model development.
Its Explore-Distill-Mount process converts discovered solutions into reusable memory builders, query tools, and skills without task reference answers.
Across benchmarks, it reduces OC-NaVQA mean position error from 33.10 m to 24.72 m and raises FindingDory success from 38.3% to 63.8%; real-robot patrol tests show reuse with fewer online tool calls.

papers.abstract: As multimodal agents engage in sustained interactions, long-term memory serves two distinct but complementary functions: fine-grained evidence recall and internalized interpretation for global understanding. Although episodic and latent memory address these demands through explicit historical records and internalized experience, neither paradigm alone can accommodate the diverse memory affinities across tasks, owing to limitations in episodic evidence coverage and integration, and in latent factual grounding. To bridge this divide, we propose a dual-memory framework, unifying a model-native latent memory as an intuitive prior with a multi-indexed episodic memory for exact evidence reconstruction via retrieval-conditioned joint alignment. At inference, the framework adaptively composes these memories through a training-free routing mechanism driven by Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) sensitivity and confidence proxies for query-dependent memory affinity. Extensive evaluations across multimodal benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, outperforming single-paradigm baselines overall (+4.67\% over vanilla Episodic), with further analysis highlighting episodic strengths in evidence-localized tasks and latent contributions to integrating dispersed information and compensating for imperfect retrieval.
authors: Qiuhe Hong, Jingya Wang, Cuzhen Geng, Shenyao Peng, Munan Ning, Yuyang Liu, Yonghong Tian
bullets: Addresses the complementary needs of exact evidence recall and broad, internalized understanding in long-term multimodal interactions.
Combines model-native latent memory with multi-indexed episodic memory through retrieval-conditioned joint alignment.
Uses training-free routing based on Jensen–Shannon Divergence sensitivity and confidence proxies to adapt memory composition.
Evaluations across multimodal benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, including a reported +4.67% over vanilla episodic memory.
Episodic memory helps evidence-localized tasks, while latent memory supports dispersed-information integration and robustness to imperfect retrieval.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained object (FO) manipulation requires robots to distinguish a specified FO from visually similar objects and execute actions reliably despite scene distractors. However, scene-level visual conditioning lacks explicit object selection, while category-level guidance cannot reliably distinguish FOs within the same category. We present a SAM3-guided visuomotor policy framework that addresses these challenges through persistent object memory and focused visual conditioning. First, we introduce FO Memory-driven SAM3 (FOM-SAM3), which learns reusable FO memory tokens from limited multi-view registration images, while keeping SAM3 fully frozen. Through one-vs-rest learning, these tokens encode persistent memories for localizing target FOs and rejecting similar alternatives, which can be stored in a memory bank for reuse. Second, we propose Focused Spatial-Appearance Encoding (FSAE), which combines in-FO appearance features with explicit bounding boxes to condition action policies, including Diffusion Policy (DP) and Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT). The effectiveness of the proposed FOM-SAM3 is validated on the FO-30 dataset comprising 30 physical objects across four coarse categories. Across three real-robot FO manipulation tasks, our FOM-SAM3-guided policies demonstrated robustness against distractors, discriminative ability of similar FOs, and extendibility to new FOs.
bullets: Targets fine-grained manipulation where scene-level or category-level guidance cannot reliably select a particular object.
FOM-SAM3 learns reusable target-object memory tokens from limited multi-view images while keeping SAM3 frozen.
FSAE combines target appearance features with bounding-box information to condition Diffusion Policy and ACT controllers.
Validated on 30 physical objects across four categories and three real-robot manipulation tasks.
The framework showed distractor robustness, discrimination among similar objects, and extension to new objects.
