papers.abstract: Zero-shot object navigation requires an embodied agent to choose where to search while retaining evidence from previous observations. HGWM couples an LLM-generated room-anchor prior with persistent spatial-semantic memory. A coarse stage assigns visual-semantic scores to candidate headings on a 0-10 scale; a fine stage measures symbolic compatibility between observed objects, room context, and the goal prior. Phase-dependent fusion combines these scores with an LLM direction recommendation before local action selection. On HM3D v0.1, the reported HGWM configuration achieves 62.6% success rate (SR) and 31.5% success weighted by path length (SPL), compared with 58.1% and 31.2% for WMNav. On MP3D, the corresponding values are 46.8% and 17.9%, compared with 45.4% and 17.2%. The results indicate higher success point estimates and modest path-efficiency gains. On HM3D v0.2, the full model obtains 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL. Additional component ablations reduce SR by 0.9-2.3 percentage points and SPL by 0.6-1.5 points. These are author-reported aggregate measurements. The accompanying implementation repairs pass offline tests; episode-level rerun records are not available. Evaluation is confined to simulation.
bullets: Uses a coarse-to-fine process: heading scoring followed by symbolic matching of observed objects, room context, and the goal prior.
Fuses phase-dependent graph scores with an LLM direction recommendation for local action selection.
Reports higher success and modestly better path efficiency than WMNav on HM3D v0.1 and MP3D.
On HM3D v0.2, the full model achieves 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL; component ablations lower both metrics.
Evaluation is limited to simulation, and episode-level rerun records are unavailable.

papers.abstract: Controlling scientific instruments requires parameters to be adjusted progressively in response to feedback from successive operations. When unobserved operating conditions evolve with operational history, responses become nonstationary, and a static mapping from actions to responses becomes inadequate for decisions across shots. Shot-to-shot tuning of neutral beam injection (NBI) ion sources in magnetic confinement fusion devices is representative of this class of problems: the conditions of electrode surfaces and vacuum are difficult to observe directly, discharge outcomes vary between shots, and experiments are costly and carry operational risks. We propose a physically grounded multimodal agent with three independently auditable components. Deterministic algorithms extract symbolic physical quantities and visual evidence from multichannel waveforms; a memory with two layers organizes trajectories from the current task, experience from earlier tasks, and procedural knowledge, from which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) generates candidate actions; and an independent action feasibility check enforces action constraints before execution. In a strictly chronological replay of 455 shots from four EXL-50U platforms, physical symbols alone outperformed waveform images alone by 0.21-0.32 in macro-F1 for quality classification across all four evaluated models. Retrieved context increased the mean agreement with historical action directions by 22.4-42.7 percentage points, whereas the contribution of visual evidence varied across models. Under supervised operation on five ion sources, the system achieved a beam-extraction rate of 86.80% across 409 executed shots. These results demonstrate the engineering feasibility of the framework for supervised sequential tuning on a physical scientific instrument.
authors: Guoyang Shi, Hongwen Li, Yiding Yu, Zhuang Fu, Siqi Ding, Zhengyuan Chen, JianGuo Chen, Hanyue Zhao, Tianyuan Liu
bullets: Addresses shot-to-shot NBI ion-source tuning when hidden operating conditions evolve and responses are nonstationary.
Combines deterministic extraction of physical and visual features, two-layer trajectory/knowledge memory, MLLM action generation, and independent feasibility checks.
In chronological replay of 455 shots across four EXL-50U platforms, physical symbols outperformed waveform images alone for quality classification.
Retrieved context improved agreement with historical action directions, while visual evidence had model-dependent effects.
Demonstrates engineering feasibility for supervised sequential tuning on five ion sources; scope is limited to supervised operation and the evaluated platforms.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require a robot to remember what it has done and what it has seen. Frontier vision-language models can plan such tasks without task-specific training, but how such a planner should remember an episode is an open question. We argue that its memory must keep track of what the planner has done and learned, and must let the planner choose what to look at, since every frame costs tokens; a note rewritten at every step meets both poorly. We propose LogLook, whose execution-grounded memory lets the system keep the record, an execution log and the model's earlier notes, while the model decides where to look: frames are returned only where it expects a change, and demonstrations are skimmed before it inspects the parts it chooses. Measured with the benchmark's motion planner, LogLook matches the success of a note-only memory with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, and fails far fewer episodes through what it remembered or saw. With direct control, LogLook solves 93.5% of the RoboMME test set.
authors: Tianyi Jiang, Tianyao Tong, Zhenshan Bing
bullets: Addresses how frontier vision-language robot planners should remember actions and observations during manipulation tasks.
Maintains an execution log alongside the model’s notes instead of rewriting a note at every step.
Uses model-directed visual access: it requests frames where changes are expected and selectively inspects demonstrations.
Matches note-only memory success with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, while causing fewer memory- or perception-related failures.
Achieves 93.5% success on the RoboMME test set with direct control.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of execution-grounded memory. At every decision, GPT-6 Astra receives the observation, the instruction and the memory, and returns a note and an action, optionally with image points to watch; the motion planner or π0.5 executes the action. The memory has two parts. The system keeps the record: one log line per executed action with the measured gripper state, and every note the model has written. The model chooses what to see: after an action only the recorded frames that changed near the watched points are returned, and a demonstration is skimmed before the model inspects the ranges it asks for. All snippets come from one MoveCube test episode: the observation, a verbatim (shortened) decision, the resulting log lines and notes, the three frames returned during the watched push, and the demonstration range the model inspected.

papers.selection_reason: Execution-grounded memory for VLM-based robot planners that selectively retrieves frames, relevant to embodied memory, VLA, and token efficiency.
papers.title: LogLook: Execution-Grounded Memory for Frontier-Model Robot Planners
papers.tldr: LogLook improves robot-planning memory by grounding it in execution logs and letting the model selectively inspect frames and demonstrations, reducing visual context while maintaining or improving task success.

papers.abstract: Humans efficiently process multimodal streams spanning hours to years, building persistent, fine-grained spatiotemporal memories that support reasoning about and predicting long-horizon events. In contrast, existing benchmarks focus on short- and medium-context tasks, and most foundation models struggle to preserve fine-grained information over long horizons. To evaluate and improve long-horizon spatiotemporal reasoning, we introduce the LongVideo dataset and the 4DMemoryBench. LongVideo comprises about 900 hours of video and over 5,000 manually reviewed questions covering visual, textual, and spatiotemporal reasoning across diverse context lengths. We further develop the 4DMemory Harness, which integrates four complementary skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and a model-specific retrieval-augmented generation system. Evaluating 13 leading models, we find that standalone foundation models struggle with long-horizon tasks, while the 4DMemory Harness improves all of them by over 50\%. Compared to previous benchmark, the same models exhibit a performance drop of more than 10\% on 4DMemoryBench. We hope 4DMemory will facilitate the development of spatiotemporal agents capable of addressing complex, long-horizon tasks.
authors: Yanhao Jia, Yi Zhu, Yiran Zhong, Weigao Sun, Feida Zhu, Pengkun Jiao, Sihan Yang, Ming Ma, Steven Hoi, Erik Cambria
bullets: LongVideo contains about 900 hours of video and over 5,000 manually reviewed questions spanning visual, textual, and spatiotemporal reasoning.
4DMemoryBench evaluates reasoning across diverse context lengths, targeting persistent memory over long video streams.
The 4DMemory Harness combines four skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and model-specific retrieval-augmented generation.
Across 13 leading models, the harness improves performance by over 50%, while models perform over 10% worse than on a previous benchmark.
The benchmark targets development of agents for complex, long-horizon spatiotemporal tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Motivation for 4DMemory Agent. (a) Traditional models with limited active context may lose access to earlier observations, leaving relevant evidence unavailable for temporal reasoning. (b) 4DMemory Agent coordinates persistent memory and task-specific skills through a harness to retrieve evidence and reason over events and their relations. 2024b; Bai et al., 2025). At the method level, adaptive spatiotemporal compression removes redundant frames and visual tokens, sparse memory consolidates dense observations into long-term representations, and query-adaptive hierarchical selection allocates computation across temporal granularities (Shen et al., 2025; Song et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b). Together, these advances improve access to long-range evidence, but their gains are typically evaluated under different datasets, interfaces, and access conditions, making it difficult to isolate improvements in the base model, evidence acquisition, memory, and final reasoning. Moreover, these components are not readily composable across systems, since methods such as LongVU require access to the internal visiontoken pipeline, whereas LongVT learns its tooluse protocol through model-specific post-training of Qwen2.5-VL-7B rather than through a modelagnostic plug-in interface (Shen et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026).

Figure 3: Overview of the LongVideo construction pipeline. Hours-level videos undergo audio-text screening, clip construction, and evidence refinement to obtain coherent clips with grounded captions. Visual evidence, audio captions, and transcripts are aligned to original source timestamps and organized into chronological multimodal evidence chains. QA pairs are then constructed from multiple evidence chains and checked for answer correctness, clip necessity, and potential shortcuts.

Figure 4: Illustration of 4DMemory Agent framework. (a) The harness builds persistent, question-independent memory of events, entities, and spatial relations, preserving source timestamps for reuse across questions. (b) A foundation model retrieves timestamped evidence and iteratively refines its queries and reasoning, with optional tools provided by a skill library.

Figure 2: Comparison of previous Video-MME (top) and LVBench (bottom) scores with 4DMemory results for the same models. All models shown score lower on 4DMemory, with dashed arrows indicating the decrease in percentage points.
Table 2: The overall performance on the 4DMemory Benchmark among 13 SOTA methods.

Table 3: Six selected standalone-video spatiotemporal subtypes. Columns denote multi-event ordering, state-change tracking, distributed counting, path and trajectory tracking, cross-modal reasoning, and cross-modal binding, respectively.

papers.selection_reason: Long-horizon spatiotemporal memory benchmark and agents; directly relevant to embodied memory and long-video understanding.
papers.title: 4DMemory: Benchmarking Long-Horizon Spatiotemporal Memory with Harness-Augmented Agents
papers.tldr: 4DMemory introduces a long-horizon video benchmark and tool-augmented harness that substantially improves foundation-model performance on spatiotemporal reasoning tasks.

papers.abstract: When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (1Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools) and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p=0.011), and even the rulebook's apparent pool-immunity collapsed on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a single 15-token caution instruction, and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook's lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We release the testbed, audited ports, seeds, and caches.
bullets: Memory gains were highly sensitive to which warmup experiences were sampled: retrieval systems beat No-Memory in only 1 of 10 pools.
A single 15-token caution instruction matched the collision-only benefit of retrieval, and caution-aware metrics removed the rulebook’s apparent lead.
More sophisticated memory representations showed no robust advantage in this evaluation.
Baseline implementation quality and uncontrolled prompts could reverse the reported conclusion about whether memory helps.
The study releases the testbed, audited ports, random seeds, and caches; findings are scoped to this testbed and decisive model setting.
papers.selection_reason: Controlled evaluation of experience memory in closed-loop LLM driving agents directly connects embodied decision-making with environment-grounded memory.
papers.title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines
papers.tldr: In one audited HighwayEnv testbed, apparent benefits from experience memory in closed-loop LLM driving agents largely vanish under resampled warmup pools and token-matched filler controls.

papers.abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to train agents that adapt quickly to unseen tasks from limited interaction, but this requires representing task evidence over long interaction histories. Classical recurrent agents compress experience into hidden states, while transformer-based agents retrieve from past trajectories at quadratic memory and computation cost. In this work, we propose Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation (METTA) for meta-reinforcement learning. It decomposes the fast adaptation phase into two temporal scales: a causal neural memory performs fine-grained within-episode adaptation with linear sequence complexity, while compact episode-level summaries support long-range cross-episode task inference without attending over the full interaction history. Moreover, equipping agents with neural memory provides sufficient expressive capacity and test-time training capability, enabling effective adaptation to unseen held-out tasks and task families at meta-test time. On unseen held-out Meta-World ML10/45 test environments, METTA achieves a success rate over $50\%$ while maintaining a low training budget and short wall-clock time. On long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks, it outperforms transformer-based baselines by exhibiting more structured exploration behavior. These results show that METTA provides an efficient path toward more adaptive and scalable long-context meta-RL.
authors: Ali Najar, Hosein Hasani, Amir Kooshan Fattah, Yasamin Rajabi, Mahdieh Soleymani Baghshah
bullets: Addresses the challenge of inferring unseen tasks from long interaction histories without the quadratic cost of full-trajectory transformer attention.
Uses a causal neural memory for fine-grained, within-episode adaptation and episode-level summaries for long-range task inference.
Supports test-time training and adaptation to unseen tasks and task families.
Achieves over 50% success on held-out Meta-World ML10/45 environments with low training and wall-clock budgets.
Outperforms transformer baselines on long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks through more structured exploration.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation (METTA) for meta-reinforcement learning, using neural memory to handle long interaction histories. This fits the Adaptation and Memory topic, specifically test-time learning and embodied memory.
papers.title: METTA: Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation for Meta-Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: METTA enables efficient long-context meta-reinforcement learning by combining linear-time within-episode memory with compact cross-episode task summaries for test-time adaptation.

papers.abstract: A conventional embodied agent in an indoor environment builds a map by accumulating noisy real-world measurements and results from heavy inference to guide navigation. While the detailed measurements may differ due to scene changes or sensor settings, the unique topological structure of navigable passages or the connectivity between rooms may provide training-free guidance that complements local observations. We propose a sparse topometric graph as an efficient structural representation for robust indoor navigation, alleviating the need for fine-grained matching, which is computationally expensive, memory-intensive, and prone to real-world variations. The map consists of nodes that encode local 3D geometry and distance-weighted edges that capture traversable connectivity. A learned graph-matching network finds consistent subgraph structures across sessions by considering both node-level geometric descriptors and neighborhood connectivity. The holistic contextual matching is robust to local ambiguities caused by weak distinctiveness or repetitive structure, and establishes stable correspondences despite local scene changes, different sensor modalities, or limited spatial overlap. We analyze the practicality of the graph through cross-session point-goal navigation, where a goal specified in a prior reference map must be reached from an unknown initial pose in a later session. Experiments show that our method achieves the highest success rates (77.1% on Gibson and 40.0% under 3D-FRONT scene changes), while reducing memory by more than two orders of magnitude compared to point-level representations. The proposed approach further supports cross-session alignment and goal-directed navigation with strong scalability and robust real-world transfer.
authors: Eun Sun Lee, Minkyun Seo, Gwangtak Bae, Junho Kim, Seunggu Kang, Jaesik Park, Young Min Kim
bullets: Represents indoor maps with nodes for local 3D geometry and distance-weighted edges for traversable connectivity.
Uses learned graph matching over geometric descriptors and neighborhood structure to establish correspondences across sessions.
Handles local ambiguities, scene changes, different sensor modalities, and limited spatial overlap without training-specific fine-grained matching.
In cross-session point-goal navigation, achieves 77.1% success on Gibson and 40.0% under 3D-FRONT scene changes.
Reduces memory use by more than two orders of magnitude versus point-level representations.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse topometric graph memory and graph-matching for cross-session indoor navigation, fitting robot navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: A Sparse Topometric Graph for Scalable Cross-Session Indoor Navigation
papers.tldr: A sparse topometric graph enables scalable, robust cross-session indoor navigation by matching room connectivity and local geometry instead of fine-grained measurements.

papers.abstract: GUI agents aim to automate complex user tasks by interacting with mobile interfaces, but ef- fective decision-making in long-horizon set- tings requires reusing prior experience rather than relying solely on the environment ob- servations. Existing memory-based methods typically store experience either at the single- action level or as entire trajectories. Single- step actions are often too fine-grained to carry meaningful semantics, since the success of an individual action does not necessarily imply progress towards the overall goal. In contrast, whole trajectories are often too coarse-grained and difficult to reuse across different tasks. We propose a subgoal-aware memory graph that distils past trajectories into structured, reusable evidence at the level of subgoals. We define a subgoal as consecutive actions shar- ing a single intent, the granularity at which progress toward the task becomes meaning- ful. To reduce redundancy and support cross- task reuse, we organise subgoal experiences as nodes in a graph, where related memories can be merged, extended, and retrieved based on the environment observation. On SPA-Bench, our method improves success rate by 11.11% over the baseline.
authors: Dezhao Luo, Daniel Beechey, Derek Yuen, Weilin Luo
bullets: Single-action memories are too fine-grained, while whole-trajectory memories are too coarse and hard to reuse.
The method defines subgoals as consecutive actions sharing one intent.
Past trajectories are distilled into graph nodes representing reusable subgoal experiences.
Related memories can be merged, extended, and retrieved using the current environment observation.
Evaluation on SPA-Bench shows an 11.11% success-rate improvement over the baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes subgoal-level memory graph for reusing interaction experience in GUI agents.
papers.title: Subgoal-aware Memory Graph for GUI Agent
papers.tldr: A subgoal-aware memory graph helps GUI agents reuse meaningful segments of past experience for long-horizon mobile tasks, improving SPA-Bench success by 11.11% over a baseline.

papers.abstract: Long egocentric videos pose a central challenge for multimodal language models: the visual stream must be compressed into a memory representation that can be searched efficiently while still preserving the evidence needed for question answering. Building on an online textual-memory framework in which first-person videos are converted into temporally grounded captions, this work systematically studies the role of retrieval in episodic-memory video question answering. We evaluate how different retrieval units, query formulations, context budgets, and reranking strategies affect multiple-choice answering on QAEgo4D-Closed, isolating retrieval as the main variable while keeping the underlying generated memory fixed. Our best configuration, Parent, matches fine-grained caption subchunks, then provides their full parent captions to the reasoner. It achieves 56.4 % accuracy, matching strong full-memory and retrieval baselines while exposing only a small fraction of the textual memory at question time. More importantly, our analysis shows that better temporal coverage does not necessarily translate into better answers: increasing the retrieval budget improves temporal Hit@K and Recall@K, but can reduce accuracy by introducing visually plausible distractors and uncertain caption evidence. These findings suggest that retrieval-augmented egocentric memory should not be optimized only for evidence recall, but also for the reliability, specificity, and answer-discriminative value of the retrieved context. The study motivates more structured episodic memories that move beyond raw caption retrieval toward evidence-aware representations for long-form egocentric reasoning.
authors: Raffaele Cali, Giuseppe Lando, Rosario Forte, Antonino Furnari
bullets: Evaluates retrieval units, query formulations, context budgets, and reranking while keeping the generated textual memory fixed.
The best setup, Parent, retrieves fine-grained caption subchunks but gives their full parent captions to the reasoning model.
Parent reaches 56.4% accuracy while exposing only a small fraction of the textual memory at question time.
Larger retrieval budgets improve temporal Hit@K and Recall@K but can hurt accuracy by adding distractors and uncertain evidence.
Results motivate structured, evidence-aware episodic memories beyond raw caption retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Studies retrieval-augmented textual memory for egocentric video QA, directly relevant to embodied memory and learning from egocentric video.
papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Online Textual Memory for Episodic Memory Video Question Answering
papers.tldr: A systematic study shows that effective retrieval for episodic video QA depends on reliable, answer-discriminative evidence—not merely broader temporal coverage.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).
authors: Chenyuan Chen, Ran Ding, Lechen Zhang, Zewen He, Yoshihiko Nakamura
bullets: Addresses non-Markovian manipulation scenes where important visual cues disappear or leave view.
Uses SAM3 to track objects and select key event frames within an adaptive memory budget.
An action expert reads selected frames via cross-attention alongside object tokens encoding appearance, geometry, and time.
Introduces HuMeGo, a benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks.
Raises success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot; also improves SIMPLE tasks from 70.2% to 86.9%.
papers.selection_reason: Object-guided perceptual memory for whole-body VLA humanoid manipulation, relevant to embodied memory and robot learning.
papers.title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: WholeBodyMem improves humanoid loco-manipulation by selectively remembering task-relevant object events from before the robot acts.

papers.abstract: Dynamic interactive object search in large-scale human environments presents substantial challenges for existing methods. Current scene representations like 3D Scene Graphs (3DSG) only provide coarse-grained spatial segmentation and cannot identify functional areas such as storage or leisure areas. Without functional area understanding, existing methods are constrained to exhaustive sequential exploration at large scales, resulting in inefficient search behaviors -- particularly in open-layout environments with numerous interactive objects such as drawers and cabinets. Moreover, these methods lack adaptability to environmental dynamics such as object relocations. To address these limitations, this paper proposes CMAR-search, a novel framework built upon Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning (CMAR). Our approach leverages commonsense about area functionalities and aggregates environmental memory to construct a Functional 3D Scene Graph (F3DSG), which organizes the environment into functional areas with their associated containers. Through this structured representation, CMAR enables hierarchical action planning at both macro-area and micro-container levels, empowering the system to efficiently identify and inspect semantically relevant areas for effective object search. Notably, CMAR continuously integrates real-time perception, accumulated memory, and commonsense to dynamically relocalize objects in changing environments. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that CMAR-search significantly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in both success rate and search efficiency for object search in dynamic interactive environments.
authors: Kaiyao Liao, Qingfeng Li, Xinlei Zhang, Chen Chen, Qing Sun, Jianwei Niu
bullets: Addresses coarse 3D scene representations, exhaustive exploration, and difficulty handling relocated objects.
Builds a Functional 3D Scene Graph (F3DSG) that organizes spaces by functional areas and associated containers.
Uses hierarchical planning to select relevant areas first, then inspect specific containers such as drawers and cabinets.
Continuously integrates perception, memory, and commonsense to relocalize objects as environments change.
Experiments in simulation and real-world settings show higher search success and efficiency than existing baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Functional 3D scene graph and memory-augmented reasoning for object search in dynamic environments fit embodied navigation and memory.
papers.title: CMAR-search: Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning for Object Search in Dynamic Interactive Environments
papers.tldr: CMAR-search combines commonsense, environmental memory, and functional scene understanding to efficiently find objects in dynamic, interactive environments.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic mapping in dynamic real-world environments is essential for embodied intelligence and long-term autonomy. However, existing methods often involve a trade-off: lightweight online mapping is efficient but captures limited semantic context, while dense mapping provides richer semantics at higher computational cost and is more vulnerable to distractors. They also struggle to relocalize objects after scene changes. To address these challenges, we propose the Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System (OASIS), a unified system for online mapping, complex open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments. Motivated by the observation that indoor scenes are organized around stable semantic anchors, OASIS represents the environment using a sparse set of anchor nodes, each maintaining a unified multimodal representation that integrates semantic descriptions, visual features, and geometric states for reasoning, verification, and navigation. Its compact anchor-centric memory supports on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval, reducing redundant storage while improving retrieval reliability. To handle scene dynamics, OASIS further reuses transient observations collected during navigation to relocalize moved objects. Experiments in both simulation and real-world environments, including standard retrieval benchmarks and navigation tasks under both static and dynamic settings, demonstrate that our system can perform complex open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation, while also enabling relocation of displaced objects after scene changes.
authors: Kaiyao Liao, Qingfeng Li, Chen Chen, Xiaoze Wu, Qing Sun, Jianwei Niu
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–semantic richness trade-off in online mapping and the difficulty of relocalizing objects after scene changes.
Represents scenes with sparse anchor nodes that combine semantic, visual, and geometric information for reasoning, verification, and navigation.
Uses on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval to reduce redundant storage while supporting complex queries.
Reuses transient navigation observations to relocalize objects that have moved.
Validated in simulation and real-world settings across retrieval benchmarks and static/dynamic navigation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Anchor-centric multimodal memory for open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation in dynamic scenes; combines spatial understanding with embodied memory.
papers.title: OASIS: Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System for Open-Vocabulary Retrieval and Navigation in Dynamic Environments
papers.tldr: OASIS enables efficient open-vocabulary object retrieval and navigation in dynamic environments using a sparse, multimodal memory built around stable semantic scene anchors.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in foundation-model agents have enabled increasingly capable embodied systems for long-horizon planning and interaction. However, embodied agents require fast, closed-loop decisions as they continuously perceive and act on a changing environment. Deploying strong cloud agents leaves the platform idle for seconds between consecutive actions, while lightweight local models respond quickly but are more vulnerable to errors. Existing hierarchical architectures typically assign models fixed roles, whereas conventional model routers make stateless per-request decisions. We present CARE, a critic-guided adaptive execution framework that dynamically determines when to escalate control from a local executor to a stronger cloud model. A lightweight critic model monitors execution reliability and triggers escalation when local execution becomes unreliable; once escalated, control persists until the agent recovers, avoiding step-wise switching. To support such control transfer, a shared handoff memory maintains execution context and task-level progress across executors, enabling the model to intervene without restarting from scratch. Across diverse embodied benchmarks, CARE improves task success by 6.3-18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline. CARE further approaches or exceeds Cloud-only success while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8-82.6%.
authors: Wei Zhang, Lirong Xiang, Charles Fleming
bullets: Targets the latency of cloud-only agents and the error vulnerability of lightweight local agents in long-horizon embodied tasks.
Uses a lightweight critic to monitor local execution and trigger persistent escalation rather than making stateless per-step routing decisions.
Maintains shared handoff memory so cloud control preserves execution context and task progress without restarting.
Across diverse embodied benchmarks, improves task success by 6.3–18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline.
Approaches or exceeds Cloud-only success while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8–82.6%.
papers.selection_reason: Critic-guided cloud/local escalation with shared handoff memory for embodied agents; improves latency while maintaining task success.
papers.title: Know When to Escalate: Critic-Guided Adaptive Execution for Cloud-Local Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: CARE adaptively escalates embodied-agent control from a fast local model to a stronger cloud model when a critic detects unreliability, improving success while reducing action latency.

papers.abstract: Unlike conventional GUI agents, personalized GUI agents require user preferences to guide sequential execution over changing GUI states. This raises two challenges: determining HOW each preference should alter execution strategy and WHEN it should take effect along the interaction trajectory. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate overall task success, offering limited insight into these questions. We introduce PrefDiag-Bench with two components: (1) a categorization of preferences into five types, characterizing HOW they affect execution; and (2) a stage-wise diagnostic framework with 1,664 probes, tracing WHEN preferences should take effect and where failures occur. We evaluate eleven GUI agent systems, including end-to-end agents and agentic workflows, under two forms of user context: explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs. Although existing agents achieve relatively high completion rates on non-personalized tasks, performance is substantially lower on preference-personalized tasks. Even the best-performing model, Seed-2.0-Pro, achieves only 47.17% on Process preferences under explicit user profiles. Agents struggle particularly with Ranking and Process preferences. Further analysis reveals two key capability bottlenecks: selecting relevant evidence from user history and recognizing when preferences should take effect during execution. Controlled interventions that explicitly provide relevant evidence improve end-to-end task success by up to 7.06%. PrefDiag-Bench offers a more systematic evaluation of GUI agents' personalization capabilities beyond overall task success. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Zhixin-L/PrefDiag-Bench.
authors: Zhixin Lin, Dongliang Xu, Jungang Li, Shidong Pan, Jun Feng, Yanbin Sun, Jing Li, Liang Liu, Yue Yao
bullets: Categorizes preferences into five types based on how they alter execution.
Uses 1,664 stage-wise probes to identify when preferences should take effect and where failures occur.
Evaluates 11 GUI agent systems using explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs.
Agents struggle most with Ranking and Process preferences; the best reported Process score is 47.17% under explicit profiles.
Providing relevant evidence from user history improves end-to-end success by up to 7.06%.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on behavioral memory logs and personalization in GUI agents, addressing the challenge of retaining and utilizing user history for agent adaptation.
papers.title: Diagnosing Personalization Failures in Mobile GUI Agents
papers.tldr: PrefDiag-Bench diagnoses how and when mobile GUI agents apply user preferences, revealing major personalization weaknesses despite strong non-personalized task performance.

papers.abstract: LLM agents that act on live Web data must combine heterogeneous evidence, remember what they have done and improve from outcomes without weakening their own safeguards. We study this problem in autonomous investing, where every action is irreversible and based on untrusted Web content. We present Steward, a multi-agent LLM system that draws the boundary of self-evolution in its type system. First, nine role-specialised agents decide jointly: four analysts read news feeds, SEC filings, macroeconomic series and market data and emit typed reports, from which a Portfolio Manager sets target positions that a protected Risk Manager audits. Second, a seven-layer shared memory, assembled by code from the system's own record, gives each decision its position context, the market narrative, calibration and the agent's past decisions. Third, the system improves itself by review: code grades every trade and forecast nightly and writes the grades into memory, and each quarter a reflector proposes prompt learnings that a deterministic gate applies reversibly and replay of recorded inputs verifies. All three operate around an invariant core of order arithmetic, risk rules and discipline-agent prompts that no self-edit can reach. In a five-month live deployment (102 trading days, 1,632 LLM calls), the system contained a 24.6% sector drawdown to a 0.3% loss; in replay of its recorded inputs, a single model given the same raw data traded more and lost 1.35 points against the market over five days where the joint design showed no significant loss, and no injected instruction was followed; and a 2015-2026 backtest shows the core alone lowering the maximum drawdown under all 50 random entry policies. The reflector traced the dominant failure to its root cause, and the gate applied a learning that the agent adopted on trigger evenings and on no control evening. Code: https://github.com/yebof/quant-agent
authors: Yebo Feng, Jingyang Dai, Liangrui Pan, Nelson Lau, Jiahua Xu, Yang Liu
bullets: Combines nine specialized agents to analyze heterogeneous financial and Web data, set positions, and audit risk.
Uses seven-layer shared memory to provide decisions with market context, calibration, and prior-action history.
Enables reversible, code-graded self-improvement through periodic reflection, deterministic gating, and replay verification.
In a five-month live deployment, it contained a 24.6% sector drawdown to a 0.3% loss; replay tests found no injected-instruction compliance.
A protected invariant core covers order arithmetic, risk rules, and discipline prompts, while backtests indicate reduced maximum drawdown across random-entry policies.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a multi-agent system with a shared memory mechanism and self-review process for agents, directly relevant to embodied memory and test-time learning in agent systems.
papers.title: Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing: A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core
papers.tldr: Steward is a governed multi-agent LLM investing system that supports self-improvement while protecting core risk and execution safeguards.

papers.abstract: Should an embodied agent's experience be baked into its policy weights, or kept external and retrieved at inference? A memory-augmented teacher (a VLM that retrieves lessons, with their episode images, from its own past attempts) produces trajectories on a vision-conditioned reach task; from the same trajectories we distil LoRA student policies and evaluate them under matched protocols, including one that re-attaches the teacher's frozen retrieval buffer to a fixed set of student weights. We pre-registered the hypotheses, arms, tests, and analysis rules before training and before any p-value. Distilling the memory-augmented behaviour into weights beat an action-only control by +1 pp (n.s.); the registered test proves underpowered for its own minimum effect, so we withdraw - rather than refute - the memory-in-weights claim. Attaching retrieval to a fixed set of student weights added +34 pp (z=5.15), reaching the pooled memory-augmented teacher reference (49.3%); the pre-registered protocol contrast agrees (+23 pp, z=3.36); under a pre-registered auto-reset sensitivity count the two are +36 and +29 pp. An exploratory behavioural probe with pre-registered per-arm predictions is consistent with behavioural distillation transferring the marginal correction but not the conditional, situation-specific correction that retrieval supplies. The recipe that follows is to externalise the memory: in follow-up controls registered before they ran, the same frozen buffer lifts the base model with no adapter to 48% (sensitivity 48%) and the other three adapters from 19-26% to 53-55% (sensitivity 17-21% to 50-55%), and the adapter adds nothing detectable once the buffer is attached. On a second, harder task, the retrieval advantage points the same direction but falls short of significance (+6 pp, 95% CI [-4.5, +16.4]); exploratory diagnostics tie the attenuation to memory coverage.
bullets: A pre-registered study compares memory-augmented retrieval, weight-distilled policies, and fixed student policies with the teacher’s retrieval buffer attached.

Distilling memory-augmented behavior into weights improved performance by only 1 percentage point over an action-only control; the test was underpowered, so the claim was withdrawn rather than refuted.
Attaching the frozen retrieval buffer to student weights produced a large gain (+34 percentage points), matching the memory-augmented teacher’s 49.3% reference performance.
Follow-up controls found the buffer substantially improved the base model and other adapters, while adapters added no detectable benefit once retrieval was attached.
On a harder second task, the retrieval advantage was smaller and not significant, with exploratory evidence linking the reduction to limited memory coverage.
papers.selection_reason: Directly studies external memory versus policy weights for embodied agents; fits embodied memory and robot learning.
papers.title: Externalise the Memory: A Pre-Registered Study of Where an Embodied Agent's Experience Should Live
papers.tldr: For this embodied reach task, keeping experience in an external retrieval buffer is more effective than distilling it into policy weights alone.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are flexible in language interaction, but using them as long-horizon planners is costly and prone to hallucinated or invalid actions. This paper targets a different role for LLMs: constrained bridges between language and symbolic planning. We propose MemPlan, a memory-conditioned PDDL planning framework for partially observable interactive text environments. MemPlan keeps the PDDL domain fixed and reconstructs the PDDL problem at each step from parsed observations, candidate hypotheses, and interaction memory. Positive graph memory assigns relevance-based action costs to candidate hypotheses for missing objects, locations, or conditions, guiding the planner toward more plausible checks. Negative memory records execution-refuted assumptions and compiles them into exclusion constraints, preventing repeated attempts at candidates already contradicted by feedback. A unified schema-conditioned language--symbol interface, trained offline with supervised fine-tuning, connects text environments to the planning loop through observation-to-fact parsing and symbolic-action-to-command grounding. Experiments on TextWorld, ALFWorld, and Robotouille show that MemPlan improves task completion and step efficiency over language-only and PDDL-aware baselines, while substantially reducing online token cost compared with LLM-planning baselines such as ReAct. The same fine-tuned interface is also reused across TextWorld task types without task-specific fine-tuning. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/tewiSong/MemPlan.
bullets: Addresses costly, hallucination-prone long-horizon planning by constraining LLMs to translate between language and symbolic planning.
Reconstructs the PDDL problem after each observation using parsed facts, hypotheses, and interaction memory.
Positive memory prioritizes plausible missing entities and conditions; negative memory excludes assumptions refuted by feedback.
Evaluated on TextWorld, ALFWorld, and Robotouille, improving task completion and step efficiency while reducing online token cost versus LLM-planning baselines.
The same offline fine-tuned interface transfers across TextWorld task types without task-specific fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-conditioned PDDL planning with interaction and environment memory for partially observable environments fits embodied memory.
papers.title: MemPlan: Memory-Conditioned PDDL Planning for Partially Observable Text Environments
papers.tldr: MemPlan combines memory-conditioned PDDL replanning with a fixed language–symbol interface to improve efficient, reliable planning in partially observable text environments.

papers.abstract: Today's multimodal assistants are typically prompted to interpret the visual evidence presented to them. To offload the cognitive burden of remembering across long horizons, wearable assistants should instead proactively acquire and maintain useful memory as the user's surroundings evolve. Doing so on the user's behalf requires identifying what matters, understanding the scene in real time, and initiating memory maintenance in the background while the user stays focused on their activities. We introduce ProactEgoMem, a benchmark that evaluates proactive memory in streaming egocentric video. Three tasks ground the evaluation in ambient environmental needs: Information Capture (IC) preserves transient yet dense visual information, State Tracking (ST) follows changing object states, and Location Tracking (LT) records object movements. The benchmark defines its protocol at two levels of proactiveness: the Notification Level asks for a single timely notification that satisfies the user's intent, while the deeper Intervention Level asks the agent to maintain memory on the user's behalf through an active start-to-stop tool lifecycle. Parallel ProactEgoMem-Daily and ProactEgoMem-Sci tracks contain 300/100 clips covering daily and scientific use cases, paired with 1000/500 questions in ProactEgoMem-QA, which measures the quality of the proactively acquired memory. Across proprietary, open-source, video-language, and streaming baselines, even the strongest models fail to capture memory both timely and accurately. ProactEgoMem provides a rigorous evaluation foundation for proactive multimodal assistance and for video agents that co-exist with their users.
authors: Ruotong Liao, Meikel Kokowski, Xiaoxiao Sun, Yongqin Xian, Laura Bravo S\'anchez, Shiye Su, Federico Tombari, Serena Yeung-Levy, Volker Tresp
bullets: Evaluates Information Capture, State Tracking, and Location Tracking for ambient memory needs.
Tests two levels of proactiveness: timely notifications and active start-to-stop memory-maintenance interventions.
Includes Daily and Scientific tracks with associated question-answering evaluations.
Finds that even strong proprietary, open-source, video-language, and streaming baselines struggle to be both timely and accurate.
Supports evaluation of proactive multimodal assistants and video agents operating alongside users.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for proactive memory in streaming egocentric video; directly targets embodied memory and video-language understanding.
papers.title: ProactEgoMem: Benchmarking Proactive Memory in Streaming Egocentric Video
papers.tldr: ProactEgoMem benchmarks whether video agents can proactively capture, update, and maintain useful memories from streaming egocentric video.

papers.abstract: Geometric structure is essential for robotic manipulation and understanding the 3D world. Most VLA models rely on 2D representations of current observations, while geometry-aware approaches often require additional 3D information. However, geometry inferred independently from individual observations is often discarded rather than accumulated into a persistent task representation. Our key insight is that action generation needs a compact, task-relevant geometric abstraction that can be continuously updated, rather than a complete, renderable 3D reconstruction at every step. We introduce GeoMem-VLA, a VLA framework that internalizes explicit 3D supervision into dedicated geometric tokens and maintains them as temporal memory for action generation, without directly aligning the VLM's native visual embeddings with the teacher feature space. During training, a frozen geometry foundation model supervises learnable GeoPlan tokens through a geometric flow-matching objective over the current scene point map and future end-effector tracks. These tokens are integrated with the memory of observation representations, where historical information is retrieved, adaptively fused with current observations, and consolidated to retain event frames as the task progresses. At inference, the policy retrieves historical representations and fuses them with the current working representation to predict actions, without invoking the 3D teacher or explicitly reconstructing the scene. After benchmark-specific downstream adaptation, GeoMem-VLA achieves 98.9% average success on LIBERO and 91.10% / 91.24% on RoboTwin's clean/randomized settings. Across five real-world tasks, GeoMem-VLA achieves 78.0% average success. These results suggest that internalizing and remembering 3D scene understanding is a promising approach to robot control.
authors: Qinfan Zhang, Yifan Luo, Haoyuan Shi, Guanlin Liu, Han Dong, Haozhe Shan, Yong Dai, Xiangcong Ren, Xiaozhu Ju
bullets: Addresses the loss of accumulated geometric information in VLA models that primarily use current 2D observations.
Learns dedicated GeoPlan tokens from frozen geometry-model supervision over scene point maps and future end-effector tracks.
Retrieves, fuses, and consolidates geometric and visual memories across time without requiring 3D reconstruction or the teacher model at inference.
Reports 98.9% average success on LIBERO, 91.10%/91.24% on RoboTwin clean/randomized settings, and 78.0% across five real-world tasks.
Scope: performance depends on benchmark-specific downstream adaptation and is evaluated on the reported simulation and real-world tasks.
papers.selection_reason: VLA framework with 3D geometric temporal memory for robot manipulation; directly fits embodied action and memory.
papers.title: GeoMem-VLA: Internalizing 3D Scene Understanding into Temporal Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: GeoMem-VLA equips vision-language-action models with compact, temporally persistent 3D geometric memory for improved robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance across embodied manipulation tasks by unifying visual understanding, language conditioning, and action generation. However, long-horizon tasks can involve non-Markovian dependencies: successful decisions may require retaining task progress and past interaction outcomes, while partial observability and execution errors compound over time. Existing work has begun to address these challenges by augmenting foundation-model policies with memory and by introducing hierarchical architectures that separate high-level planning from low-level execution. We organize the high-level VLM as a robotic agent through an editable harness to maintain task context and improve planning through execution experience. We instantiate this approach as SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), with a fixed VLA executor providing low-level control. The harness maintains and updates task context using observations and execution feedback to guide subsequent planning. Self-evolution uses environment rollouts to propose and evaluate harness revisions, with the selected configuration fixed before held-out testing. On RoboMME, SERA achieves 51.38% overall success with autonomous selection, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. Our exploration suggests that agentic planning is a promising direction for history-dependent robotic manipulation.
authors: Tingwen Du, Haoyu Guo, Hanxue Zhang, Xuanxu Wang, Junting Dong, Chao Gao, Mingfei Han, Tao Lu, Mulin Yu, Chunhua Shen, Xiaojun Chang, Zhihui Li
bullets: Targets non-Markovian manipulation tasks where progress, past outcomes, partial observability, and errors affect future decisions.
Uses an editable harness around a high-level VLM, paired with a fixed VLA executor for low-level control.
Maintains task context from observations and execution feedback to guide later plans.
Self-evolves by proposing and evaluating harness revisions through environment rollouts before held-out testing.
On RoboMME, autonomous self-evolution improves overall success from 44.38% to 51.38%.
papers.selection_reason: VLA-based robotic manipulation with self-evolving memory harness for history-dependent tasks.
papers.title: From VLM Planners to Robotic Agents: Self-Evolving Harnesses for History-Dependent Manipulation
papers.tldr: SERA turns a high-level vision-language model into a self-evolving robotic agent that uses execution history to improve long-horizon manipulation planning.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires a robot to remember task-relevant information beyond its short observation window. Existing memory-augmented policies typically retrieve relevant information from history and reason over it at execution time, placing a heavy reasoning burden on the high-level model. To address this challenge, we propose PAL (\textbf{P}lan first, \textbf{A}ct \textbf{L}ater), a hierarchical memory framework for vision-language robot manipulation. It maintains a short-term visual buffer, a semantic-event memory, and an executable \texttt{subtask\_list}. A high-level vision-language model (VLM) converts streaming visual observations into the \texttt{subtask\_list}. At execution time, the VLM selects the currently relevant subtask from the \texttt{subtask\_list} and passes it to a low-level vision-language-action (VLA) policy. To teach the model what to write to memory and when to update it, we introduce a two-stage data generation procedure that first expands sparse update supervision and then uses self-labeling with task-grounded verification to generate training data that better match the state distribution encountered during execution. We evaluate our approach on memory-dependent benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks. On RoboMME, PAL achieves a \textbf{56.05\%} success rate, outperforming the strongest baseline, FrameSamp-Modul, at 44.51\%. In real-world experiments across four manipulation tasks, \pal{} reaches \textbf{60.83\%} overall success, surpassing MemER (45.00\%) and FrameSamp-Modul (28.33\%). These results show that proactively writing future-relevant subtasks into hierarchical memory improves long-horizon visual reasoning and robot control. Code and videos can be found on our website: https://qinghangliu.github.io/pal-webpage/
authors: Qinghang Liu, Conglin Wang, Zongsheng Li, Boyong He, Han Gao, Pengcheng Wang, Tao Sun, Lige Liu, Chang Liu
bullets: Targets the heavy reasoning burden of retrieving and interpreting history during execution.
Uses hierarchical memory: a short-term visual buffer, semantic-event memory, and executable subtask list.
A high-level VLM converts streaming observations into subtasks, then selects relevant subtasks for a low-level VLA policy.
Trains memory updates with staged supervision expansion and task-grounded self-labeling.
Achieves 56.05% success on RoboMME and 60.83% overall success across four real-world manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical memory with VLM-generated subtask lists for vision-language robot manipulation fits embodied memory and VLA control.
papers.title: Plan First, Act Later: Streaming Reasoning for Executable Memory in Robot Control
papers.tldr: PAL improves long-horizon robot manipulation by planning future-relevant subtasks into executable memory before action time.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic operation requires memory that scales with essential information rather than execution time. We present a parameter-space memory framework where each episode is stored as a separable object. A neural implicit representation is fitted to episode video from a shared, meta-learned initialization; the resulting weight delta constitutes the memory. Crucially, this delta remains a fixed size regardless of whether the episode spans a hundred or a hundred thousand frames. A learned projector maps the weight delta into token embeddings, conditioning a language model for question answering and a decoder for joint command regression, without frame retrieval at query time. On RoboMME, the language model exceeds chance across all question types, and the decoder achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.51. Replacing the delta with matched noise drops performance by 11.4 points, while random-origin weights are non-decodable, proving the meta-learned initialization is essential for embedding episode content. By representing individual experiences as fixed-size weight deltas in a common parameter space, this approach decouples memory cost from time horizon and provides a basis for scalable streaming memory.
authors: Leann Alhashishi, Christos Margadji, Sebastian William Pattinson
bullets: Addresses the challenge of scaling long-horizon robotic memory with episode duration.
Fits a neural implicit representation to episode video from a shared meta-learned initialization; the weight delta becomes the memory.
Projects each delta into tokens for language-model question answering and a decoder for joint-command regression.
On RoboMME, the language model performs above chance across question types, while action decoding reaches mean R² = 0.51.
Noise replacement reduces performance by 11.4 points, and random-origin weights are non-decodable, highlighting the importance of meta-learned initialization.
papers.selection_reason: Parameter-space episodic memory for robot episodes enables recall and action, directly relevant to embodied memory and robot learning.
papers.title: inr2action: Encoding Robot Episodes as Neural Implicit Representations for Recall and Action
papers.tldr: inr2action stores each robot episode as a fixed-size neural-network weight delta that supports memory-based question answering and action prediction without retrieving frames.

papers.abstract: 4D scene graphs require persistent object identity when an object disappears inside an opaque carrier and later reappears as a fresh detection. When appearance and target-centric motion are unavailable, identity recovery must rely on relational history. We formulate cross-visibility-gap identity persistence as historical-node recovery through a remembered target--carrier binding. We introduce CVG-SGM, a perception-frontend-compatible transfer--maintain--read memory. Geometry-weighted cross-node interaction transfers target-specific evidence into carrier states, a shared per-node GRU maintains this information during transport, and a two-time readout combines stored carrier--identity compatibility with current detection--carrier geometry to recover the historical identity. In the controlled one-identity-per-carrier setting, CVG-SGM achieves 1.000 re-link accuracy, compared with 0.570 for both no-memory and parameter-count-matched no-write controls. It also generalizes to scene-disjoint, unseen longer visibility gaps. On real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level episodes, it correctly re-links 36/36 held-out detections, compared with 28/36 for the strongest fixed carrier--identity control. Counterfactual carrier-memory swaps redirect predictions according to the swapped bindings, supporting the role of stored relational information in identity recovery. The current approach remains limited by shared-carrier identity ambiguity and does not provide end-to-end raw-video re-identification.
authors: Jiahui Hu, Li Gao, Yu Liu, Pengzhan Zhou
bullets: Addresses identity recovery when objects disappear inside opaque carriers and later reappear as new detections.
Uses geometry-weighted target-to-carrier transfer, per-node GRU memory during transport, and a two-time compatibility readout.
Achieves 1.000 re-link accuracy in the controlled one-identity-per-carrier setting, versus 0.570 for both no-memory controls.
Correctly re-links 36/36 held-out real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level detections, compared with 28/36 for the strongest fixed-binding control.
Generalizes to unseen longer gaps, but remains limited by shared-carrier ambiguity and lacks end-to-end raw-video re-identification.
papers.selection_reason: Memory mechanism for persistent object identity across visibility gaps in 4D scene graphs, combining spatiotemporal memory with 3D scene understanding.
papers.title: Cross-Visibility-Gap Identity Persistence for 4D Scene Graphs
papers.tldr: CVG-SGM preserves object identities across visibility gaps by storing target–carrier relational bindings, achieving perfect re-linking in controlled and reported real-feature episodes.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are moving beyond reactive responses toward proactive assistance that anticipates user needs without explicit requests. However, existing proactive agents primarily address immediate needs, while many everyday situations involve delayed intentions that can only be acted on hours or days later. Humans handle such intentions through prospective memory, the ability to remember to act on an intention when the right moment arises. In this paper, we introduce ProMemAgent, the first proactive agent to incorporate prospective memory over everyday sensory contexts for long-horizon proactive assistance. ProMemAgent organizes past sensory perceptions (e.g., egocentric video and audio) into context-aware memory, generating prospective cues and linking earlier events with subsequent developments for future retrieval. Given the current context, it retrieves relevant past events and performs memory-augmented proactive reasoning to determine whether assistance is needed. We further introduce CPMBench, the first benchmark for evaluating long-horizon proactive assistance over sensory contexts, comprising 1,000 instances across eight everyday categories. Extensive experiments show that ProMemAgent achieves the best memory retrieval performance and consistently outperforms all baselines on long-horizon proactive assistance.
authors: Lilin Xu, Linyang He, Kaiyuan Hou, Yuang Fan, Minghui Zhao, Xuhai Xu, Xiaofan Jiang
bullets: Addresses the gap between immediate-response agents and delayed everyday intentions that require action hours or days later.
Organizes egocentric video and audio perceptions into context-aware memories with prospective cues linking earlier events to later developments.
Retrieves relevant past events from the current context and performs memory-augmented reasoning to decide whether assistance is needed.
Introduces CPMBench, a benchmark with 1,000 instances across eight everyday categories for evaluating long-horizon proactive assistance.
Experiments report the best memory retrieval performance and consistent improvements over all evaluated baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Prospective memory over egocentric sensory contexts directly targets embodied memory for long-horizon proactive assistance.
papers.title: ProMemAgent: Long-Horizon Proactive Assistance with Context-Aware Prospective Memory from Sensory Perceptions
papers.tldr: ProMemAgent enables long-horizon proactive assistance by using prospective memory over past sensory contexts to anticipate future user needs.

papers.abstract: Experience generated during deployment offers an opportunity for robots to improve policy reliability through learning from their own executions. However, learning through human corrections requires teleoperators to monitor execution and intervene when policies fail, a demand that is difficult to meet as robot fleets grow. We introduce collective experience learning (CEL), a learning paradigm in which deployed robots share their execution experience to improve a common policy. We realize CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT), which uses failure contexts from robot executions to retrieve relevant trajectory segments from the fleet's shared successful experience and uses their actions as supervision for policy updates, without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) coordinates experience collection, policy optimization and policy distribution despite local interruptions within the robot fleet. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from training data collection. With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience and FERT generally achieves higher success rates across the evaluated sizes. On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots increases success from 79.2% to 98.3%. These results support collective experience as a practical basis for scalable robot learning and a path towards improving policy reliability during deployment without collecting additional expert corrective actions.
bullets: Problem: Human monitoring and corrective interventions do not scale as robot fleets grow.
Method: FERT retrieves relevant successful trajectory segments using failure contexts and fine-tunes the policy with their actions as supervision.
System: FATS asynchronously coordinates experience collection, training, and policy distribution despite robot interruptions.
Results: Across five real-world manipulation tasks, policies reached 93.3–99.2% success on robots excluded from data collection; larger fleets generally improved performance.
Scope: Demonstrated for deployment-time learning in real-world manipulation, including phone packaging, where 96 robots improved success from 79.2% to 98.3%.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a collective learning paradigm (CEL) and a specific fine-tuning method (FERT) for robot fleets, directly addressing robot manipulation and learning from deployment experience.
papers.title: Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots
papers.tldr: Collective experience learning lets robot fleets improve a shared policy from deployment failures and successful trajectories without additional expert corrections, achieving high reliability across manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Long-term personalized agents are required to reason over distributed history across modalities and evolving dialogue states. While existing flat cross-modal methods compress visual evidence prematurely and struggle with temporally stale observations, they neglect the necessity to unify multimodal and cross-session evidence. Crucially, raw multimodal memories are inherently entangled and heterogeneous, making fine-grained visual grounding and cross-modal reasoning computationally prohibitive. To this end, we present latent multimodal memory reasoning, i.e., LMMR, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that shifts long-term multimodal memory organization into a continuous latent space. Specifically, (i) instead of converting images to text and relying on static retrieval, LMMR maps both textual hidden states and visual patch features into a shared Sparse Autoencoder concept space, establishing sparse activations as common semantic addresses to dynamically construct a turn-level multimodal memory graph. (ii) A graph encoder then aggregates cross-modal and temporal dependencies across the task-specific latent subgraph, injecting the graph readout as a continuous residual rollout into the generation backbone while retaining native visual tokens to preserve fine-grained details. Extensive experiments on nine Mem-Gallery tasks and twelve MemEye settings demonstrate that LMMR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in capturing complex multimodal dependencies while enabling faithful and grounded responses.
authors: Cai Ke, Xinghao Chen, Yuanchen Bei, Yuni Lai, Keyu Chen, Ruizhi Qiao, Siyu An, Junnan Dong, Ruifeng Xu, Xing Sun
bullets: Addresses distributed, evolving multimodal history, including temporally stale observations and heterogeneous raw memories.
Maps text hidden states and visual patch features into a shared Sparse Autoencoder concept space with sparse semantic addresses.
Builds turn-level multimodal memory graphs and uses a graph encoder to aggregate cross-modal and temporal dependencies.
Injects graph representations into the generation backbone while retaining native visual tokens for fine-grained grounding.
Experiments across nine Mem-Gallery tasks and twelve MemEye settings report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in multimodal dependency capture and response faithfulness.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a neuro-symbolic framework for long-term multimodal memory reasoning, mapping visual and textual evidence into a shared latent space to handle spatiotemporal dependencies.
papers.title: Latent Multimodal Memory Reasoning
papers.tldr: LMMR organizes long-term multimodal memories in a shared latent concept space and reasons over their temporal and cross-modal relationships for more faithful responses.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied agents face temporal confusion and incomplete or distorted records, recurring errors from fixed memory rules, and growing storage and retrieval costs. We present BetaMem, a framework for building and evolving traceable long-term memory through six linked layers: working, spatial, entity, episodic, experiential, and procedural memory. A dual-level write contract constrains operation executability and source support for content: supervised fine-tuning learns compliant memory operations, while reinforcement learning combines repeated sampling with teacher verification of the original observations to reward complete, accurate records and penalize omissions, distortion, and unsupported content. We formulate failure-driven policy recursive self-improvement through diagnosis along the causal sequence of memory operations and local rule repairs gated by independent replay. Atomic tools frame storage, updates, retrieval, and forgetting as cost-utility allocation under storage and read budgets. Using the open-source Qwen3.5-9B model for memory generation, BetaMem achieves overall scores of 48.08% on M3-Bench-robot, 92.08% on LoCoMo, 72.6% on OpenEQA EM-EQA, and 62.4% on EgoLifeQA, the highest among the listed memory methods under their respective evaluation protocols. Training the model for memory generation raises the contract pass rate from 50.9% to 86.2% while reducing output tokens per stored action by 47.3%. A separate Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluation on EMem-Bench achieves an average success rate of 38.4% and an average error recurrence rate of 24.9%. We perform best among evaluated methods using comparably sized open-source models. Category results show that we have advantages in integrating information across observations, recalling events over long histories, and inferring personal habits.
authors: Mai Liu, He Sun, Siru Zhong, Kerun Chen, Hao Yan, Xiaohui Lv, Shuai Tao, Wulong Liu
bullets: Addresses temporal confusion, incomplete or distorted records, recurring memory errors, and rising storage/retrieval costs.
Uses six linked memory layers: working, spatial, entity, episodic, experiential, and procedural.
Combines contract-constrained memory operations, supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning with teacher verification, and failure-driven rule repair.
Models storage, updates, retrieval, and forgetting as cost–utility allocation under storage and read budgets.
Reports strong results across several benchmarks, including 48.08% on M3-Bench-robot, 92.08% on LoCoMo, and improved contract compliance from 50.9% to 86.2%.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-layer embodied memory framework directly matches embodied memory subtopic.
papers.title: BetaMem: Learning to Remember a Changing World for Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: BetaMem is a layered, self-improving memory framework that helps embodied agents maintain accurate, traceable long-term memories under changing environments and resource limits.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) relies on retaining and using relevant observations. Yet growing histories introduce redundancy, and retained information may remain underused. We introduce ReInsBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines history utilization through controlled continuation trials. Its results show that history-review reinstruction can recover navigation failures using the existing task context. Motivated by this finding, we propose ReInsVLN, a training-free framework supporting memory construction and utilization in frozen navigators. Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression constructs compact visual context through temporal redundancy reduction, coverage-aware protection, and instruction-guided token selection. Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders guide navigators to revisit retained observations according to a predefined schedule, without additional model calls. On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN improves success rates by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points over the native StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1, reaching 64.27% and 64.44%, respectively. Visual compression largely preserves navigation performance while reducing prefill latency and KV cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%, respectively, on matched observation workloads. Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the applicability of ReInsVLN to sequential instruction following and ordinal navigation.
authors: Siwei Cheng, Hao Wu, Zitong Qi, Xinming Zhang, Haoyu Xi, Peiran Yin, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Xiaoyu Shen, Wei Zhang
bullets: ReInsBench diagnoses how effectively vision-and-language navigators use historical observations through controlled continuation trials.
Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression removes temporal redundancy while preserving instruction-relevant visual context.
Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders prompt frozen navigators to revisit retained observations on a predefined schedule without extra model calls.
On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN reaches 64.27% and 64.44% success, improving over StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1 by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points.
Visual compression reduces prefill latency and KV-cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%; robot trials support broader sequential instruction-following use.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free VLN with history compression and reminders, improving navigation while reducing KV cache; fits VLN, embodied memory, and token/cache efficiency.
papers.title: ReInsVLN: Revisiting Historical Evidence for Training-Free Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: ReInsVLN is a training-free memory framework that compresses and periodically reactivates navigation history, improving VLN performance while reducing inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation often depends on short-term cues - such as brief contacts, temporary occlusions, and intermediate object states - that are ambiguous in a single frame and can only be resolved by integrating observations over time. However, injecting historical information solely by enlarging the history window is computationally costly and frequently yields limited gains due to substantial redundancy and task-agnostic, inflexible sampling of observations. We propose CondenseVLA, a multi-frame VLA policy with a learnable decoder-side history condensation module for using short-term visual context in action decoding. Given a sequence of cached per-frame features from the VLM backbone, CondenseVLA distills observation history into a fixed set of slot tokens using learnable queries and multi-head cross-attention. Simple auxiliary regularization penalizes overlap among slot attention maps and decorrelates slot embeddings, encouraging complementary attention and reducing slot redundancy. Across the evaluated tasks, CondenseVLA improves Simpler-WidowX success from 58.7% to 69.8% (+11.1 percentage points), achieves 97.2% on LIBERO, and reaches 52.8% on real-world tasks. It achieves 21.6% success on memory-dependent RMBench tasks. These results support selective condensation of bounded recent visual evidence for action decoding, while harder multi-observation tasks expose the limits of a finite history window. Project page: https://github.com/FeiyangHong/CondenseVLA
authors: Feiyang Hong, Yujie Wei, Bo Zhao, Xiu Su, Hongxun Yao, Shuo Yang
bullets: Targets short-term cues such as contacts, occlusions, and intermediate object states that single frames cannot resolve.
