Uses decoder-side learnable queries and multi-head cross-attention to compress cached per-frame VLM features into a fixed set of history slots.
Regularizes slot attention and embeddings to encourage complementary, non-redundant representations.
Improves Simpler-WidowX success from 58.7% to 69.8%, reaches 97.2% on LIBERO and 52.8% on real-world tasks.
Achieves 21.6% on memory-dependent RMBench tasks, highlighting limits of a finite recent-history window.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes CondenseVLA, a VLA policy that condenses visual history into slot tokens for efficient robot manipulation. This directly addresses robot manipulation and embodied memory mechanisms.
papers.title: CondenseVLA: Learnable History Condensation for Efficient Multi-Frame VLA
papers.tldr: CondenseVLA efficiently integrates recent visual history into robot actions by learning to condense redundant frame features into complementary slot tokens.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) can complete a task despite local execution errors that are corrected, bypassed, or carried forward without individually determining its outcome. We call these implicit failures (IFs) and study them as signals for process observability beyond final task outcome. Across 1,828 traces from nine MAS-benchmark configurations, IFs occur in 54.3% of successful and 75.2% of failed traces. We develop taxonomies of error types and subsequent absorption mechanisms, supported by human and cross-model annotation audits. Counterfactual replay further probes how repairing an IF changes the final outcome. To examine the practical value of IFs, we evaluate IF-based best-of-N trace selection against existing process reward models, and introduce a novel RL algorithm, IF-GRPO, that uses IF costs to refine preferences among successful trajectories in GRPO. Experiments show that IF-GRPO exhibits some gains in accuracy and process metrics. Importantly, it exposes trade-offs between task performance, IF count and cost, and token-normalized IF density. Overall, our results show that IFs provide complementary process observability into how MAS reach their outcomes, including error recovery, propagation, and IF-based process differences that final task success alone does not expose.
authors: Yanwei Huang, Arpit Narechania, Atanu Sinha
bullets: IFs appear in 54.3% of successful traces and 75.2% of failed traces across 1,828 traces from nine benchmark configurations.
The study taxonomizes error types and absorption mechanisms, validated through human and cross-model annotation audits.
Counterfactual replay examines how repairing implicit failures affects final outcomes.
IF-based trace selection and the IF-GRPO reinforcement-learning method use implicit-failure costs to refine process preferences.
Results indicate some gains in accuracy and process metrics, while revealing trade-offs among task performance, IF count and cost, and token-normalized IF density.
papers.selection_reason: Studies 'implicit failures' in multi-agent systems to provide process observability. This relates to retaining interaction history and error recovery, relevant to embodied memory mechanisms.
papers.title: MASIF: Implicit Failures for Process Observability in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.tldr: Implicit failures—local errors absorbed without changing the final outcome—offer a complementary way to observe and improve multi-agent system processes beyond task success alone.

papers.abstract: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) enables agents to adapt to new tasks without parameter updates, relying on memory to retain what they learn from experience. For agents operating continually, existing approaches using memory trade off bounded cost against access to past experience. Approaches using growing memories, such as full-history attention and accumulating summaries, incur storage and per-decision costs that increase with task length. Fixed-size memories bound storage but restrict access: sliding windows discard older steps, while recurrent networks compress even recent interactions into a hidden state. We introduce Recurrent Summary Memory (RSM), a Transformer policy that attends exactly to a short working buffer of recent interactions and carries a fixed-capacity summary of earlier experience. When the buffer fills, RSM rewrites the summary from its previous contents and the buffer, then clears the buffer, so deployment memory and per-decision cost stay $O(1)$ in task length. On long-running partially observable tasks, frozen RSM policies sustain their adapted performance for eight times the training horizon with about 1% of full-history memory, ending ahead of every evaluated baseline while growing memories deteriorate. When the task configuration changes mid-run, RSM re-adapts better than growing and recurrent memories. Clearing the summary or blocking the policy's access to it removes its benefit, while swapping in another task's summary steers behaviour towards that task. Together, these results show that our fixed-capacity summary can sustain in-context adaptation far beyond the training horizon.
authors: Jiawen Wang, Cheng Xue, Peng Zhang, Jochen Renz
bullets: Targets the trade-off between bounded memory and retaining older experience in continual in-context reinforcement learning.
Uses a Transformer policy with a short recent-interaction buffer plus a fixed-capacity summary of earlier experience.
Rewrites the summary when the buffer fills, keeping deployment memory and per-decision cost O(1) with task length.
On long partially observable tasks, maintains adapted performance for 8× the training horizon using about 1% of full-history memory, outperforming evaluated baselines.
Summary access is necessary for the benefit; changing or swapping summaries alters adaptation and behavior toward the corresponding task.
papers.selection_reason: Bounded-state in-context RL with recurrent summary memory directly addresses continual adaptation and memory for agents.
papers.title: Remember Less, Adapt Longer: Bounded-State In-Context Reinforcement Learning with Recurrent Summary Memory
papers.tldr: Recurrent Summary Memory lets a fixed-capacity policy retain useful experience and adapt over long-running tasks without growing memory or per-decision costs.

papers.abstract: We present \'{E}pi, an autonomous research agent that sustains investigations across model sessions and evolves its methods through accumulated experience. \'{E}pi combines persistent research history, hierarchical memory, branching and independent review to maintain research continuity, learn from experiments, and explore and revisit alternative approaches. Its experiments run across session boundaries, and a fixed verifier evaluates their outputs. \'{E}pi produced 120 record-setting results, comprising 20 numerical bound records across 12 families and 100 construction records across eight families. These include an approximately 84-fold narrower interval for the $n$-queens constant and a more than 3.6-million-fold narrower rigorous interval for the quartic Feigenbaum attractor dimension. Exact dual certificates establish that the Cohn-Elkies linear-programming bound cannot be sharp in dimensions 10 and 11. Beyond numerical improvements, \'{E}pi gives a computer-assisted proof of Tuza's conjecture for split graphs with an eight-vertex clique part and at most three triangle-active neighborhood types, with arbitrary multiplicities. We extend this research process to algorithmic coding with \'{E}pi-turbo, a lightweight configuration that develops executable solvers for tasks including vehicle routing, scheduling and production planning. On 30 FrontierOR tasks, \'{E}pi-turbo achieves a 5.4% higher total benchmark score than Codex at 64% of its model cost, using the same underlying model and reasoning effort. \'{E}pi is designed to support human understanding by connecting computational results to explicit methods and mathematical arguments that researchers can examine and build upon.
authors: Yue Huang, Zhangchen Xu, Xiaonan Luo, Zheyuan Liu, Lichi Li, Yiping Wang, Peiyang Song, Eric Gabriel Ramos, Enze Xie, Olexandr Isayev, Paul Liang, Nouha Dziri, Huan Sun, Jianfeng Gao, Ying Liu, Misha Sra, Xiangliang Zhang, Alex Pentland, Zichen Chen
bullets: Addresses the challenge of maintaining continuity and improving methods across autonomous research sessions.
Uses persistent history, hierarchical memory, branching, independent review, and a fixed output verifier.
Reports 120 record-setting mathematical results, including tighter bounds, exact dual certificates, and a computer-assisted partial result related to Tuza’s conjecture.
Its coding variant, Épi-turbo, outperformed Codex by 5.4% on 30 FrontierOR tasks while using 64% of its model cost.
Designed to expose explicit methods and mathematical arguments for human inspection and further development.
papers.selection_reason: Presents Epi, a persistent, self-improving agent for autonomous research. It maintains research history across sessions and evolves methods, which is a strong fit for Embodied Memory and Continual/Online Learning.
papers.title: Epi: Towards a Persistent, Self-Improving Agent for Autonomous Research
papers.tldr: Épi is a persistent, self-improving research agent that carries investigations across sessions, learns from prior experiments, and produces verifiable mathematical and algorithmic results.

papers.abstract: Agent networks require reliable ways for requesting agents to verify where data is located, how it can be accessed, and whether the data received matches what the data owner made available. Checksum mismatches can reflect either altered content or serialization differences that preserve data equivalence under specified rules. Data identification mechanisms for agents, such as DataFacts, describe where data can be accessed and provide checksums for checking received data against published references. We propose a serialization-invariant identification method that assigns the same identifier to data representations equivalent under explicit rules. We use DataFacts as a case study, retaining its existing checksum alongside the proposed identifier. In a controlled agent study, we compare the proposed configuration with ordinary-tool and checksum baselines across equivalent re-encodings, altered content, and unavailable references. The study includes three model tiers from each of two providers. For equivalent re-encodings, the proposed configuration increased expected-outcome rates by 80.4 percentage points over the ordinary-tool baseline and by 70.2 percentage points over the checksum baseline. The proposed configuration also increased evidence-supported rejection of altered content by 3.5 percentage points over the checksum baseline. We contribute a serialization-invariant identification method with explicit equivalence rules, an integration approach illustrated through DataFacts, and an empirical evaluation against ordinary-tool and checksum baselines.
bullets: Addresses checksum failures caused by harmless serialization differences in agent-published datasets.
Defines explicit equivalence rules and assigns one identifier to equivalent representations.
Integrates the identifier with DataFacts while retaining its existing checksum.
In a controlled study across model tiers and providers, improved expected outcomes for equivalent re-encodings and slightly improved rejection of altered content.
Evaluates against ordinary-tool and checksum baselines across equivalent, altered, and unavailable-reference cases.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses data integrity and verification in agent networks. While specific to serialization, the concept of ensuring reliable data access and integrity for agents aligns with Embodied Memory and Adaptation and Memory.
papers.title: Same Data, Different Bytes: Serialization-Invariant Integrity Checks for Agent-Published Datasets
papers.tldr: A serialization-invariant identifier helps agents recognize equivalent data representations while still detecting altered content.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents in human-centered environments require memory that integrates what they observe with what humans tell them over time. However, existing embodied memories are built primarily from visual experience, leaving open how dialogue with humans can be grounded in the objects encountered throughout that experience. We introduce DialogMem, a two-phase benchmark in which agents build memory from time-aligned streams of posed RGB-D observations and dialogue, and later use it for instance-level object navigation and question answering (QA). DialogMem provides 142 episodes across 27 real-world 3D scenes, with 14,193 QA pairs and 11,890 navigation instructions. We evaluate nine memory representations within a unified framework of memory formation, evidence retrieval, and reasoning for task outputs. In experiments, appending dialogue to visual memory at evaluation time substantially improves QA but yields negligible navigation gains, suggesting that relevant dialogue is present in memory but not grounded to specific objects. Controlled diagnostics show that navigation improves with link quality but falls short of ground-truth object-level memory even under perfect linking. Retrieving the correct object entry and recovering its spatial location remain further bottlenecks. These results identify three bottlenecks for dialogue-grounded embodied memory: grounding and organizing dialogue at object-level entries during formation, retrieving the correct entry, and localizing it accurately.
authors: SeongJun Jeong, Junghyun Kim, Gi-Cheon Kang, Byoung-Tak Zhang
bullets: Introduces a two-phase benchmark using time-aligned posed RGB-D observations and human dialogue across 27 real-world 3D scenes.
Evaluates nine memory representations through memory formation, evidence retrieval, and reasoning.
Adding dialogue improves QA substantially but provides negligible navigation gains when not grounded to specific objects.
Diagnostics identify bottlenecks in object-level dialogue grounding, correct-entry retrieval, and spatial localization.
Even perfect object linking does not match ground-truth memory performance, indicating additional retrieval and localization challenges.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces benchmark for dialogue-grounded embodied memory in 3D environments, fitting embodied memory subtopic.
papers.title: DialogMem: Evaluating Dialogue-Grounded Embodied Memory in 3D Environments
papers.tldr: DialogMem benchmarks how well embodied agents integrate dialogue with visual experience for object navigation and QA in 3D environments.

papers.abstract: Frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies cannot incorporate previously encountered failures without updating the underlying model. We present retrieval-triggered projection correction (RTPC), an auditable external-memory wrapper for frozen OpenVLA policies that retrieves stress-collected local-depth records and applies translation-only projection correction while keeping rotation and gripper commands unchanged. RTPC is evaluated on CALVIN single-task manipulation using primary and independent replication cohorts. In the primary evaluation, RTPC reduced a depth-based near-collision or stall proxy event rate without changing task-success count. However, this reduction was not reproduced in the independent replication, and retrieved correction directions were not distinguishable from random same-family directions. Analysis identifies endpoint coupling, batch sensitivity, and the lack of a trigger-matched memory-free baseline as limitations for attributing effects to retrieval-based correction. These findings do not establish physical safety improvement or memory-specific benefits, but provide an empirical evaluation and failure analysis of retrieval-conditioned intervention for frozen VLA policies.

papers.abstract: Online scene change detection requires an agent to detect what has changed in a previously mapped environment while it is still on site, observing from unconstrained viewpoints and without access to future observations. This causal setting is strictly harder than its offline counterpart, and online methods have consistently trailed offline accuracy. O-SCD closed that gap by treating change as a persistent property of a 3D Gaussian splatting map of the reference scene, surpassing the strongest offline methods in change detection accuracy while operating at over 10 frames per second. O-SCD optimizes a change field over the Gaussians of the reference map, refitting it to all past cue maps at every frame, a step that consumes more than half of the per-frame budget and forces accuracy to be traded against speed. We present a replay-free formulation that eliminates this trade-off. Because the reference map stays fixed, rendering the change field is a linear operation. Each new observation can therefore be carried onto the map's Gaussians directly, by a single backward pass of the renderer, which reduces multi-view fusion to an exact two-scalar recursion per Gaussian. Past observations are never stored or revisited. The self-supervised objective that O-SCD minimizes by descent also determines the decision threshold exactly, by sorting, yielding a label-free per-frame cutoff whose margin provides a selective-prediction signal. On PASLCD, our method improves mean intersection over union from 0.489 to 0.575 and throughput from 11.8 to 25.6 frames per second, even exceeding O-SCD's offline result while remaining strictly causal.
authors: Chamuditha Jayanga Galappaththige, Jason Lai, Lloyd Windrim, Timothy Patten, Donald G. Dansereau, Niko Suenderhauf, Dimity Miller

papers.title: O-SCD++: Replay-Free Online Scene Change Detection via Recursive Evidence Fusion
papers.tldr: O-SCD++ enables faster, replay-free causal scene change detection by recursively fusing evidence directly into a fixed 3D Gaussian map.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems have achieved rapid progress by learning unified policies that map sensor observations directly to driving trajectories. However, once deployed, these systems typically remain frozen: they may repeat similar decisions in similar scenes, and failures can only be addressed through costly data collection and retraining. This sharply contrasts with human drivers, who improve lifelong through experience, memory, and reflection. In this work, we ask whether autonomous driving systems can achieve similar post-deployment self-evolution to human drivers. We propose EvoAD, a self-evolving autonomous driving framework via latent world-model guided post-hoc reflection. EvoAD stores driving experiences in a bird's-eye-view feature memory pool, retrieves scene-relevant precedents according to geometric and semantic similarity, and uses a latent world model to evaluate the future consequences of candidate trajectories in a compact planning-oriented space. Instead of treating memory as external textual contexts or using world models only for pre-action simulation, EvoAD transforms executed driving outcomes into reusable improvement signals for future decisions. This enables the system to diagnose how prior trajectories could have been improved and to refine behavior in similar future scenarios without retraining the base driving policy. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 show consistent improvements across reflection rounds and state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating the potential of world models as reflective mechanisms for post-deployment self-evolution in autonomous driving.

papers.title: EvoAD: Self-Evolving Autonomous Driving via Latent World-Model Guided Post-hoc Reflection
papers.tldr: EvoAD enables autonomous driving systems to improve after deployment by reflecting on past driving outcomes with a latent world model, without retraining the base policy.

papers.abstract: Geometric and Semantic Foundation models are becoming increasingly popular tools for generating spatial maps for robots. Recent work (e.g., FOUND-IT) has leveraged these tools to construct real-time, task-driven, and open-set 3D scene graphs from a single uncalibrated camera. However, while classical robot mapping techniques have undergone extensive system demonstrations, limited work has been done to develop both the fundamental and the systems wide advancements needed to integrate these new types of robot spatial memory into a full, useable autonomy pipeline. In this paper, we bridge this gap, and in doing so we also evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of this type of 3D memory. Towards this end, we integrate FOUND-IT into a mobile manipulator platform and demonstrate it is well-suited to support multiple objectives such as object change detection, support for multiple mapping sessions, determination of navigable paths, and directly support object grasping for the task of scene re-arrangement. Furthermore, we provide nuanced insights into the effectiveness and limitations of a monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph construction system using observations from rigorous on-robot experiments. Code is available at https://github. com/MIT-SPARK/FOUND-IT.
authors: Dominic Maggio, Lorenzo Shaikewitz, Aryan Naveen, Kris Hauser, Luca Carlone

Reports rigorous on-robot experiments assessing the system’s effectiveness and limitations.

It demonstrates the integration of this memory system into a full autonomy pipeline for tasks like object grasping, path planning, and scene rearrangement, directly fitting 3D foundation models, robot manipulation, and embodied memory.

papers.abstract: When we say that a robot uses memory, does that memory actually play a role? Success-rate ablations alone cannot establish the use of task-relevant facts: they change information and computation together, while aggregate rates can hide offsetting gains and losses. We propose an Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol (IMEP) for vision-language-action (VLA) systems to address four questions: (1) Does memory provide a net benefit? (2) Under what conditions does memory help? (3) Do changes to memory alter task outcomes? (4) Are these effects specific to task-relevant facts? At the retrieval interface, we compare target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal numerical perturbations, and exact replicas, while assessing decision correctness separately from motor execution success. We evaluate within-episode, cross-episode, and agentic memory. In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) intervention, including its installation procedure, changes 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts produces no clear additional effect over fact-preserving replacements. To examine when memory helps, we introduce ChainBench, where correct decisions require historical information unavailable in current observations. The full memory configuration raises task success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under shared recorded executions. These results show that correct history can support robot decisions, but establishing whether a memory system realizes this benefit requires fact-specific evidence beyond aggregate success rates.
authors: Keyuan Luo, Yi Xie, Wanyun Ling, Yuanzhe Li, Ziyue Li, Zhuoqi Zeng

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic tasks expose a fundamental limitation of current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models because their restricted temporal context pre-vents effective accumulation and reuse of past experiences. As a result, memory has become a fundamental component for enabling embodied agents to perform long-horizon reasoning and adaptive decision-making. This survey presents a systematic taxonomy of VLA memory mechanisms based on memory scope and persistence, categorizing existing approaches into five representative paradigms and one emerging frontier. Based on this taxonomy, we compare representative VLA memory systems in terms of memory characteristics, architectural com-plexity, and open-source maturity, revealing a clear trade-off in which increasing architectural complexity is generally accompanied by decreasing open-source ma-turity. Finally, we discuss the key challenges in building full-lifecycle memory systems, including efficient memory management and lifelong knowledge evolu-tion. Overall, this survey provides a unified perspective on memory architectures for VLA agents and offers insights into the development of lifelong embodied in-telligence.
authors: Yong Wang, Boyu Shen, Xinwei Zhang, Yizheng Li, Keyuan Luo
bullets: VLA models struggle with long-horizon tasks because limited temporal context hinders the accumulation and reuse of experience.
It proposes a taxonomy based on memory scope and persistence, covering five established paradigms and one emerging frontier.
Representative systems are compared by memory characteristics, architectural complexity, and open-source maturity.
The survey identifies a trade-off: greater architectural complexity generally corresponds to lower open-source maturity.
Key open challenges include efficient memory management and lifelong knowledge evolution.

papers.title: From Sliding Windows to Self-evolving Lifelong Memory: A Dual-perspective Survey of Memory Paradigms for Long-Horizon Robotics VLA Models
papers.tldr: This survey organizes memory mechanisms for long-horizon robotics VLA models and highlights the trade-offs and challenges involved in building lifelong embodied agents.

papers.abstract: Continuous aerial search builds target hypotheses from sparse, viewpoint-dependent observations. When later evidence contradicts a stored hypothesis, however, the candidate can remain available to the planner and continue triggering approach or verification actions. We call this trajectory-level failure false candidate persistence (FCP). We equip SkyAgent with Revisable Target Memory (RTM), which associates evidence with persistent candidates, discounts correlated views, and revises each candidate through Tentative, Confirmed, and Rejected states. The key interface binds every generated waypoint to its source candidate: rejection therefore invalidates stale goals, while conservative reactivation protects temporarily occluded targets. Across four splits from the CityAVOS, UAV-ON, and OpenUAV benchmarks, our SkyAgent equipped with RTM outperforms all competitors, improving SR by 2.90--6.31 points while substantially reducing Behavior-FCP and post-contradiction travel with a low false-rejection rate. Across 35 matched real-world DJI scenarios per method, RTM consistently improves task success and behavioral reliability, further validating its state-to-action correction under physical deployment conditions.
authors: Kaibo Yang, Xingyu Wu, Enze Zhu, Yajie Chai, Xuyang Li, Jiahui Cui, Xiaoxuan Liu, Lei Wang, Zhan Chen

Associates evidence with persistent candidates, discounts correlated views, and tracks Tentative, Confirmed, and Rejected states.
Binds waypoints to their source candidates so rejecting a candidate invalidates stale goals; conservative reactivation handles temporary occlusion.
Across benchmark splits, improves success rate by 2.90–6.31 points while reducing behavioral FCP and post-contradiction travel.
Real-world DJI scenarios show improved task success and behavioral reliability with a low false-rejection rate.

papers.title: SkyAgent: Revisable Target Memory for Continuous Aerial Search
papers.tldr: SkyAgent’s Revisable Target Memory lets aerial-search agents revise contradicted target hypotheses and cancel stale actions, improving success and reducing wasted post-contradiction travel.

papers.abstract: Heterogeneous robot teams enable complex, long-horizon tasks by combining complementary sensing, mobility, and manipulation capabilities across multiple embodiments. Yet existing systems struggle to retain execution-time corrections as reusable experience, maintain task-relevant context memory across space and time for reliable handoffs, and explicitly represent the inter-robot dependencies required for structured collaboration. In order to address these challenges, we present InstAgent, a recursively self-improving (RSI) Agent Operating System for heterogeneous robot collaboration. InstAgent organizes team behaviors as agentic behavior trees (BTs) that explicitly model capability assignment, inter-robot dependencies and handoff checks. The RSI mechanism updates these collaboration programs from execution feedback and preserves successful revisions for reuse in future tasks, while shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory provides context for planning and handoff validation. Experiments on 20 real-world multi-robot tasks with three high-level models show consistent gains in task success, first-attempt completion, and execution efficiency.
authors: Haoyang Luo, Junhao Qin, Jingyan Cao, Yi Huang, Guangjie Yang, Xiaoyu Chen, Haotao Lu, Tianxiang Gui, Ye Shi, Jingya Wang
bullets: Targets reusable execution-time corrections, reliable context-aware handoffs, and explicit inter-robot dependency modeling.
Represents collaboration with agentic behavior trees for capability assignment, dependencies, and handoff checks.
Uses recursive self-improvement to revise collaboration programs from feedback and retain successful revisions.
Provides shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory for planning and validating handoffs.
Experiments across 20 real-world multi-robot tasks and three high-level models report gains in task success, first-attempt completion, and execution efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Self-improving multi-robot agent system with shared spatiotemporal memory and execution-feedback-driven revision.
papers.title: InstAgent: A Recursively Self-Improving Agent Operating System for Heterogeneous Robot Collaboration
papers.tldr: InstAgent enables heterogeneous robot teams to improve collaboration over time by combining behavior-tree coordination, shared spatio-temporal memory, and feedback-driven program revision.

papers.abstract: Spatial memory enables robots to reuse past observations for localization, navigation, and question answering. Designing such memory involves jointly deciding what to retain and how to retrieve it for diverse semantic, metric, and temporal needs. We investigate whether coding agents can automate this design process through iterative implementation and evaluation. Under a fixed development budget, a Designer Agent writes and revises code for memory construction and retrieval using feedback from a fixed Query Agent. The resulting implementations are frozen before building memories from held-out observation histories, without access to downstream questions, and evaluated across five complementary task tracks using the same Query Agent. Across three independent design searches, Codex / GPT-6 Astra averages 44.23 on the equally weighted five-track score, versus 29.32 for ReMEmbR, the strongest evaluated baseline supporting all five tracks, a 50.9% relative improvement. Qualitative analysis relates performance differences to evidence retention and retrieval, while identifying grounding and evidence-use failures. These results demonstrate the potential of coding agents to automate spatial memory design, while revealing task-dependent trade-offs in performance and computational cost. Project page: https://ba-fa-3344.github.io/.
authors: Qianwei Wang, Ce Zhang, Zhanpeng Luo, Pengpeng Su, Shuo Yang, Hao Xu

A Designer Agent iteratively implements and evaluates memory construction and retrieval with feedback from a fixed Query Agent.
Designs are frozen before evaluation on held-out observation histories and five task tracks, without access to downstream questions.
Across three searches, Codex / GPT-6 Astra scores 44.23 versus 29.32 for ReMEmbR, a 50.9% relative improvement.

papers.selection_reason: Automated design of spatial memory for robots directly fits embodied memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Spatial Memory by Agents, for Agents
papers.tldr: Coding agents can automatically design spatial memories for robots, substantially improving multi-task performance while exposing trade-offs in grounding, evidence use, and computational cost.

papers.abstract: Agents operating over long horizons need an effective memory that allows them to reuse their experience throughout long interactions. If the entire history of an interaction is retained, it becomes difficult to find the relevant experience, while compressing it into summaries may result in the loss of visual and spatial details that are required later on. We present \textbf{MFM}, a multimodal filesystem memory architecture that keeps complementary types of agent memory. \textbf{Episodic memory} stores the observations, actions, and outcomes, and \textbf{spatial memory} associates experiences with locations. \textbf{Semantic and procedural memory} build up general knowledge and reusable methods of acting, and \textbf{working memory} holds the current plans. MFM makes use of searchable textual records to connect these different representations to the underlying multimodal episodes. The agents are able to find previous experiences by means of contextual cues and to examine the original observations in order to recover details that are missing from their textual descriptions. Through consolidation, the agents convert experience into higher-level knowledge and procedures while still keeping references to the original episodes. In the case of long-horizon Minecraft and computer-use tasks, MFM leads to improved performance with three base models. With GPT-6-Astra, MFM completes \emph{Mine Diamond from Scratch} and reaches 16 out of 24 milestones on the \emph{Ender Dragon} task, as against 12.7 for the best baseline. On CUABench-KiCad it attains a mean reward of 0.440, as compared to 0.400 for the best baseline and 0.267 in the case of no persistent memory.
authors: Chloe Su, Jiahan Li, Zhenting Qi, Chaoran Cheng, Haoyu Chen, Sejoon Jun, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of retrieving relevant history while preserving visual and spatial details over long interactions.
Combines episodic, spatial, semantic, procedural, and working memory in a filesystem-based architecture.
Uses searchable textual records to retrieve experiences and inspect their underlying multimodal observations.
Consolidates experiences into reusable knowledge and procedures while retaining links to source episodes.
Improves results across three base models, including stronger performance on long-horizon Minecraft and CUABench-KiCad tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal filesystem memory for long-horizon embodied agents, directly matching embodied memory.
papers.title: Multimodal Filesystem Memory For Long-Horizon Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: MFM gives long-horizon embodied agents a searchable multimodal memory that links textual knowledge to original visual-spatial experiences, improving performance on Minecraft and computer-use tasks.

papers.abstract: Tiny robots have limited computation and memory, yet visual navigation systems often maintain more state than a task requires. We ask whether persistent memory can instead be shaped by the task. We present \textbf{RingNav}, a \(10.6\)k--parameter visual heading estimator that constrains its memory to the circular manifold \(S^1\). RingNav learns only the turn between consecutive images, while heading is composed directly on the circle. On the TartanAir Visual SLAM Challenge, RingNav reduces mean absolute turn error by \(27\%\) and accumulated heading error over $4$ sec by \(15\%\) relative to a similarly sized learned-memory model. The structured update also gives exactly zero turn for identical frames and exact cancellation under sequence reversal. Without fine-tuning, RingNav transfers to real-world drone experiments and continues estimating heading under severe visual degradation. RingNav runs at $27.3$Hz on Raspberry Pi Zero 2W and can be deployed on an ultra-low power GAP8 processor at $33.4$Hz.
bullets: Addresses the excessive state maintained by visual navigation systems on computation- and memory-constrained robots.
Uses a 10.6k-parameter model that predicts only the turn between consecutive images and composes heading directly on the circle S¹.
Reduces mean absolute turn error by 27% and 4-second accumulated heading error by 15% versus a similarly sized learned-memory model on the TartanAir Visual SLAM Challenge.
Provides exact zero turn for identical frames and exact cancellation under sequence reversal.
Transfers without fine-tuning to real-world drone experiments and runs at 27.3 Hz on Raspberry Pi Zero 2W and 33.4 Hz on GAP8.
papers.selection_reason: Learned visual heading estimator for tiny robots with task-shaped circular memory; relevant to robot navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: RingNav: Task-Shaped Circular Memory for Visual Heading
papers.tldr: RingNav is a tiny visual heading estimator whose memory is constrained to the circular manifold, enabling efficient and robust navigation on resource-limited robots.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video provides a continuous first-person record of everyday activities, making it a natural foundation for wearable AI assistants. Unlike offline video understanding, streaming systems must process observations as they arrive, while queries may refer to experiences from the distant past. Recent work has begun to explore whether information can be recalled across long temporal gaps. Yet remembering how far is only part of the challenge: recurring objects, actions, and locations also require models to remember exactly which detail belongs to which event. We introduce EgoProbe, a benchmark that evaluates streaming egocentric memory along these two complementary dimensions: long-range retention, i.e., how far, and event-specific recall under interference, i.e., how exact. Built on long-form egocentric videos, EgoProbe uses an event-grounded data engine to extend recall intervals, identify related events, and construct event-grounded distractors, followed by human verification. It contains two subsets: EgoProbe-Base, which evaluates long-range recall without intervening related events, and EgoProbe-Echo, which challenges models with similar intervening events and event-grounded distractors. EgoProbe-Echo adopts coarse-to-fine multi-turn probing: the first turn evaluates coarse-grained event recall, while the second tests whether the model can retrieve the target-specific detail associated with the designated event. Extensive evaluation across diverse models reveals substantial limitations in long-range recall, with further challenges in recovering target-event details among related experiences. Even when models correctly answer coarse-grained questions, they often fail to recall the specific details of the designated event. EgoProbe exposes this underexplored failure mode and provides a testbed for advancing long-range and exact memory in streaming egocentric video understanding.

Introduces EgoProbe-Base for unobstructed long-range recall and EgoProbe-Echo for recall amid similar events and distractors.
Uses an event-grounded data engine with human verification to construct extended recall intervals and targeted probes.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for long-range and exact memory in streaming egocentric video.
papers.title: EgoProbe: Benchmarking Long-Range and Exact Memory in Streaming Egocentric Videos
papers.tldr: EgoProbe benchmarks whether streaming video models can both remember distant egocentric events and retrieve the exact details tied to the correct event.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation fundamentally requires memory: agents must retain task-relevant information from past observations and interactions and use it to guide future actions. Existing approaches typically preserve raw historical observations, compressed visual tokens, or language summaries, but these representations either expose the action policy to increasingly long histories or risk discarding task-relevant temporal, semantic, and perceptual information. We introduce Mem4Act, a framework for learning effective latent memory as a fixed-size representation explicitly optimized for long-horizon robotic control. Mem4Act addresses three coupled challenges: how to efficiently cover long histories, what information memory should retain, and how to ensure the policy actually relies on memory. To this end, it organizes history via multi-granularity temporal aggregation, preserves complementary semantic and perceptual information through question-answering supervision and key-frame DINO feature reconstruction, and employs memory-first two-stage training to encourage greater use of memory by the action policy. The resulting memory captures both high-level task state and fine-grained perceptual evidence while providing a bounded interface to the action policy. Across RoboMME, RMBench, and four real-world manipulation tasks, Mem4Act achieves state-of-the-art performance on memory-dependent control, with success rates of 49.88%, 61.0%, and 81.5%, respectively. Extensive ablations further demonstrate the importance of temporal aggregation, complementary memory supervision, and memory-first training.

Uses multi-granularity temporal aggregation to efficiently cover long interaction histories.
Combines question-answering supervision with key-frame DINO feature reconstruction to retain complementary semantic and perceptual information.
Applies memory-first two-stage training to encourage the action policy to rely on the learned memory.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across RoboMME, RMBench, and four real-world manipulation tasks, with success rates of 49.88%, 61.0%, and 81.5%.

papers.title: Mem4Act: Learning Effective Latent Memory for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: Mem4Act learns a fixed-size latent memory that preserves task-relevant temporal, semantic, and perceptual information for long-horizon robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: We introduce REKI, a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) pretrained exclusively on public data that sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size: on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365, it is outperformed only by models about twice its size. REKI consists of a vision-language model (VLM) followed by a flow-matching action expert, and is pretrained on a curated mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision-language data. Additionally, we endow it with a memory that gives the policy access to its recent past at negligible cost: a few register tokens in the action expert summarise the output of the VLM at each frame and persist in the expert's cache. This memory improves success in simulation and on real robots, and makes oscillations between poses about four times rarer. REKI uses a simple model design and training paradigm, and is optimised to be efficient at training and inference. We release the full code across data curation, training, inference and evaluation, deployment, and all pretrained and finetuned model weights: https://github.com/kyutai-labs/reki.
authors: Juliette Marrie, Paul Pacaud, Adrien Ramanana Rahary, Shizhe Chen, Moritz B\"ohle

Combines a vision-language model with a flow-matching action expert.
Uses register tokens to summarize recent VLM outputs in the action expert’s cache at negligible cost.
Improves simulated and real-robot success, while making pose oscillations about four times rarer.

papers.title: REKI: Registering Knowledge in VLAs
papers.tldr: REKI is a compact 2.4B vision-language-action model with efficient register-token memory that improves robot-control performance and reduces pose oscillations.

papers.abstract: Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT) is an essential capability for intelligent robots in human-robot collaboration, requiring an agent to follow a designated target person in dynamic environments relying solely on egocentric visual perception. However, persistent pedestrian occlusions in dynamic scenes pose critical challenges to existing EVT methods. Lacking proactive visibility preservation, reactive tracking methods frequently experience prolonged target loss under severe occlusions. Therefore, we propose VP-EVT, a framework that treats target visibility as an explicit objective of motion control rather than a by-product of following. Acting on this objective requires understanding both what obstructs the target and how robot motion can change that obstruction. VP-EVT therefore uses language-guided perception to extract separate target and pedestrian observations. When occlusion makes current observations incomplete, VP-EVT combines visual history with ego-motion to maintain estimates of their relative positions and motion. Using these estimates and the current following waypoints, VP-EVT predicts whether continued following will sustain the obstruction. When the predicted risk is low, the original following motion is retained; otherwise, a recurrent controller combines updated estimates with maneuver context from preceding decisions to coordinate viewpoint adjustment and the return to stable following. Moreover, we introduce OccEVT-Bench for closed-loop evaluation of persistent occlusion and collect expert demonstrations for training. On its Risk split, VP-EVT improves success rate by 121.4% relative to a competitive baseline and reduces visibility deficit and longest target-loss duration by 78.8% and 74.4%, respectively.
authors: Yanci Wen, Tianle Zeng, Jianwei Peng, Weixi Situ, Hanjing Ye, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses prolonged target loss caused by pedestrian occlusions in dynamic environments.
Uses language-guided perception to separate target and occluder observations, then combines visual history with ego-motion to estimate relative motion during partial visibility.
Predicts whether continued following will maintain occlusion and selectively triggers viewpoint-adjustment maneuvers through a recurrent controller.
Introduces OccEVT-Bench and expert demonstrations for closed-loop evaluation and training.
On the Risk split, improves success rate by 121.4% and reduces visibility deficit and longest target-loss duration by 78.8% and 74.4%.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied visual tracking with proactive visibility preservation, using ego-motion history and recurrent control for target following.
papers.title: VP-EVT: Active Visibility Preservation for Embodied Visual Tracking
papers.tldr: VP-EVT enables embodied visual trackers to proactively avoid persistent occlusions by adjusting the robot’s viewpoint while maintaining target following.

papers.abstract: Indoor service robots often enter unmapped buildings whose layouts and task constraints are already familiar to users. We address this human-familiar, robot-unseen setting with AVALON, a topological navigation framework organized around human-seeded layered spatial memory, node-verified topological execution, and task-triggered, evidence-gated human--robot memory co-updating. The robot has no prior on-site traversal or site-specific training. Deployment requires only a floor plan, place clues, and an initial topology-odometry alignment. Visual depth point-goal navigation leverages verified node arrivals to perform translational re-anchoring, without requiring a robot-constructed global SLAM map. Human--robot memory co-updating fuses complementary sources of information. Human operators specify task constraints that are unobservable via vision and report offline environmental modifications, whereas the robot provides physical-state evidence through active in-situ validation. Task relevance governs whether human-reported environmental changes undergo robot validation during the active mission. Field-collected perceptual evidence gates memory updates, maintaining an explicit separation between human-specified permissions and robot-observed traversability. Our experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that AVALON with X-NavDP completes a 12.81 m Intersection-to-Dining mission in 46.4 s (5/5) with no mapping, 40.9% less robot time than DimOS-Go2 (78.5 s, 4/5), while policy-only X-NavDP times out in all of the 5 runs. These demonstrate the superiority of the proposed topological navigation framework.
authors: Jing Xia, Changyan Li, Yuduo Wang, Guiyin Tian, Bo Wang, Yifan Liao, Mingjun Li, Shiyan Hu
bullets: Targets service robots entering unmapped buildings without prior on-site traversal or site-specific training.
Uses a floor plan, place clues, and initial topology–odometry alignment instead of a robot-built global SLAM map.
Combines human task constraints and environmental reports with robot-verified physical-state evidence.
Verified node arrivals support translational re-anchoring for visual depth point-goal navigation.
On a Unitree Go2, AVALON completed the reported mission in all 5 runs and avoided timeouts seen with policy-only X-NavDP.
papers.selection_reason: Indoor topological navigation with human-seeded spatial memory and robot navigation, fitting embodied navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: AVALON: Zero-Shot Indoor Navigation with Human-Seeded Topological Memory
papers.tldr: AVALON enables zero-shot indoor robot navigation in human-familiar but robot-unmapped buildings using human-seeded topological memory and evidence-gated memory updates.

papers.abstract: Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (STMM) requires robots to respond to sound events by navigating to the associated objects and performing appropriate physical interactions. Existing STMM evaluations primarily vary object layouts within limited architectural structures, leaving challenges to unseen scenes insufficiently explored. We introduce Multi-scene Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (MuSTMM), a dataset that combines spatial audio rendering and physical interaction across 31 scenes with diverse architectures and object layouts. MuSTMM contains 14.36 million precomputed binaural Room Impulse Responses (RIRs) and a scene-disjoint split for evaluating single-event and multi-event settings in unseen scenes. We further augment the Navigation Policy Model with explicit spatial memory that complements acoustic cues with observed geometry. Specifically, we accumulate pose-aligned depth observations in a shared coordinate frame and project this memory into an egocentric Bird's-Eye View (BEV) occupancy map. Fusing map features with sound context produces a goal descriptor that provides both target-location and scene-structure priors, guiding navigation to the target region required for subsequent physical interaction. This policy achieves a 2.60% success rate boost over existing methods, while component ablations further support the effectiveness of spatial memory. MuSTMM and the navigation policy provide a testbed for the new challenge of studying sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen scenes. The code and dataset will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Hao Ju, Feng Yan, Zhihao Zhong, Heng Yang, Shaofei Huang, Zhedong Zheng
bullets: Addresses the limited evaluation of sound-triggered manipulation across diverse, unseen architectural scenes.
Provides 31 scenes, spatial audio and physical interactions, 14.36 million precomputed binaural RIRs, and scene-disjoint single- and multi-event splits.
Augments navigation with pose-aligned depth memory projected into a Bird’s-Eye View occupancy map.
Fuses spatial-memory features with sound context to guide robots toward target regions for physical interaction.
Reports a 2.60% success-rate improvement over existing methods; ablations support the value of spatial memory.
papers.selection_reason: Sound-triggered mobile manipulation with spatial memory and navigation policy; directly relevant to embodied navigation, manipulation, and embodied memory.
papers.title: MuSTMM: Learning Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation across Multiple Scenes
papers.tldr: MuSTMM introduces a multi-scene benchmark and spatial-memory navigation policy for sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen environments.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering interactions that are no longer visible. We introduce Latent Transition Memory (LTM), which stores history as compact latent transitions between consecutive observations. Instantiated on $\pi_{0.5}$ as LTM-$\pi$, our method uses a frozen latent action encoder, a lightweight adapter, and causal KV caching for incremental inference without memory-specific semantic annotations or external reasoning-model calls. With DreamDojo transitions, LTM-$\pi$ achieves 58.54% success on RoboMME and 80.5% on LIBERO-Mem, performing best among baselines without external reasoning models or memory-specific annotations. Ablations support the contribution of transition content beyond temporal cues and the efficiency of delayed memory admission. Scaling RoboMME demonstrations tenfold improves success from 57.67% to 87.50%, while a Cup Swap diagnostic highlights the role of process supervision in temporal composition. Under a 200-token memory budget, success remains 84.00%, versus 87.50% without compression. Finally, real-robot counting success improves from 11.25% to 82.50%. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency of latent transition memory, highlighting its capacity for complex temporal information, bounded-context operation, and real-world robotic control.
authors: Qixin Sun, WenLong Gao, Xiansheng Chen, Zhongyuan Wang, Si Liu, Pengwei Wang
bullets: Stores consecutive-observation transitions in latent form rather than retaining full visual history.
Combines a frozen latent action encoder, lightweight adapter, and causal KV caching for incremental, annotation-free inference.
LTM-π reaches 58.54% success on RoboMME and 80.5% on LIBERO-Mem without external reasoning models or memory annotations.
Memory scales effectively: RoboMME success rises to 87.50% with tenfold more demonstrations and remains 84.00% under a 200-token budget.
Real-robot counting success improves from 11.25% to 82.50%; a Cup Swap diagnostic underscores the importance of process supervision for temporal composition.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces latent transition memory for vision-language-action robotic manipulation, directly relevant to embodied memory and VLA policies.
papers.title: LTM: Latent Transition Based In-Context Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: LTM gives vision-language-action robots compact latent memories of past state transitions, substantially improving manipulation that depends on hidden history.

papers.abstract: Proactive robots should anticipate user needs and provide assistance before being explicitly asked. A straightforward approach is to infer human intentions from commonsense knowledge, but the same observed behavior can imply different needs across users, potentially leading to unwanted assistance. We observe that everyday routines in the real world exhibit recurring patterns, so learning these patterns can reduce ambiguity in proactive decisions. Based on this, we propose a memory-based agentic framework in which a VLM task predictor reads a Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) alongside the current observation to decide when to assist and what task to perform, and a VLA executor performs the predicted task. PAM is structured as a finite-state machine over activity phases, per-state assistance rules, and event-driven transitions; a reflection VLM revises PAM from each day's interaction trace without weight updates or retraining. In our 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, memory-free baselines remain conservative, with limited recall on proactive tasks. Our system improves consistently with accumulated experience, achieving the highest precision, recall, and F1 and reducing first-fire delay from approximately 5 seconds on Day 1 to 1 second by Day 5. Our approach also adapts to changes in the user's routine through continued memory reflection, recovering from memory--routine misalignment after a single memory update. The project page is available at https://davian-robotics.github.io/PAM/
authors: Dohyun Lee, Minho Park, Jeonghoon Park, Dongyoon Hwang, Junha Hyung, Sungwon Hwang, Byungkun Lee, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in proactive assistance, where identical behaviors may indicate different user needs.
Uses a VLM task predictor with Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) to select when and how to assist, and a VLA executor to perform tasks.
Represents routines as a finite-state machine with activity phases, assistance rules, and event-driven transitions.
A reflection VLM updates PAM from daily interaction traces without weight updates or retraining.
In a 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, the system improved with experience, achieved the best reported precision, recall, and F1, and reduced first-fire delay from about 5 seconds to 1 second.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic proactive robot framework with procedural assistance memory and VLA executor; relevant to embodied memory and VLA.
papers.title: An Agentic Framework for Proactive Robots with Procedural Assistance Memory
papers.tldr: A memory-based agentic framework helps robots proactively assist users by learning and updating personalized routine patterns without retraining.

papers.abstract: Agent memory architectures define how LLM agents store and reuse experience across tasks, but they are typically fixed after deployment, limiting their adaptability across task types. Recent self-evolving approaches instead adapt these memory architectures using execution feedback, typically represented as evaluation scores or compressed summaries. However, such coarse-grained feedback is insufficient for precise failure localization in current agent systems, where long-horizon task execution involves multiple interacting components. Without a precise failure location, existing approaches lack a clear code-level target for modification, leaving the update scope weakly constrained and often leading to large-scale rewrites of an otherwise capable memory architecture. We propose MemScope, a framework for evidence-grounded, localized evolution of an existing memory architecture. Its tool-using Patch Agent jointly inspects raw execution traces, runtime memory state, and current architecture code to identify repair targets and apply bounded, in-place edits under provider-identity and memory-compatibility constraints. On GAIA, the trace-and-memory inspection variant achieves 86.67% accuracy, compared with 70.00% for trace-only and 63.33% for summary-only feedback. Under xBench tasks, the evolved memory architecture improves over its original version from 49 to 55 correct answers with DeepSeek V3.2 and from 50 to 53 with Kimi K2.7 Code. On disjoint ALFWorld unseen tasks, success rises from 50.75% to 71.64%. Across archived architecture-snapshot transitions, the median code-change ratio is 4.4%. These results support fine-grained execution evidence as a basis for localized, in-place memory-architecture evolution.
authors: Miao Su, Yucan Guo, Zixuan Li, Long Bai, Zhongni Hou, Xiaolong Jin, Jiafeng Guo
bullets: Targets the difficulty of locating failures in long-horizon agent executions using only coarse scores or summaries.
A Patch Agent jointly analyzes raw traces, runtime memory state, and architecture code to identify repair targets.
Applies bounded in-place edits while preserving provider identity and memory compatibility.
Improves performance on GAIA, xBench, and unseen ALFWorld tasks, with a median code-change ratio of 4.4%.
papers.selection_reason: Evolving agent memory architectures with execution feedback directly targets LLM/agent memory and deployment-time adaptation.
papers.title: MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair
papers.tldr: MemScope evolves LLM-agent memory systems through evidence-grounded, localized code repairs instead of broad rewrites.

papers.abstract: Passive human videos of everyday activity offer robots access to a massive amount of human experience without requiring a demonstration for each task. However, using this experience requires recovering knowledge from unstructured video recordings and adapting it to a different body (i.e., the robot). To overcome these challenges, we present mobile code-as-policy (MoCaP), an agentic framework that turns passive human video recordings into guidance for an end-to-end mobile manipulation policy. MoCaP extracts spatial memory and cues of how people prepare to interact with objects, which inform navigation and the search for a manipulation-ready configuration. Guided by passive human experience and current observations, MoCaP uses a closed-loop code-as-policy to coordinate planning and tool use primitives to solve motions under the robot's geometry and kinematic constraints. On a real mobile manipulator, MoCaP achieves 80% success on each of two mobile manipulation tasks in an indoor environment whereas existing approaches cannot succeed at the task. Video-derived spatial memory improves object-navigation success from 70% to 100%, and human approach prior raises the rate of finding a reachable base pose from 0% to 100% at an unfavorable start location. Videos and code are available on the project website: https://mocap-7.github.io/MoCAP-page/.
authors: Yiyang Cai, Tatsuya Kamijo, Ninghao Lu, Zijin Hu, Sherry Yang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring knowledge from unstructured human videos to robots with different bodies and constraints.
Extracts spatial memory and human approach cues to guide object navigation and selection of manipulation-ready base poses.
Uses a closed-loop code-as-policy agent to coordinate planning and tool-use primitives under robot geometry and kinematic constraints.
On a real mobile manipulator, achieves 80% success on each of two indoor tasks where existing approaches fail.
Video-derived memory improves object-navigation success from 70% to 100%, while human approach priors improve reachable-base-pose discovery from 0% to 100% in an unfavorable start setting.
papers.selection_reason: Turns passive human videos into spatial memory and code-as-policy for mobile manipulation; directly relevant to embodied manipulation, human-video learning, robot navigation, and embodied memory.
papers.title: MoCaP: Mobile Code-as-Policies for Zero-Shot Mobile Manipulation from Passive Human Videos
papers.tldr: MoCaP converts passive human videos into spatial and behavioral guidance for zero-shot mobile manipulation by a robot.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal agents have made significant progress in interacting with open worlds. However, their ability to self-evolve remains limited. Supervised fine-tuning enables imitation but not active experience organization, while outcome-based reinforcement learning promotes exploration yet underuses intermediate trajectory information. Therefore, we propose EvolvingBrain, which uses an adaptive skill system as the brain for agent self-evolution, consisting of two following components. Stratified Skill Self-Evolution: extracts Procedural Patterns and Problematic Patterns from model-specific trajectories, summarizes experience by generating skills, and evolves through multiple interactions with the open world, ultimately forming a Stratified Skill Architecture consisting of Domain, Plan, and Action/Trap Skills, which provides the agent with a multi-granularity knowledge repository and a novel evolution approach. State-Aware Adaptive Execution: summarizes long-horizon interactions into Structured Abstractive Memory and uses it to guide the State-Aware Skill Fusion Strategy, enabling the agent to utilize knowledge according to its current state. Experiments on VAB-Minecraft and DiscoveryWorld demonstrate that EvolvingBrain improves success rates on open-world tasks and exhibits generalization capabilities. Our code is provided in the supplementary materials and will be publicly released in the camera-ready version.
authors: Runxuan Liu, Jingqi Shi, Baoxin Wang, Honghong Zhao, Haoyuan Xu, Yueqing Sun, Jiafeng Liang, Tao He, Dayong Wu, Qi Gu, Shijin Wang, Ming Liu, Bing Qin
bullets: Addresses the limits of imitation learning and outcome-only reinforcement learning in organizing and exploiting intermediate experience.
Extracts procedural and problematic patterns from trajectories to generate skills through repeated world interactions.
Builds a stratified skill architecture with domain, plan, and action/trap skills for multi-granularity knowledge storage.
Uses structured abstractive memory and state-aware skill fusion to select and combine skills during long-horizon interactions.
Improves open-world task success rates and demonstrates generalization on VAB-Minecraft and DiscoveryWorld.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive skill system and structured memory for self-evolving agents in open worlds.
papers.title: EvolvingBrain: An Adaptive Skill System for Multi-modal Agents Self-Evolution in Open Worlds
papers.tldr: EvolvingBrain enables multimodal agents to self-evolve in open worlds by continually learning structured skills from experience and adapting their use to the current state.

papers.abstract: Existing robot policy memories typically evolve with observation sequences, implicitly treating each update as the same amount of physical time. Yet identical observation histories can span different durations and require different actions, exposing physical time as a missing dimension of policy memory. We introduce Temporal Flow Policy (TFP), which learns memory dynamics to retain past events and evolve the memory state over measured time intervals. Observations and prior memory determine the content and time scales of each transition; elapsed time determines how far the state advances. TFP conditions diffusion and flow-matching policies through this memory state and is trained with their native imitation objectives. We evaluate TFP with Diffusion Policy and $\pi_{0.5}$ through controlled comparisons of memory designs. These experiments show that successful timing depends on both measured intervals and retained history. TFP achieves higher average success than the recurrent and state-space memories we equip with the same intervals and than a variant that feeds the interval to a learned gate. Memory readouts recover the time since an event and motion information after occlusion. Changing the supplied intervals systematically delays or advances actions, linking time inputs to behavior. Real-robot tasks requiring timing or memory, together with LIBERO evaluations, demonstrate benefits in physical and general manipulation. These results suggest viewing robot memory not as stored observation history, but as a state that retains past events and evolves with physical time.
authors: Yushen Liang, Yue Peng, Baosheng Jin, Tianluo Zhang, Xinyu Zhang, Shuyi Zhou, Zhuoran Chen, Xinqi Liu, Shenji Wan
bullets: Problem: Standard robot memories treat each update as equal time, so identical observations over different durations can produce inappropriate actions.

Method: TFP learns memory dynamics where observations and prior memory determine transitions, while measured elapsed intervals control state evolution; it conditions diffusion and flow-matching policies.
Results: Controlled comparisons with Diffusion Policy and π₀.₅ show higher average success than matched recurrent, state-space, and interval-gated memories.
Evidence: Memory readouts recover event timing and motion after occlusion, while changing supplied intervals systematically delays or advances actions.
Scope: Real-robot timing and memory tasks plus LIBERO evaluations indicate benefits for physical and general manipulation.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces physical time into robot policy memory, directly relevant to embodied memory and policy learning.
papers.title: Physical Time as a Missing Dimension of Robot Policy Memory Dynamics
papers.tldr: Temporal Flow Policy adds measured physical time to robot policy memory, enabling actions that depend on both what happened and how long ago it occurred.

papers.abstract: Geometry foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D scene structure from video sequences, but maintaining consistent reconstructions over long horizons remains challenging. Feed-forward models process long sequences as independent, fixed-length frame windows and align their predictions, causing pose and reconstruction errors to accumulate across windows. Streaming models retain information from past frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when later observations reveal errors. To address this, we introduce Scaffold MemOry for Revision (SMORE), a framework equipping frozen geometry foundation models with a revisable external memory for long-horizon inference. Inspired by hippocampal associative memory in biological brains, which links spatial context with sensory experience, SMORE associates where an observer is with what it observes, enabling past observations to be stored, retrieved, verified against new evidence, and revised when inconsistencies are detected. We evaluate SMORE with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across all evaluated models, SMORE consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. By retaining corrected poses and observations, SMORE further improves the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. These results establish revisable external memory as a flexible interface for extending pretrained geometry models beyond fixed-context prediction toward iterative, error-correcting inference over long visual sequences.
bullets: Addresses error accumulation from fixed-window and non-revisable streaming inference on long video sequences.
Associates spatial context with observations so past geometry can be stored, retrieved, checked against new evidence, and revised.
Evaluated with eight geometry models across five tasks, including pose, depth, point-cloud reconstruction, SLAM, and novel view synthesis.
Consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, with reported reductions of up to 58% in depth error and 43% in Chamfer distance.
Achieves trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM and improves large-scale scene consistency.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a revisable external memory (SMORE) for long-horizon 3D geometry, fitting World Models (long-horizon prediction) and Adaptation and Memory.
papers.title: Remember, Revisit, Revise: Scaffold Memory for Long-Horizon 3D Geometry
papers.tldr: SMORE adds revisable external memory to frozen 3D geometry models, enabling long-horizon predictions to retrieve, verify, and correct past estimates for more consistent reconstructions.

papers.abstract: Object-goal navigation requires an embodied agent to explore an unfamiliar environment, identify a target object, navigate toward candidate instances, and reliably determine whether the observed object satisfies the mission goal. This work investigates this problem through a two-stage development process. In Stage I, a fixed modular framework is used to examine combinations of exploration, object detection, and target validation methods. The results reveal clear trade-offs among navigation performance, validation reliability, execution time, and model-related cost, with no single fixed configuration remaining preferable across all evaluated conditions. These observations motivate F2A-ObjectNav (Fixed-to-Adaptive Object-Goal Navigation), an adaptive agentic architecture in which a rule-based Supervisor coordinates specialized components for navigation and exploration, object detection, target validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory. The architecture uses event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional semantic guidance while retaining lightweight execution during normal operation. F2A-ObjectNav is evaluated over 25 episodes in each of AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, achieving success rate (SR) / success-weighted path length (SPL) values of 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37, respectively. In addition to task-level metrics, architecture-specific behavioral metrics are used to characterize semantic-guidance usage, strategy switching, recovery activation, memory-supported behavior, and decision stability. The results show different patterns of adaptive intervention across the three environments, with higher intervention frequencies observed in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR than in AI2-THOR.
bullets: Object-goal navigation requires exploration, object detection, target validation, and reliable mission completion in unfamiliar environments.
A fixed modular study found trade-offs among navigation performance, validation reliability, execution time, and model cost, motivating adaptive coordination.
A rule-based Supervisor dynamically manages navigation, exploration, detection, validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory.
Event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional guidance support adaptive behavior while keeping normal execution lightweight.
Across AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, SR/SPL were 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37; adaptive interventions were more frequent in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive agentic architecture for object-goal navigation with mission memory and recovery.
papers.title: F2A-ObjectNav: An Adaptive Agentic Architecture for Object-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: F2A-ObjectNav adaptively coordinates specialized navigation components to improve object-goal navigation across varied environments.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong performance on local robot manipulation, yet their success does not readily translate to long-horizon mobile manipulation. In our experiments, a pretrained subtask VLA achieves 80% success rate on atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when these skills are composed into mobile manipulation. We argue that this gap stems from failures across the execution process rather than from local manipulation capability alone. To uncover these bottlenecks, we systematically diagnose failures in long-horizon mobile manipulation and identify three dominant regimes: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation. Based on this diagnosis, we develop failure-guided agentic intervention that augments a fixed subtask VLA with demonstration-based planning guidance, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment. On RoboCasa365, these interventions progressively improve task success from 19% to 47%, with the finalized system reaching 49% on held-out episode seeds, compared with 18% for the baseline. The same design improves performance from 14% to 37% on BEHAVIOR-1K and from 5/20 to 13/20 on real-robot tasks. These results suggest that reliable mobile manipulation can be advanced by diagnosing and intervening on the current bottleneck, rather than uniformly scaling the underlying policy. Our code will be released at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/Cracking-Mobile-Manipulation.git.
authors: Zixuan Wang, Jia-Ning Li, Yinzhou Tang, Yanzhao Yu, Biao Wu, Meng Fang, Xin Li, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: A pretrained VLA succeeds on 80% of atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when skills are composed for mobile manipulation.
Failures primarily arise in task planning, navigation/base positioning, and local manipulation.
The proposed system adds demonstration-based planning, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment to a fixed subtask VLA.
Success improves from 19% to 47% on RoboCasa365, reaching 49% on held-out seeds versus 18% for the baseline.
The approach also improves results on BEHAVIOR-1K and real-robot tasks, supporting bottleneck-focused intervention over uniform policy scaling.
papers.selection_reason: Failure-guided agentic interventions for long-horizon mobile manipulation with adaptive visual memory.
papers.title: Cracking Mobile Manipulation: From Failure Diagnosis to Agentic Robot System
papers.tldr: Diagnosing bottlenecks across planning, navigation, and manipulation enables targeted agentic interventions that substantially improve long-horizon mobile manipulation.

papers.abstract: Retrieving useful context for a robot requires matching its task, execution stage, and the continuation that should follow. We introduce Robota-Embed, to our knowledge the first vision-language-action (VLA) embedding model to jointly encode all three modalities in both current-state queries and recorded future continuations. Predictive retrieval training aligns these endpoints, enabling historical continuations to serve as context at inference time. We construct a multi-source corpus of 1,695,684 cleaned training anchors and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench, with 4,000 queries and a shared 8,000-entry gallery. Robota-Embed achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, exceeding action-free Gemini Embedding 2 by 22.09 and 33.47 percentage points. Controlled retrieval studies show that removing native action degrades retrieval more than removing vision. We study two complementary applications. Embed2ICL uses retrieved experience for training-free and training-based policy conditioning, increasing success from 47.0% to 56.3% in DROID-Sim and from 86.4% to 92.8% on the LIBERO difficult subset, while improving task progress on real robots. Embed2Evolve uses execution feedback to grow task-local memory and refine context use around a frozen GPT-6 Astra policy. Across five ManiSkill tasks, it achieves 68% success, compared with 24% for GPT-6 Astra Direct and 33% for a harness independently evolved with Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B under the same protocol. Relative to the latter, it uses approximately 79.5% fewer policy tokens per test rollout, counting both successes and failures. These results show that a unified, action-aware retrieval space can support robot in-context learning and task-local context evolution.
authors: Yunze Liu, Jing Wang, Shenrui Wu, Wenkun He, Guanqi Zhan, Xianzheng Ma, Junyu Chen, Wenhang Ge, Haozhan Tang, Yuchao Gu, Zhuoyang Zhang, Zekai Wang, Dantong Niu, Zhen Dong, Yuke Zhu, Trevor Darrell, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Song Han, Han Cai
bullets: Jointly encodes task, execution stage, and future action continuations in both current-state queries and recorded experiences.
Uses predictive retrieval training and a corpus of 1,695,684 training anchors; introduces a 4,000-query benchmark with an 8,000-entry gallery.
Achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, outperforming the action-free Gemini Embedding 2 baseline in the reported comparisons.
Retrieved experience improves policy success in DROID-Sim and LIBERO, and execution-feedback memory evolution improves performance across five ManiSkill tasks.
Ablations indicate that removing action information harms retrieval more than removing vision; evaluation focuses on the reported simulated and real-robot settings.
papers.selection_reason: Unified VLA retrieval embeddings for robot in-context learning and task-local memory evolution.
papers.title: Robota-Embed: Unified VLA Embeddings for Robot In-Context Learning and Evolution
papers.tldr: Robota-Embed learns a unified vision-language-action retrieval space that helps robots retrieve useful past experience for in-context learning and task-specific evolution.
