papers.abstract: Multimodal models and agents have emerged to enable AI systems to learn from and interact with the real world more like humans by integrating information across multiple modalities. However, enabling multimodal agents to continually acquire useful information from complex, heterogeneous multimodal data remains a significant challenge as they move toward long-horizon tasks and lifelong settings. Addressing this challenge requires effective memory mechanisms that can maintain continuity across sessions, adapt to changing users and environments, and refine memory-management policies through accumulated experience. We introduce a two-axis analytical framework for multimodal agent memory structured around two key questions: how multimodal information is formed and represented (Axis I, Formation and Representation), and how its management adapts with accumulated experience (Axis II, Memory Management). Axis I, Formation and Representation, characterizes what information is retained and how it is encoded (e.g., modality-specific embeddings, textual and structured records, latent and parametric representations) to support subsequent reasoning and action. Axis II, Memory Management, distinguishes three tiers: T1 Static Memory reuses fixed memory; T2 Dynamic Memory updates memory through a stable policy; and T3 Self-Evolving Memory updates memory through an evolving policy. Based on this framework, we synthesize recurring design patterns and derive principles for balancing source fidelity with abstraction, maintaining temporal validity and provenance, grounding memory use in recoverable evidence, and evolving memory policies over time. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and potential future directions for the memory mechanism of multimodal agents.
authors: Minghao Guo, Qingyue Jiao, Xiujin Liu, Jianhong Pang, Ruimeng Yang, Naihao Xu, Liwei Che, Haochen Xue, Ziqi Wang, Xinying Cai, Jiaxuan Luo, Jiaxin Deng, Xuesong Ye, Jintao Qu, Wenyao Gao, Jingwen Gu, Chenyang Zhao, Shichun Liu, Guibin Zhang, Zefang Liu, Siyin Wang, Wujiang Xu, Danrui Li, Zeru Shi, Woongyeong Yeo, Shuang Liu, Wei-Chieh Huang, Weizhi Zhang, Tianyu Yang, Kangsan Kim, Yebowen Hu, Bowen Wen, Bowen Jiang, Haohao Su, Ming Yin, Sheldon Yu, Mian Zhang, Yuyan Chen, Hanrong Zhang, Kai Mei, Zihao Zhang, Mingyu Jin, Xi Zhu, Hengyi Wang, Tianxin Wei, Linyong Nan, Zhenwen Liang, Zhendong Chu, Ziqi Huang, Yongye Su, Sixun Dong, Shujian Liu, Kaiqu Liang, Jiaojiao Han, Zhaoye Fei, Kun Wang, Shihan Dou, Zhichun Guo, Xingjian Diao, Zeqi Gu, Heng Wang, Tao Feng, Cheng Qian, Hamid Palangi, Silei Xu, Xi Yun, Yi Zhu, Shilong Liu, Qingsong Wen, Sung Ju Hwang, Zuxuan Wu, Yu-Gang Jiang, Yiyu Shi, Dimitris N. Metaxas, Jiaxuan You, Julian McAuley, Mengdi Wang, Jiawei Han, Philip S. Yu, Ziyi Ye
bullets: Motivated by the difficulty of continually retaining useful information from complex, heterogeneous multimodal data.
Axis I classifies memory by how information is formed and represented, including embeddings, textual or structured records, and latent or parametric forms.
Axis II categorizes memory management into static, dynamically updated, and self-evolving policies.
The framework synthesizes design patterns and principles for abstraction, temporal validity, provenance, evidence grounding, and policy evolution.
It outlines open challenges and future directions for multimodal agent memory.
papers.selection_reason: Framework for multimodal agent memory, relevant to memory mechanisms for embodied agents and long-horizon adaptation.
papers.title: Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory
papers.tldr: This paper presents a two-axis framework for understanding how multimodal agents form, represent, manage, and evolve memory for long-horizon, lifelong interaction.

papers.abstract: Memory for long-horizon video generation must satisfy two competing requirements: it must remain bounded so generation can continue indefinitely, while still recovering what was observed at a place when the camera returns, regardless of how long ago it was seen. Reconstruction-based memories provide spatial recall by caching and reprojecting explicit geometry, but require growing storage and depend on estimated 3D structure. Recurrent memories keep a constant-size state, but retention is governed by temporal recurrence, causing old observations to fade with time. We introduce SMART, a slot memory addressed by region tokens, which combines bounded storage with spatially addressed recall. SMART stores content in a constant-size slot recurrence whose writes are addressed by the observing camera and whose reads are queried by the rendering camera, without constructing an explicit 3D representation or maintaining a growing cache. Consequently, recall is conditioned on inter-view geometry rather than on recency. Each read additionally provides a confidence estimate that conditions a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, allowing it to selectively trust retrieved content while relying on its generative prior elsewhere. On long trajectories in Memory Maze and Minecraft, SMART maintains high-fidelity recall far beyond its training horizon while using constant memory and per-step cost.
authors: Eren Cetin, Julius Erbach, Vukasin Bozic, Hyojun Go, Zixiang Zhao, Nikolai Kalischek, Federico Tombari, Konrad Schindler, Dominik Narnhofer
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between bounded memory and recalling observations when the camera revisits a location.
Uses a constant-size slot recurrence with writes keyed by the observing camera and reads queried by the rendering camera.
Avoids explicit 3D reconstruction and growing caches by conditioning recall on inter-view geometry.
Provides confidence estimates to a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, which balances retrieved content with its generative prior.
On Memory Maze and Minecraft trajectories, maintains high-fidelity recall beyond the training horizon with constant memory and per-step cost.
papers.selection_reason: Bounded spatially addressed memory for long-horizon video generation, relevant to video world models and embodied memory.
papers.title: Long-horizon Video Generation with Slot Memory Addressed By Region Tokens
papers.tldr: SMART enables long-horizon video generation with constant memory by retrieving past visual content based on spatial camera regions rather than recency.

papers.abstract: Frontier language-model agents can now improve robots on their own: they write control code, test it, and keep what works as skills and memories for the next task. We introduce SEAR (Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics), a framework and benchmark built around two questions. Is the agent really learning, or just trying more often? And does what it learns still help on new tasks, in a new simulator, and on a real robot? The framework runs an agent in three modes: it writes code that becomes the policy (code-as-policy), acts live in the control loop (agent-as-policy), or works as a researcher that fine-tunes a vision-language-action model (auto-research). The benchmark adds controls that separate retained experience from repeated attempts, familiar tasks, privileged simulator state, larger budgets, and luck. Across seven frontier language models, 330 simulated and five physical tasks, and over four years of agent runtime, we highlight three findings. First, the learning curve of a robotic agent depends both on the overall time budget and the task difficulty relative to model capability. Harder tasks make longer sessions worthwhile; on easier tasks, re-rolling short attempts does just as well. Second, control code and shared routines transfer across tasks and simulators, while task-specific solutions do not. On a real robot, we observe a performance gap between agent-designed practice and novel human-designed scenes. Third, different models evolve more effectively in different ways. Some do best acting live, others writing code first. And a text-only model keeps pace with a comparable multimodal one: perception helps with error assessment, but agentic reasoning and tool use can matter more. We release the benchmark and codebase to support future research.
authors: Xinyi Wang, Bangzheng Li, Hanyu Wang, Lin Zhang, Andrea Yaoyun Cui, Zhenggang Tang, Shyamal Buch, Dejia Xu
bullets: Evaluates three modes: code-as-policy, agent-as-policy, and auto-research fine-tuning of a vision-language-action model.
Introduces controls to distinguish retained learning from more attempts, familiar tasks, privileged state, larger budgets, and chance.
Across seven models, simulated tasks, and physical-robot tasks, longer learning helps mainly when tasks are difficult relative to model capability.
Reusable control code and routines transfer across tasks and simulators, but task-specific solutions transfer poorly; a real-robot gap remains for novel human-designed scenes.
Models differ in their best evolution strategy, and text-only models can match comparable multimodal models when reasoning and tool use compensate for weaker perception.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving agentic robotics framework retains skills and memories across tasks, fitting robot learning and embodied memory.
papers.title: SEAR: Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics
papers.tldr: SEAR benchmarks whether language-model agents genuinely improve robotic skills and transfer them beyond repeated trial-and-error.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents accumulate progress in persistent task state, yet repeatedly process interaction histories describing how that progress was achieved. This raises a natural question: can long-horizon context instead be organized around reusable progress rather than the history that produced it? In this paper, we introduce CarryOn, an object-oriented context runtime that organizes continuation around reusable task objects. Rather than treating compressed histories or reconstructed accounts of progress as the primary basis for continuation, CarryOn builds a context view from continuation carriers, complementary execution context, and a live tail of recent interactions. A core challenge is keeping this reusable basis valid after its surrounding history is retired: how can CarryOn update the basis without reconstructing the full representation at every fold? CarryOn maintains carrier records across folds, revising affected records against bound evidence and applicable environment checks while carrying forward unaffected records and jointly updating execution context. Experiments on OSWorld 2.0 and BrowseComp-Plus show improved gains of 5.8% and 7.0% while reducing total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%, respectively. Project page: https://ethannju.github.io/carryon
authors: Yuchen Lu, Julian McAuley, Lei Zhang
bullets: Targets redundant processing of histories in persistent, long-horizon tasks.
Builds context from reusable continuation carriers, execution context, and a recent-interaction tail.
Maintains carrier records across context folds, updating only affected records using evidence and environment checks.
Reports gains of 5.8% on OSWorld 2.0 and 7.0% on BrowseComp-Plus.
Reduces total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9% on the respective benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces CarryOn, an object-oriented context runtime for long-horizon agents that organizes context around reusable progress to reduce token usage and improve efficiency.
papers.title: Pack Light, CarryOn: Building Object-Oriented Context for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.tldr: CarryOn organizes long-horizon agent context around reusable task objects instead of repeatedly replaying full interaction histories, improving performance while reducing token usage.

papers.abstract: A robot's world model must remember objects that leave the camera's view. FloWM, a learned world model, keeps them in a spatial grid of features that it moves with five built-in velocities. A node memory instead keeps each object's position and velocity as numbers. We compare them in FloWM's own block world, with an oracle-fed Kalman tracker as the node memory. How the grid is read changes its score: a single-cell probe finds 66% of out-of-view blocks, while FloWM's own probe 89%. FloWM also scores 8 points higher in view although no frame is shown, which we attribute to its write-back of its own predictions. Out of view, the tracker reaches FloWM's range in 14KB against 5.6MB, with no probe. On diagonal motion, outside its five velocities, FloWM finds 11% of blocks even after fine-tuning, while the unchanged tracker keeps 93%. Faster blocks defeat both until one more allowed speed takes the tracker to 94%, where FloWM's built-in shifts would need 25 copies of its grid. A learned node memory must still replace the oracles and handle velocity under noise, long gaps, and the bounce.
bullets: FloWM stores object information in a spatial feature grid with five built-in velocities; the comparison uses an oracle-fed Kalman tracker as node memory.
Probe design strongly affects FloWM’s apparent recall: single-cell probing finds 66% of hidden blocks versus 89% with FloWM’s own probe.
Without camera frames, FloWM scores 8 points higher in view, attributed to writing back its predictions.
Out of view, the tracker matches FloWM’s range using 14KB versus 5.6MB and handles diagonal motion at 93% recall versus FloWM’s 11%.
Both struggle with faster motion; the tracker reaches 94% when given one additional allowed speed, while FloWM would require 25 grid copies.
papers.selection_reason: Studies object memory in learned robot world models under partial observability, directly relevant to embodied memory and world models.
papers.title: Grid or Nodes? Probing Object Memory in World Models Under Partial Observability
papers.tldr: In FloWM’s block-world tests, a compact oracle-fed node memory matches or exceeds grid-based object recall while using far less memory and handling unseen motion better, though it is not yet fully learned.

papers.abstract: An embodied agent must prioritise among competing bodily needs. In active inference, it can respond to an urgent need by increasing the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. We compare these two interventions, separately and together, in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, and ask how each changes survival, perception and the body model the agent learns. Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival. Preference reweighting keeps bodily states further from their lethal boundaries and changes the states from which the agent learns, so its learned model covers fewer need levels, with lower quality across all levels but slightly higher quality on the levels it visits. An experiment on 72 further layouts does not establish the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts, but both interventions improve average survival there and their interaction is positive. Survival alone therefore gives an incomplete account of how a model prioritises needs and learns about its body.
authors: St John Grimbly, Nicolas Kuske, Evert A. Boonstra, Charel van Hoof, Rowan Hodson, Benjamin Rosman, Ryan Smith, Mark Solms, Jonathan P. Shock
bullets: Precision increases the reliability of interoceptive information, sharpening posteriors and improving survival.
Preference reweighting prioritises need-relieving outcomes, keeping bodily states farther from lethal boundaries.
Preference reweighting changes which bodily states are experienced and learned, narrowing model coverage while slightly improving accuracy in visited states.
Across 72 additional layouts, both interventions improved average survival and interacted positively, but the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts was not established.
Survival alone does not fully reveal how an agent prioritises needs or learns its body model.
papers.selection_reason: Explores interoceptive prioritization in an embodied agent using active inference, comparing precision and preference reweighting to learn body models and survival strategies.
papers.title: Two Routes to Interoceptive Prioritisation: Dissociating Likelihood Precision and Preference Reweighting in Active Inference
papers.tldr: Precision and preference reweighting are distinct routes to prioritising bodily needs, producing different effects on survival, perception, and learned body models.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have shown strong potential for embodied vision-language navigation (VLN), yet their performance degrades on long-horizon trajectories due to context-length limits, redundant historical observations, and unstable spatial alignment across time. These issues make it difficult to both compress long navigation histories and reliably reuse past spatial experience. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{MemoryVLN}, a unified memory-driven navigation system built around memory construction and management. During memory construction, \emph{Long Sequence Compression} employs forgetting-curve-inspired temporal sampling to preserve dense recent evidence and sparse yet representative distant observations under a limited token budget. \emph{Ego-Aware Memory Representation} further integrates 2D semantic tokens, 3D geometric tokens, and 6D agent poses, allowing each memory to encode both what was observed and where it was observed. During memory management, \emph{Hierarchical Memory Bank} maintains in-episode and context-level memories through cross-context warm-start and confidence-controlled write-back. \emph{Memory Enhancement} then retrieves the Top-$K$ relevant memories according to the current navigation state and fuses them with the current visual tokens. Together, these mechanisms transform raw navigation history into compact, spatially grounded, selectively retrievable, and reusable navigation experience. Extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE demonstrate consistent improvements over the state-of-the-art baselines by a substantial margin (i.e., 2\% and 6.5\% in successful rate).
authors: Xueyao Wei, Yifei Wang, Delun Li, Shaoan Wang, Junzhi Yu, Wenjie Song, Xingyu Chen
bullets: Addresses context-length limits, redundant observations, and unstable spatial alignment in long trajectories.
Compresses history with temporal sampling that preserves recent evidence and representative distant observations.
Represents memories using 2D semantics, 3D geometry, and 6D agent poses for spatial grounding.
Maintains hierarchical in-episode and cross-context memory, retrieves relevant memories, and fuses them with current visual tokens.
Reports successful-rate gains of 2% on R2R-CE and 6.5% on RxR-CE over state-of-the-art baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces MemoryVLN, a memory-driven system for vision-language navigation that constructs ego-aware memory representations and manages hierarchical memory banks, directly fitting Embodied AI and Adaptation and Memory.
papers.title: MemoryVLN: From Ego-Aware Memory Representation to Cross-Context Memory Reuse in Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: MemoryVLN improves long-horizon vision-language navigation by compressing, spatially grounding, and selectively reusing navigation history.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory has become a core component of large language model (LLM) agents. As agents accumulate personal information over long-term use, users increasingly ask them to delete sensitive or outdated facts. A memory system should honor such requests. It should remove exactly what was requested and keep the rest of its memory intact. However, existing memory benchmarks evaluate only memory writing, retrieval, and organization, so whether agents can forget at the user's explicit request remains under-evaluated. To address this gap, we propose Bemula, the first benchmark dedicated to memory unlearning. It comprises 50 multi-session dialogue instances, 135 forget requests of six types, and 1,742 test questions. Each dialogue has a control version without the requests, so that only systems that have stored the target can earn credit for forgetting. Across the paired versions, five test suites measure storage, removal of the requested information, preservation of unrelated memories, relearning of similar facts, and resistance to extraction attacks. On Bemula, we evaluate six mainstream memory systems under three backbone LLMs, together with the Full Context LLM on two of them. The results are negative. Across all evaluated systems and backbones, no system passes more than 1.5% of forget requests end to end, and most pass none at all. These systems either leave the requested information extractable under simple attacks or delete far more than requested. Memory unlearning therefore remains an open challenge for agent memory design. We release our data and code at https://github.com/Nboxff/bemula-benchmark.
authors: Bofan Xie, Chaokun Wang, Guanchen Ge, Songyao Wang, Fang Niu, Hang Zhang, Wei Wang
bullets: Addresses the gap in evaluating explicit memory deletion in long-term LLM agents.
Introduces 50 multi-session dialogues, 135 forget requests across six types, and 1,742 test questions, with paired control versions.
Evaluates storage, targeted removal, unrelated-memory preservation, relearning, and resistance to extraction attacks.
Tests six memory systems with three backbone LLMs, plus Full Context LLM on two backbones.
No evaluated system passes more than 1.5% of forget requests end to end; failures involve residual extraction or excessive deletion.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Bemula, a benchmark for memory unlearning in LLM agents, and investigates the technical challenges of removing specific information while preserving the rest of the memory state.
papers.title: Can Agents Forget When Asked? A Benchmark for Memory Unlearning in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Bemula benchmarks whether LLM agents can selectively forget user-requested memories while preserving unrelated information, finding that current systems largely fail.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in real-world environments often requires long-horizon operation under partial observability and evolving goals. Existing mapless navigation approaches predominantly assume fixed goals throughout an episode, limiting applicability to practical scenarios where goals change online during execution. We study online chained-goal navigation, where goals evolve through existing-goal redirection or new-goal emergence without explicit transition signals. Under this setting, we find navigation may require either continued exploration or strategic revisitation, creating conflicting memory requirements. We propose Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Belief Learning (GLST), a memory-decomposition framework that separates latent beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations for long-horizon reasoning. We further introduce goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation under evolving goals. Extensive experiments in simulation across diverse terrains demonstrate improved chained-goal navigation performance over baselines. Real-robot experiments using the Spot quadruped further validate our memory decomposition framework.
authors: Yousef Liang, Ryan Ardalan, Yarden Goraly, Chenhao Zhu, Yue Yin, Jonas Frey, Claire Tomlin, Marco Pavone, Shankar Sastry
bullets: Targets chained-goal navigation under partial observability, where goals may be redirected or newly introduced without explicit transition signals.
Separates latent beliefs into global/local spatial and long/short temporal representations to support exploration and strategic revisitation.
Uses goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation as goals evolve.
Experiments in simulated diverse terrains and on a Spot quadruped show improved chained-goal navigation over baselines.
The approach is evaluated in simulation and real-robot settings; broader scope beyond these settings is not established in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a memory decomposition framework (GLST) for online chained-goal navigation that separates beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations, directly addressing long-horizon reasoning and memory requirements in embodied agents.
papers.title: GLST: Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Memory Decomposition Framework for Online Chained-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: GLST enables mapless robots to navigate long-horizon environments with goals that change online by decomposing memory across spatial and temporal scales.

papers.abstract: Spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents navigating and interacting with the physical world. As observations arrive incrementally, agents must reason in a streaming manner. Yet streaming understanding must also be closed-loop: task-relevant evidence may require both recalling past observations and actively acquiring new views. Existing streaming approaches largely emphasize processing incoming observations, leaving task-driven active exploration underexplored. We introduce MemAct, a framework for streaming spatial understanding with memory and action. A shared vision--language model incrementally writes structured historical memory, retrieves records and past frames on demand, and acquires additional evidence through movement and turning. Retrieved evidence and action observations inform subsequent decisions, enabling the agent to continue exploring or answer within a unified reasoning loop. We develop the MemAct suite, a data generation pipeline and collection across real and simulated environments, with approximately 1M training examples for spatial reasoning, memory writing, retrieval, and exploration. Its MemAct-bench comprises 20,000 main QA pairs evaluating current-observation understanding, historical evidence use, and active exploration, plus 2,000 separate Timing questions. MemAct combines supervised fine-tuning for memory and interaction with counterfactual action optimization using cumulative evidence gains, action costs, and terminal answer quality to improve exploration and stopping decisions. Experiments show that MemAct outperforms existing spatial understanding and streaming baselines and approaches frontier multimodal models on MemAct-bench while retaining streaming inference efficiency.
authors: Yuxi Wei, Wei Huang, Qirui Chen, Lu Hou, Xiaojuan Qi
bullets: Addresses the gap between passive streaming observation and task-driven exploration that acquires missing evidence.
Uses a shared vision-language model to write structured memories, retrieve past frames, and guide movement or turning.
Introduces MemAct data and benchmarks spanning current observations, historical evidence, active exploration, and timing.
Trains memory and interaction with supervised fine-tuning plus counterfactual action optimization for evidence gain, action cost, and answer quality.
Outperforms existing spatial and streaming baselines, approaches frontier multimodal models, and maintains streaming inference efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming spatial understanding with embodied memory and active exploration; directly fits embodied memory, spatial intelligence, and vision-language-action.
papers.title: MemAct: Streaming Spatial Understanding with Memory and Active Exploration
papers.tldr: MemAct enables embodied agents to understand spaces over time by combining structured memory, on-demand retrieval, and active exploration in a unified streaming loop.

papers.abstract: Existing embodied navigation tasks commonly assume that traversability and object states remain fixed during an episode. Yet reaching a goal may require opening a door to access a room and then opening a container to reveal a hidden target. We formulate interactive navigation beyond reachability, unifying channel-induced changes in spatial connectivity, container-induced changes in target visibility, and their sequential dependencies. We introduce MultINav-Bench, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark in MolmoSpaces spanning channel, container, and mixed tasks, with interaction-necessity annotations covering required and unnecessary episodes. Its data generation pipeline automates task construction across multiple task types. The evaluation protocol separately measures navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and cost. We further propose MultINav-Agent, a three-stage agentic framework built on a persistent, state-conditioned interaction graph. Semantic interactive perception grounds entities and interaction states; a vision-language model selects task-relevant actions based on expected changes in connectivity and target observability; and post-interaction verification updates the graph to guide subsequent navigation, exploration, or interaction. Experiments on MultINav-Bench show that MultINav-Agent consistently outperforms adapted baselines across channel, container, and mixed tasks.
authors: Delun Li, Xueyao Wei, Rui Chen, Yifei Wang, Junzhi Yu, Wenjie Song, Xingyu Chen
bullets: Models navigation where interactions change spatial connectivity, target visibility, or both sequentially.
Introduces MultINav-Bench, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark covering channel, container, and mixed tasks with interaction-necessity annotations.
Evaluates navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and interaction cost separately.
Proposes MultINav-Agent with interactive perception, expected-change action selection, and post-interaction graph verification.
Reports consistent improvements over adapted baselines across all task types.
papers.selection_reason: Interactive embodied navigation benchmark and agentic framework with persistent state-conditioned interaction graph; fits robot navigation, VLA, and embodied memory.
papers.title: Interactive Navigation Beyond Reachability: Benchmark and Agentic Framework
papers.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark and agent framework for navigation tasks requiring interactions such as opening doors and containers to reach or reveal goals.

papers.abstract: Studying event memory requires defining events and their relationships within remembered experience. Autobiographical narratives provide evidence of this organization, but their analytical units must first be established. This study introduces a large language model framework for constructing event representations from narratives and modeling their structure and dynamics with excerpt-level traceability. Explicit boundary rules and a feature schema informed by hippocampal models of episodic memory and navigation guide event construction. In a proof-of-concept application to interviews from five participants, the framework constructed 256 event-states. Multiple correspondence analysis embedded these states in feature-based spaces, with analyses focused on a selected 4-D geometry and 10-D and 13-D reference geometries. Consecutive event-states were significantly closer than expected under randomized narrative order. In the selected 4-D ten-basin solution, similarity between basin-state feature profiles corresponded with similarity between one-step routing profiles; context, mechanism, and theme differentiated full-system pathway engagement. A successor representation modeled expected basin-state occupancy across successive steps. Correlations between basin-centroid distances and complete successor-profile distances were positive across all five basin solutions, with exploratory tests supporting correspondence in at least two solutions across all three geometries. These findings connect feature-based event representations with observed narrative transitions and modeled multistep organization. The framework translates hippocampal principles into source-linked event boundaries and state representations, providing an analytical basis for testing neural accounts of event segmentation and predictive organization during naturalistic recall.
bullets: Defines event boundaries and feature schemas informed by hippocampal models of episodic memory and navigation.
Applied to interviews from five participants, producing 256 traceable event-states.
Multidimensional analyses found consecutive event-states were closer than expected under randomized narrative order.
Basin-state similarity aligned with one-step routing profiles, while context, mechanism, and theme differentiated pathway engagement.
Successor-representation analyses linked feature-space distances with modeled multistep occupancy patterns across tested geometries.
papers.selection_reason: LLM framework for event memory and narrative dynamics with hippocampal/navigation-inspired structure, relevant to embodied memory.
papers.title: Event Memory and Narrative Dynamics: A Large Language Model Framework for Multidimensional State Spaces
papers.tldr: A source-traceable LLM framework represents autobiographical narratives as multidimensional event states and models their sequential organization, linking narrative transitions to hippocampal-inspired memory principles.

papers.abstract: World models capture environment dynamics and support counterfactual reasoning for planning. In image-goal navigation, where the target often lies beyond the current field of view, the agent must not only model environmental dynamics but also maintain a persistent spatial memory of the scene. Existing approaches either introduce spatial context by fine-tuning pretrained models on the target task, which underexploits their spatial priors, or rely on external 3D reconstruction, which is computationally expensive for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose the Geometry Grounded World Action Model (G$^2$WAM) for image-goal navigation. G$^2$WAM encodes spatial cues through a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, yielding a stable and consistent spatial context that enables efficient navigation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Following the world-action-model paradigm, G$^2$WAM jointly predicts future states and actions, eliminating the need for costly cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning. In addition, G$^2$WAM operates entirely in latent space, avoiding the computational burden of pixel-level reconstruction and substantially reducing inference cost. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, G$^2$WAM reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2%, respectively. In closed-loop navigation experiments, it improves the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and the success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining high efficiency.
authors: Ke Gui, Chenghao Shi, Ziyue Wang, Longwen Chen, Xieyuanli Chen, Huimin Lu
bullets: Addresses image-goal navigation when targets are outside the current view and persistent spatial memory is required.
Uses learned scene-coordinate localization to anchor current, goal, and history frames in a shared reference frame.
Jointly predicts future states and actions in latent space, avoiding pixel reconstruction and CEM-style planning.
Reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2% across four trajectory prediction benchmarks.
Improves closed-loop success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and SPL from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-grounded world action model for image-goal navigation with latent state-action prediction and persistent spatial memory.
papers.title: G$^2$WAM: World Action Models for Efficient and Geometry Grounded Image-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: G$^2$WAM enables efficient image-goal navigation by combining geometry-grounded spatial memory with latent world-action modeling, improving trajectory prediction and navigation success without explicit 3D reconstruction or costly planning.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robotic manipulation by jointly predicting future visual states and actions, yet most existing methods make decisions primarily from the current observation. This limits their reliability in long-horizon tasks, where visually similar states may correspond to different interaction histories and task stages. Moreover, directly incorporating historical observations can introduce stale, stage-mismatched, or error-contaminated information, leading to inaccurate world prediction and accumulated closed-loop errors. We propose RM-WAM, a reliable memory-augmented World Action Model that treats memory as a context-dependent predictive resource rather than universally useful historical context. RM-WAM represents history using complementary short-term visual state memory and latent event memory, which respectively capture recent interaction dynamics and longer-term state transitions. A counterfactual memory learning scheme varies the accessible history while keeping the current inputs and prediction targets fixed, enabling the model to learn a context-dependent utility estimate for historical memory. Based on this estimate, a utility-aware gating mechanism adaptively controls memory injection into the world-action backbone. Experiments demonstrate that RM-WAM highlights the importance of reliable and selective memory utilization in long-horizon tasks.
authors: Cui Miao, Junhao Yu, Ping Liu, Ning Yang, Xuhua Chen, He Zheng, Xiaodong Wang, Tao Zhang
bullets: Long-horizon manipulation is challenging because similar observations can reflect different histories or task stages.
Naively using history may introduce stale, mismatched, or error-contaminated information.
RM-WAM combines short-term visual-state memory with longer-term latent event memory.
Counterfactual memory learning estimates when historical context is useful, while utility-aware gating controls its injection.
Experiments demonstrate the importance of reliable, selective memory use in long-horizon tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces RM-WAM, a memory-augmented World Action Model that uses counterfactual learning and utility-aware gating to handle long-horizon tasks and stale information.
papers.title: RM-WAM: Reliable Memory-Augmented World Action Models for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: RM-WAM improves long-horizon robot manipulation by selectively using reliable historical visual and event memories to make better world-action predictions.

papers.abstract: Camera-first agents must act on the visual world as it unfolds. We argue that the central obstacle for future camera-first agents is not recognition ability - multimodal models (vision-language and live/streaming alike) generalize well through language and remain the right tool for semantic reasoning - but time. Many visual targets are ephemeral: they appear, are query-relevant, and leave within a short window. Binding memory to the same end-to-end path as reasoning means that by the time a monolithic pipeline completes, the evidence is gone. We formalize this as Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) and a Perceptual Deadline Contract separating a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline, grounded in the bounded, passive nature of sensory and working memory. We propose a two-deadline architecture: an always-on, bounded, non-semantic fast path; an active remembering mechanism that commits a moment to durable memory before it is overwritten (event-driven in v1); and a deferred deliberation layer (multimodal model + tools). We instantiate the contract on real MOT17 track windows, a consistency check, and calibrate the single-path baseline from measured frontier-model latency: even a short answer takes 1.2-9.3 s, and an agentic identify-and-search longer. Answers can be late; evidence cannot be missed.
authors: Xiaofan Wu, Xi Zeng, Miaoxia Chen, Peishan Chen, Shuyan Li, Chen Wang, Jiyun Yao, Hanyong Zhong, Jiahao Zhu
bullets: The key bottleneck is timing, not visual recognition or semantic reasoning.
Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) describes targets that appear and disappear before processing finishes.
A Perceptual Deadline Contract separates a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline.
The proposed architecture combines an always-on bounded fast path, active durable-memory capture, and deferred multimodal deliberation with tools.
Measured frontier-model latency suggests answers may take 1.2–9.3 seconds or longer, while evidence can disappear sooner.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes memory architecture and perceptual deadlines for camera-first embodied agents acting on ephemeral visual targets.
papers.title: How Should a Camera-First AI Agent Work?
papers.tldr: Camera-first agents should capture fleeting visual evidence immediately, then reason about it later, because semantic processing may outlast the moment an object is visible.

papers.abstract: Versatile quadruped locomotion depends on a tight coupling between what the robot perceives and what its body can execute. Yet existing visual controllers typically organize depth history using fixed temporal patterns, overlooking that the same temporal span corresponds to different spatial ranges as the robot's speed, posture, and gait phase change. Consequently, the same visual history may be insufficient in one motion state but outdated or misaligned in another. To address this limitation, we propose TempoLoco, a body-aware dynamic visual perception framework that organizes visual memory according to the robot's current locomotion state. TempoLoco learns multiple complementary temporal views from a long depth buffer, encodes them within a shared feature space, and dynamically aggregates them using proprioceptive history and multi-scale terrain evidence. This enables a single policy to align visual anticipation with the robot's current motion capabilities across complex terrains, including stairs, platforms, gaps, discrete obstacles, rough ground, and slopes. From the experiment analysis, TempoLoco achieves a 78.4% success rate, compared with 58.2% for the strongest fixed-history baseline and 62.1% for uniform multi-scale fusion. In separate capability evaluations, it completes 41/45 simulated trials across nine terrain types and 23/25 real-world trials on a Unitree B2 with a fixed arm, demonstrating robust and deployable locomotion through body-aware dynamic visual perception.
authors: Hao Zhang, Yuping Yan, Yitian Hong, Luying Feng, Tianhong Wang, Fengqi Dai, Wei Chen, Yaochu Jin
bullets: Fixed temporal visual histories can become spatially mismatched as speed, posture, and gait phase change.
TempoLoco learns multiple temporal views from a long depth buffer in a shared feature space.
Proprioceptive history and multi-scale terrain evidence dynamically select and fuse the most relevant views.
It achieves a 78.4% success rate versus 58.2% for the strongest fixed-history baseline and 62.1% for uniform multi-scale fusion.
The system completes 41/45 simulated trials and 23/25 real-world trials on a Unitree B2 across diverse terrains.
papers.selection_reason: Motion-adaptive temporal visual memory for quadruped locomotion; fits embodied navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: Beyond Fixed Visual History: Learning Motion-Adaptive Temporal Receptive Fields for Complex-Terrain Quadruped Locomotion
papers.tldr: TempoLoco dynamically adapts visual-history timescales to a quadruped’s motion state, improving locomotion across complex terrains.

papers.abstract: It is widely appreciated that robotic policies require long-term memory to perform complex tasks. However, directly conditioning policies on all past observations leaves policy learning susceptible to learning spurious shortcuts, and introduces large latency at policy deployment. As such, today's memory-augmented policies curate what to remember, either by retaining only recent frames, selected keyframes, or textual summaries, or by learning latent representations of the visual stream alone. In this work, we propose an alternative approach IMPRINT, a policy-agnostic latent memory framework that augments vision-language-action (VLA) models with multi-stream memory without explicitly constraining what the policy should remember. IMPRINT compresses different streams into a latent memory that is updated incrementally at inference, enabling low latency. To avoid shortcut learning, IMPRINT adopts a two-stage training procedure, first supervising memory to reconstruct multiple streams (observations, actions, proprioception) of past information, as well as estimate current task progress, followed by end-to-end finetuning, jointly with the policy, on action prediction. Across both simulation and real-world tasks demanding memory, IMPRINT improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26%, outperforming popular alternatives, and maintaining lowest inference latency among memory-augmented VLAs. Through careful ablations, we demonstrate the utility of incorporating diverse information streams into robotic memory, validating the advantages of foregoing history curation. Project website: https://yilin-wu98.github.io/imprint_website/.
authors: Yilin Wu, Rutav Shah, Shuaiyi Huang, Sumedh A. Sontakke, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Andrea Bajcsy, Max Simchowitz, Guanya Shi
bullets: Addresses shortcut learning and deployment latency caused by conditioning on all past observations.
Compresses observations, actions, and proprioception into incrementally updated latent memory for VLA policies.
Uses two-stage training: reconstruct past information and estimate task progress, then jointly fine-tune for action prediction.
Improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26% across simulation and real-world tasks.
Reports the lowest inference latency among evaluated memory-augmented VLAs; ablations support using diverse streams without history curation.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-stream latent memory for VLA robot policies, directly relevant to embodied memory and robot learning.
papers.title: Memory Without Curation: Learning Multi-Stream Latent Memory for Robot Policies
papers.tldr: IMPRINT gives robot policies low-latency, multi-stream latent memory without manually curating history, improving success on memory-intensive tasks.

papers.abstract: Zero-Shot Object Navigation (ZSON) in unknown multi-floor environments presents a significant challenge. Recent methods, mostly based on semantic value greedy waypoint selection, spatial topology-enhanced memory, and Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as a decision-making framework, have led to improvements. However, these architectures struggle to balance exploration and exploitation for ZSON when encountering unseen environments, especially in multi-floor settings, such as robots getting stuck at narrow intersections, endlessly wandering, or failing to find stair entrances. To overcome these challenges, we propose AERR-Nav, a Zero-Shot Object Navigation framework that dynamically adjusts its state based on the robot's environment. Specifically, AERR-Nav has the following two key advantages: (1) An Adaptive Exploration-Recovery-Reminiscing Strategy, enables robots to dynamically transition between three states, facilitating specialized responses to diverse navigation scenarios. (2) An Adaptive Exploration State featuring Fast and Slow-Thinking modes helps robots better balance exploration, exploitation, and higher-level reasoning based on evolving environmental information. Extensive experiments on the HM3D and MP3D benchmarks demonstrate that our AERR-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot methods. Comprehensive ablation studies further validate the efficacy of our proposed strategy and modules.
authors: Jingzhi Huang, Junkai Huang, Haoyang Yang, Haoang Li, Yi Wang
bullets: Targets common failures such as getting stuck at narrow intersections, wandering indefinitely, and missing stair entrances.
Uses an Adaptive Exploration-Recovery-Reminiscing Strategy to select navigation states based on environmental conditions.
Its exploration state combines Fast- and Slow-Thinking modes to balance exploration, exploitation, and higher-level reasoning.
Experiments on HM3D and MP3D report state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot methods, with ablations supporting the proposed components.
papers.selection_reason: Zero-shot object navigation with adaptive exploration-recovery-reminiscing and MLLM-based decision-making; directly fits embodied navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: AERR-Nav: Adaptive Exploration-Recovery-Reminiscing Strategy for Zero-Shot Object Navigation
papers.tldr: AERR-Nav improves zero-shot object navigation in unseen multi-floor environments by adaptively switching among exploration, recovery, and reminiscing behaviors.

papers.abstract: Active exploration and semantic navigation require an embodied agent to build memory from partial observations, predict how the evolution of observed spatial memory may support future motion, and convert that prediction into actionable plans. We present GLAM, a goal-conditioned latent world model trained over global spatiotemporal memory, and GLAM NAV, the complete navigation system built around it. Given historical map tokens, a navigation goal, and the current robot pose, GLAM jointly predicts future map representations and robot-centric waypoint latents, allowing future spatial context and navigation intent to be inferred in a shared representation space. The model follows a JEPA-like latent prediction paradigm, operates directly on map-level latent tokens rather than RGB reconstruction, and uses a pretrained waypoint encoder-decoder to supervise and decode navigation plans within GLAM NAV. Training data are collected by replaying ObjectNav expert trajectories in Habitat over HM3D v0.2 scene assets and slicing them into multi-timescale prediction samples. On a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav subset reproduction setting, GLAM NAV improves over a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline in both success rate and success weighted by path length.
bullets: Uses historical map tokens, the navigation goal, and robot pose to jointly predict future map representations and robot-centric waypoint latents.
Applies JEPA-like latent prediction directly to map-level tokens instead of reconstructing RGB observations.
GLAM NAV combines the world model with a pretrained waypoint encoder-decoder to generate actionable navigation plans.
Trained on replayed ObjectNav expert trajectories in Habitat using HM3D v0.2 scenes and multi-timescale prediction samples.
On a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav reproduction subset, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length over a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Latent world model over global spatiotemporal memory for active exploration and navigation.
papers.title: GLAM: Training a latent world model over global spatiotemporal memory for active exploration and navigation
papers.tldr: GLAM learns a goal-conditioned latent world model that predicts future spatial memory and navigation waypoints for active exploration and semantic navigation.

papers.abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source-target boundary. For each probe, no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source
authors: Jingwei Song, Zhisheng Chen, Bingfan Zeng, Jing Tang, Yubo Hou, Jinhao Jing, Zhengwei Xie, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: Tests whether interaction history yields reusable skills rather than merely preserved resources or successful actions.
Uses 19 registered evolution chains, task-state graphs, stage verifiers, reset target worlds, matched source conditions, and provenance tracking.
Compares no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled experience under matched step budgets and five seeds using TSR, WGP, and VMP.
Finds a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed agents, while related experience shows no stable transfer.
Stage audits identify early wood-collection and crafting failures that can prevent later capabilities from being observed.
papers.selection_reason: Controlled benchmark for embodied agents' experience-driven self-improvement, capability transfer, and interaction memory.
papers.title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
papers.tldr: MC-EvoBench is a controlled Minecraft benchmark showing that agents’ prior experience does not yet reliably produce durable, transferable capabilities.

papers.abstract: Memory-dependent manipulation requires a policy to track execution state and recover visual evidence that is no longer observable. We propose dual-stream memory for vision-language-action policies, assigning these requirements to complementary representations. A task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet compresses history into one temporal token, supervised by progress prediction and action-conditioned feature reconstruction. A task-conditioned retriever retains frames above a fixed relevance threshold; linear multi-scale fusion encodes each frame into sixteen spatial tokens. We then freeze the temporal compressor and jointly optimize retrieval and policy learning. Across sixteen RoboMME tasks, the complete model achieves 49.22% mean success versus 44.51% for the published FrameSamp+Modul reference, improving fourteen tasks and all four suite means. On four real-robot tasks, mean success reaches 62.5% versus 37.5%, with the largest gains on repeated actions requiring execution-stage discrimination. These results support combining execution context with selective visual access, while failures under cup swaps expose persistent identity tracking as an unresolved requirement.
authors: Yang Wang, Ping Liu, Ruiyu Wang, Xuhua Chen, Lingfeng Zhang, Tao Zhang
bullets: Targets manipulation tasks where execution state must be tracked and previously visible evidence recovered.
Uses a task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet temporal compressor with progress prediction and action-conditioned reconstruction.
Adds a task-conditioned frame retriever and encodes selected frames with 16 spatial tokens; the compressor is frozen during joint retrieval-policy training.
On 16 RoboMME tasks, mean success is 49.22% versus 44.51% for FrameSamp+Modul; real-robot mean success is 62.5% versus 37.5%.
Cup-swap failures indicate persistent object-identity tracking remains unresolved.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces memory mechanisms for VLA policies, directly relevant to VLA and embodied memory.
papers.title: Dual-Stream Memory for Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.tldr: Dual-stream memory improves vision-language-action manipulation by combining compressed execution history with selective retrieval of relevant past frames.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies fail on memory tasks, behaviour that depends on events observed long before the current frame, because their training data is overwhelmingly Markov and mapping episodic memory directly to action chunks is hard. Yet the same policy, finetuned once to follow a privileged oracle's grounded-subgoal text, nearly solves these tasks: the difficulty lies entirely in mapping memory to a grounded symbolic subgoal. Existing work entrusts this stage to a single VLM that selects keyframes and reasons over raw frames, and falls far short of the oracle: key identities and dynamics are buried in noisy pixels, the reasoning spans hundreds of frames in an unbounded context, and hallucination corrupts the memory itself. We instead present GAMMA (Grounded multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit), which builds the stage as a collaborating two-agent memory system: a detector tool (SAM-3) for spatial grounding, a VLM writer that distils each replan window into one grounded text line, an append-only text memory bank, and a VLM reasoner that reads the bank and emits the next grounded subgoal at the oracle's cadence, wrapped in a propose-verify harness that admits, defers, corrects, or rejects every agent claim against mechanical visual evidence, at training-corpus construction and at deployment alike. On a sixteen-task memory-manipulation suite GAMMA recovers a large fraction of the oracle ceiling with the policy held fixed, reaching the ceiling on several tasks, and transfers with unchanged contracts to a second benchmark.
authors: Yudong Liu, Yueqian Lin, Zijia Tang, Yuxi Zheng, Yuan Li, Shuai Zhang, Yi Li, Taotao Jing, Shuangjun Liu, Dashan Gao, Ning Bi, Jingwei Sun, Yiran Chen, Hai Helen Li
bullets: Addresses VLA failures on tasks requiring information from events far before the current frame.
Uses SAM-3 for spatial grounding, a VLM writer for concise episodic summaries, and a VLM reasoner to produce grounded subgoals.
Maintains an append-only text memory bank and verifies, corrects, defers, or rejects claims using mechanical visual evidence.
Recovers much of the privileged-oracle performance on a 16-task suite, reaching the oracle ceiling on several tasks.
Transfers to a second benchmark without changing its contracts; performance is scoped to the tested memory-manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Grounded multi-agent memory system with mechanical audit for memory-intensive VLA manipulation.
papers.title: Gamma: Grounded Multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit for Memory-Intensive Manipulation
papers.tldr: GAMMA combines grounded visual detection, structured text memory, multi-agent reasoning, and mechanical verification to help fixed VLA policies solve long-horizon memory-based manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to retain task-relevant history while revising conclusions no longer supported by physical evidence. Retaining observations alone does not specify which completed conditions should be withdrawn after a disturbance or which obligations require repair. We introduce REMM, Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation, a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor. REMM separates an append-only evidence history from revisable task state and explicitly links derived relations and completed conditions to their supporting facts. When accepted evidence changes a supporting fact, it withdraws dependent conclusions and schedules targeted recovery at verified skill boundaries without updating the executor. Across 51 physical trials, including operator-assisted runs, REMM improves mean recorded task progress over the strongest baseline from 57% to 91% in intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% in sequence recall. Complementary video diagnostics show improved grounding of retained history into the next instruction, including comparisons with $\pi_{0.5}$-compatible high-level planner adaptations. These results support revisable memory as a practical interface for continued manipulation without policy retraining. Project: https://revanthsenthil.github.io/remm/.
authors: Revanth Krishna Senthilkumaran, Ruwan Wickramarachchi, Alessandro Oltramari, Jonathan Francis
bullets: Targets long-horizon manipulation, where robots must retain useful history while retracting unsupported conclusions.
Uses a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor, without policy retraining.
Links derived relations and completed conditions to supporting facts, then withdraws affected conclusions when evidence changes.
Schedules targeted recovery at verified skill boundaries after disturbances.
Across 51 physical trials, mean recorded progress improved from 57% to 91% for intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% for sequence recall.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces revisable embodied memory layer for manipulation with frozen VLA executor, directly fitting embodied memory and robot manipulation.
papers.title: REMM: Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation
papers.tldr: REMM helps robots recover from manipulation disturbances by maintaining evidence separately from revisable task state and repairing only conclusions invalidated by new evidence.

papers.abstract: Memory allows large language model (LLM) agents to use past experience, often stored as textual records, when responding to requests. For embodied agents that control robots, visual and spatial observations introduce a broader choice of memory modalities, affecting both the information available for subsequent tasks and the model inference costs of constructing and using memory. We introduce MeMoREval, a benchmark for studying this problem through a controlled experience-request protocol. Agents first experience a sequence of events without knowing the subsequent tasks, and subsequently they use memory to respond to information and action requests without receiving new observations. The benchmark comprises 53 tasks across four simulated indoor environments and measures task success alongside the inference costs of memory construction and use. Our reference evaluations reveal that storing frames outperforms storing generated descriptions at lower write-time inference cost for the primary model, while storing frames with scene graphs achieves the highest aggregate task success for every tested model. Extensions to accumulated experience, selective frame retention, and visual input to memory writers demonstrate how the benchmark accommodates further memory-design investigations. Two physical-robot demonstrations establish the feasibility of applying its protocol beyond simulation.
authors: Junxiang Wang, Yuchen Liu, Yi Wu, Guofei Chen, Nir Pechuk, Tao Chen, Zackory Erickson, Yuzhe Qin, Tianyu Li
bullets: Evaluates memory through a controlled protocol: agents observe events first, then answer information and action requests without new observations.
Covers 53 tasks across four simulated indoor environments, measuring success plus memory construction and usage costs.
For the primary model, storing frames outperforms generated descriptions while requiring lower write-time inference cost.
Combining frames with scene graphs achieves the highest aggregate task success across all tested models.
The protocol also supports studies of experience accumulation, selective frame retention, visual memory writers, and physical-robot deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Fits embodied memory benchmarking for LLM-driven embodied agents.
papers.title: What Should Embodied Agents Remember? Benchmarking and Evaluating Memory Modality for Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: MeMoREval benchmarks how different memory modalities affect embodied agents’ task success and inference costs when using past visual-spatial experience.

papers.abstract: Memory-augmented mobile GUI agents store successful execution trajectories and reuse them in later tasks, but a stored trajectory rarely matches a new task exactly. The new task may use different parameters, share only some of its steps with a stored trajectory, or have no relevant record in memory. Forcing the agent to use irrelevant memory can mislead it, whereas discarding memory that may still be useful deprives it of guidance from past experience. To address this dilemma, we propose DeltaReplay, a step-level memory reuse framework that decides how to use existing memory without modifying it. We observe that the reusable part of a stored record is determined not by the record itself but by its relation to the new task, mainly through two factors: page-level consistency and action-level generality. We therefore store execution trajectories as paths in a transition graph, whose nodes (pages) and edges (actions between pages) capture these two factors. At reuse time, the action on each edge is split into a task-independent operation and task-specific parameters. DeltaReplay then compares each recorded step with the new task and the current screen, and decides whether to follow it, execute it after replacing its parameters, or leave it to the base agent. On AndroidWorld and SPA-Bench, DeltaReplay improves the task success rate over a base agent with the same backbone by up to 10.3 and 25.0 percentage points, respectively. These results indicate that deciding at each step how to use retrieved memory lets agents benefit even from partially matching trajectories.
authors: Yudong Bai, Yihong Chen, Quanming Yao, Yaqing Wang
bullets: Addresses the risk of both misusing irrelevant trajectory memories and discarding partially useful ones.
Represents trajectories as transition-graph paths, capturing page-level consistency and action-level generality.
Splits each action into task-independent operations and task-specific parameters for flexible reuse.
At each step, chooses to follow the recorded action, replace its parameters, or defer to the base agent.
Evaluated on AndroidWorld and SPA-Bench, with improvements of up to 10.3 and 25.0 percentage points over the same-backbone base agent.
papers.selection_reason: Step-level trajectory memory reuse with task-relative matching is transferable to embodied memory for agents.
papers.title: DeltaReplay: Task-Relative Memory Reuse for Mobile GUI Agents
papers.tldr: DeltaReplay enables mobile GUI agents to selectively reuse only the relevant parts of past trajectories, improving task success by up to 10.3 and 25.0 percentage points on AndroidWorld and SPA-Bench.

papers.abstract: Lux AI Season 3 requires agents to act under partial observability, randomized episode level dynamics, and a best of five match structure that rewards both tactical execution and fast adaptation. We present HORIZON, a hierarchical agent that combines symmetry aware spatial perception, dual memory belief tracking, relic centric graph attention, information gain driven exploration, and an opponent conditioned policy mixture. HORIZON separates short horizon control from cross match meta reasoning, while auxiliary belief and world model objectives stabilize learning. Trained with PPO in a large scale JAX simulator, the resulting agent explicitly infers hidden game parameters and opponent style. Experiments show consistent gains in match win rate, episode win rate, adaptation gain, and league rating over strong recurrent and feed forward baselines.
bullets: Targets randomized dynamics, hidden information, and best-of-five matches where rapid adaptation matters.
Uses symmetry-aware perception, dual-memory belief tracking, relic-centric graph attention, and an opponent-conditioned policy mixture.
Separates short-horizon action control from cross-match meta-reasoning, with auxiliary belief and world-model objectives.
Trained with PPO in a large-scale JAX simulator, it consistently outperforms recurrent and feed-forward baselines on win rate, adaptation gain, and league rating.
papers.selection_reason: Learned hierarchical navigation agent with belief memory and opponent adaptation in partially observable multi-agent environments.
papers.title: Hierarchical Belief Modeling for Zero-Shot Opponent Adaptation in Partially Observable Multi-Agent Navigation
papers.tldr: HORIZON improves zero-shot adaptation in partially observable multi-agent navigation by combining hierarchical memory, opponent modeling, and information-seeking exploration.

papers.abstract: A generalist robot should not only perform diverse tasks but also improve through experience, turning what it learns during execution into capabilities that later tasks can reuse. Robot agents that act through code can already repair programs from execution feedback, yet it remains a central challenge to organize this experience around the task structure that gives it meaning, so that each repair is attributed to the responsible capability, supported by execution evidence, and validated before it is reused. We introduce RoboRSI, a robot self-improvement system built on Top-Down Skill Refinement (TSR). TSR decomposes tasks into compound, atomic, and base skills with scoped responsibilities and explicit input--output contracts, attributes each execution outcome to the responsible branch, and confines revision to that branch. Building upon this structure, a Manager, Planner, Engineer, and Reviewer coordinate planning, execution, diagnosis, and the validated release of new skills, while people steer the process through objectives and corrections; stable skill sequences are further consolidated into reusable compound skills. On a mobile manipulator, RoboRSI develops multi-object household cleanup over 104 rounds. In simulation, it achieves the highest success rate on LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.7 to 11.0 percentage points.
authors: Zimo Wen, Yijin Chen, Yuxuan Cao, Wendi Chen, Yanwen Zou, Wenye Yu, Fuhang Kuang, Han Xue, Jun Lv, Chuan Wen, Cewu Lu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of organizing execution experience so repairs can be linked to responsible capabilities and reused reliably.
Uses Top-Down Skill Refinement to decompose tasks into compound, atomic, and base skills with scoped responsibilities and explicit input–output contracts.
Coordinates planning, execution, diagnosis, engineering, and review through Manager, Planner, Engineer, and Reviewer agents, with human guidance.
Consolidates stable skill sequences into reusable compound skills.

A mobile manipulator improved multi-object household cleanup over 104 rounds; in simulation, RoboRSI achieved the highest success rate across four benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by 2.7–11.0 percentage points.
papers.selection_reason: Robot self-improvement via structured skill refinement and reuse combines embodied skill learning with continual experience accumulation.
papers.title: RoboRSI: Stable, efficient, and reusable robot self-evolution in complex real-world environments
papers.tldr: RoboRSI enables robots to safely improve and reuse skills by attributing execution failures to specific task branches and validating targeted revisions.

papers.abstract: Streaming 3D reconstruction must preserve evidence from each frame while processing an expanding scene online. Spatial memory is a natural fit because it organizes history by reconstructed 3D location. Yet Point3R uses spatial proximity both to associate a new observation with an existing memory entry and to decide whether to fuse it, conflating co-location with state identity. Because pointers summarize image patches, nearby pointers may encode distinct surfaces, viewpoints, or visibility conditions; averaging them can destroy complementary evidence before later frames disambiguate it. We argue that location should determine address, not whether observations must merge. Slot3R realizes this principle as a training-free, set-associative retrofit that lets multiple states coexist at a shared address while keeping the pretrained Point3R backbone frozen. A bounded sparse readout further decouples persistent storage from per-frame decoder access. At 300-500 sampled frames, Slot3R reduces Point3R's point-cloud accuracy error (Acc) by 57.1%-63.1% on 7Scenes and 64.0%-72.0% on NeuralRGBD, lowers Sim(3)-aligned absolute trajectory error (ATE) on all three pose benchmarks, and remains competitive on video-depth estimation. It completes all evaluated settings from 600 to 1000 sampled frames at about 19 FPS under the same protocol, whereas Point3R and InfiniteVGGT run out of memory at 800 frames and beyond.
authors: Xiyuan Zhang, Yanming Yang, Kaiyuan Xu, Ruibo Li, Chi Zhang
bullets: Spatial proximity can conflate co-location with state identity, causing complementary surface or viewpoint evidence to be averaged away.
Slot3R is a training-free, set-associative retrofit with multiple memory slots per address and a bounded sparse readout.
It keeps the pretrained Point3R backbone frozen while separating persistent storage from per-frame decoder access.
At 300–500 sampled frames, it substantially reduces Point3R’s point-cloud accuracy error on 7Scenes and NeuralRGBD, and lowers aligned trajectory error across pose benchmarks.
It completes evaluated 600–1000-frame settings at about 19 FPS, while Point3R and InfiniteVGGT run out of memory from 800 frames onward.
papers.selection_reason: Set-associative spatial memory for streaming 3D reconstruction, relevant to embodied memory mechanisms and 3D foundation model retrofits.
papers.title: Slot3R: Set-Associative Spatial Memory for Streaming 3D Reconstruction
papers.tldr: Slot3R improves streaming 3D reconstruction by allowing multiple distinct states to share a spatial memory address instead of prematurely fusing them.

papers.abstract: Latent reasoning enables vision-language-action (VLA) models to transform multimodal observations into task-relevant internal states before generating continuous robot actions. While existing methods learn to generate or refine such states for each policy query, they discard successful reasoning after execution and therefore reconstruct similar computation from scratch. We present Reasoning and Flow Memory (FLOWMEM), a unified VLA model that turns successful latent computation into reusable reasoning experience. Rather than appending a fixed retrieved context, FLOWMEM dynamically retrieves and recomposes compatible latent fragments as the embodied context evolves, forming a reasoning route that follows the temporal structure and progress of successful computation. The route is then refined using current visual and proprioceptive evidence before it conditions action generation. Experiments on RoboMME and LIBERO-Plus show that FLOWMEM attains 48.0% and 77.3% success, outperforming memory-free policies by 1.7 and 4.1 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate the value of reusing successful latent computation for closed-loop VLA control.
authors: Hongyu Shi, Sen Zhao, Zuyu Zhang, Lifeng Shen, Ding Zou, Xinyu He, Xu Zhang, Qinghua Zhang
bullets: Existing VLA methods often recompute latent reasoning for every policy query and discard successful reasoning after execution.
FLOWMEM stores successful latent computations as reusable reasoning experience.
It dynamically retrieves and recomposes compatible latent fragments as the robot’s context and task progress evolve.
The retrieved reasoning route is refined with current visual and proprioceptive evidence before action generation.
It achieves 48.0% success on RoboMME and 77.3% on LIBERO-Plus, improving over memory-free policies by 1.7 and 4.1 percentage points, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: VLA model that reuses and recomposes successful latent reasoning via memory for closed-loop robot control; directly fits VLA and embodied memory.
papers.title: Recompose and Refine Latent Reasoning Flows for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: FLOWMEM helps vision-language-action models reuse and adapt successful latent reasoning paths to improve closed-loop robot control.

papers.abstract: Robotic systems operating over extended tasks must maintain a world state assembled from observations arriving at different times, with varying confidence and potential revisions. Conventional representations emphasize latest estimates, hindering fact provenance, decision reproduction, or execution auditing. We present Traceable World State (TWS), a middleware-neutral semantic representation and reference runtime for provenance-aware robot world state. A TWS snapshot captures entities, relations, observations, confidence, and revision metadata. Validated update operations transform snapshots immutably, ordered updates support deterministic replay, and a canonical SHA-256 hash chain ensures tamper-evident logs. We evaluate TWS through schema conformance, complete state lifecycles, deterministic replay, and fault injection. Passing 38 tests across Python 3.10-3.14, the framework detects record corruptions, broken hash links, sequence discontinuities, and world mismatches. Across ten public BEHAVIOR-1K task definitions, TWS imported 153 entities and 146 relations with successful validation. On 103 NVIDIA Unitree G1 simulated trajectories containing 78,369 frames, TWS achieved exact terminal-state replay in all episodes and detected 412/412 injected corruptions with a 1.72% storage overhead over Plain JSONL.
bullets: Represents entities, relations, observations, confidence, and revisions rather than only latest estimates.
Applies validated immutable updates and ordered operations to reproduce state evolution deterministically.
Uses a canonical SHA-256 hash chain to detect tampering, broken links, sequence gaps, and world-state mismatches.
Passed 38 tests, replayed all 103 simulated trajectories exactly, and detected all 412 injected corruptions.
Imported 153 entities and 146 relations from ten BEHAVIOR-1K task definitions with 1.72% storage overhead over Plain JSONL.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Traceable World State (TWS), a provenance-aware state representation framework for robotic systems that supports immutable updates, deterministic replay, and tamper-evident logging.
papers.title: Traceable World State: A Provenance-Aware State Representation and Deterministic Replay Framework for Robotic Systems
papers.tldr: Traceable World State provides provenance-aware, immutable robot state snapshots with deterministic replay and tamper-evident logging for auditable long-horizon tasks.

papers.abstract: Learning to act in unfamiliar environments requires agents to infer how the world works and revise that understanding as new evidence arrives. Yet limited observations can support multiple world models that explain past interactions but predict different outcomes in unseen states. We introduce Memento 3, building on the Memento series to enable frozen LLM agents to continually learn explicit world models through external memory. The agent maintains a natural-language rulebook as persistent semantic memory, recording revisable hypotheses about environment dynamics while leaving unknown aspects underspecified. It compiles this rulebook into executable code for prediction and planning. Through a continual loop of observation, reflection, rule revision, compilation, and verification, the agent uses prediction errors to refine both the rulebook and its code. Updated code is accepted only when the LLM judges it faithful to the rulebook and cell-exact replay reproduces the observed transitions. We investigate this process as a model-based route to recursive self-improvement (RSI): the agent autonomously explores the environment, revises its world model, and uses verified updates to guide subsequent interaction and learning, while the underlying LLM remains fixed. A population extension maintains multiple world models in parallel, sharing interaction evidence and using their predictions to guide exploration.
